5. Mr. Syed JR Modassir Hossain, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the petitioner, submits that the Court of appeal below committed an error of law in not adverting to the findings of the learned trial Court with proper and sound reasonings. Mr. Hossain argues that the learned Court of Appeal below has committed serious error of law in not considering the basic documents filed by the defendant Government such as Exhibits 'A', 'B', 'H' and 'K' which would positively indicate that the land in question and all the land surrendered to the Government by that Tea Estate as excess of khas lands had vested in the Government. Mr. Modassir Hossain also argues that there are errors of law on the face of record and as such the impugned judgment and decree must be set aside. 

 "The High Court Division may call for the record of any case which has been decided by any Court subordinate to the High Court Division and in which no appeal lies thereto, and if such subordinate Court appears to have committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice, the High Court may make such order in the, case as it thinks fit." 

 8. By the Ord. No. XLVIII of 1983 amendment the words "apparent on the face of the record" in the decision it has been substituted by "resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice", and further beyond the old section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure stood in the form. 

 9. The High Court may call for the record of any case which has been decided by any Court subordinate to such High Court and in which no appeal lies thereto, and if such subordinate Court appears- 

 Thereafter powers under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure was squeezed and limited to "errors of law on the face of the record". Section 100 was omitted by Ord. XLIX of 1978 with effect from 1.6.79. Litigants could only invoke the jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure when no appeal lies against any order or decree. But with the repeal of section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure and re-enactment of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in its new garb, the powers of the High Court has increased to a large extent. Now under the newly amended provision as made in section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code, the grounds for interference has been stretched from jurisdictional point of view for stretching and superseding the errors on the face of the record into errors of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 13. Now coming to the question on merit let us now concentrate to observe how upon being faced with the pleadings of the parties, the evidence on record both oral and documentary, the court of appeal reacts; whether the court below proceeds in accordance with law or commits errors of law in the course of the trial occasioning failure of justice or commits an error in procedure affecting in the decision occasioning any failure of justice. 

 (1) of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, Government acquires interest of the proprietors, tenure holders and rent receivers including khas lands (beyond the retainable limit) by publication of notification from the date mentioned therein and these interests vest in the Government absolutely free from all encumbrances. By Exhibit 'R' Baraura Tea Estate through their Manager surrendered the excess khas land to the Government. The learned trial Court found that the excess land so surrendered by Baraura Tea Co. Ltd. in favour of the Government was duly accepted by the Government and compensation assessment' roll was also published. Rent-receivers having khas lands in the capacity of a rent receiver are stripped of their excess khas lands on the very moment of the publication of notification under sub-section 1 of section 3, and the same vests in the Government absolutely free from all encumbrances. It may be noted that the lands in schedule of the plaint falls within surrendered excess khas land. It may also be noted that the records of right and the compensation roll were prepared in the name of the Baraura Tea Company and not in the name of the plaintiff. Had the plaintiff occupied the lands in question as a rayati or under rayati, record of right or the compensation roll would also have been prepared in his name and the Baraura Tea Company would definitely have excluded the plots in question from the lands surrendered as in the statement Ext. 'H'. 

 34. The scheme of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, would reveal that special provision has been made in Chapter II of Part-II of the Act in regard to acquisition of rent-receiving interests and special provision for acquisition of the interests of certain rent-receivers. According to this provision, rent-receiving interest can be acquired by notification under section 3 of the Act even before the general provisions of the aforesaid Act have been given effect to. Before acquisition of the interests of the rent-receivers and tenure holders or Taluks or rayati or the khas lands of the tenure holders or rent-receivers, preparation of the record of rights is necessary. Thereafter, the compensation assessment roll is prepared and published in order to give effect to such provision of law. Sub-section 2(a) in section 3 of the Act was introduced by amendment empowering the Government to publish notification in respect of rent-receiver by name with reference to areas where such interests exist in the manner the Government might determine and notifications were issued District-wise but the rent-receiving interests and vesting of khas lands in the Government shall vest in the Government with effect from 14.4.1956 in terms of those notification issued.

full_judgment: 18. Scrutinizing the connected papers on records it further appears that both the courts below considering the C.S. khatians as well as the fact of gifting ¼ land of the Khatian by Abbas vide Ext-"Cha" and of ¼  land of the Khatian in the name of Abdul being sold in auction, concurrently held that Osman, Abbas, Abdul and Sadhu were the owners of the suit land and the daughters of Sheikh Mohar had no subsisting interest in the said land. Therefore, no title would be conferred upon the defendants, those who purchased of land from the daughters of Sheikh Mohar. In this context the provisions of sections 143, 144 and 144A of the state Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 are relevant and the decision reported in 61 DLR 18 (Para-30) as referred from the side of the opposite-parties can be relied on.

full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This appeal by the defendant No. 1, by leave, is against the judgment and decree dated August 13, 1996 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 208 of 1995 allowing the appeal and thereupon decreeing the suit upon reversing the judgment and decree dated March 19, 1995 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Gazipur, in Title Suit No. 44 of 1993 dismissing the suit which was filed seeking declaration of title in the land in suit and for a further declaration that names of Ananda Mohan Mondal, Gobinda Chandra Mondal, Fatik Chandra Mondal and Ganesh Chandra Mondal, sons of Durga Charan Mondal as well as name of Ganesh Chandra Mondal, son of late Joy Gopal Mondal have been wrongly recorded in the finally published SA record of rights as well as in the RS record along with the names of plaintiffs vendor Krishna Mondal and others and the land in suit has been wrongly recorded in the RS record in the name of the Custodian of Vested Property. 

 2. The plaintiff-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 filed the aforesaid suit stating, infer alia, that the land of CS Khatian No. 122 comprising 34.64 acres of land belonged in equal share to Raj Chandra Mondal and Lechu Mondal, sons of late Kanai Mondal. Raj Chandra Mondal died leaving wife Rajrani Mondal and son Rai Charan Mondal. Rajrani Mondal sold her interest to Keru Mondal and Khetra Mondal and delivered possession to them. Keru Mondal died leaving 2 sons, Fatik Mondal and Natu Mondal and they inherited the property left by their father. Khetra Mondal died leaving 2 daughters by name Kazali Dasi and Bilashi Dasi. Kazali Dasi recorded the land she got in the name of her minor son Dowri Mondal in the RS record and Bilashi Dasi recorded her share of the property in the name of her minor son Sree Mohon in the RS record. On the death of Rajrani Mondal her son Rai Charan Mondal inherited her remaining interest. Rai Charan Mondal died leaving wife Maha Dasi who sold her inherited share measuring 2.82-1/2 acres of land to Narendra Sarker, son of Umesh Sarker. Lechu Mondal died leaving sons-Krishna Mondal and Joy Gopal Mondal. Krishna Mondal sold 1.98 acres of land out of his share to Abdur Rahman and Torap Ali Dewan and delivered possession to them. Torap Ali Dewan sold 0.33 acre of land to Mofazzal and his wife and they exchanged the same with the plaintiffs. Joy Gopal Mondal died leaving 2 sons, Kartik Mondal and Gonesh Mondal. Gonesh Mondal exchanged his share with his brother Kartik Mondal and thereby Kartik Mondal became 16 annas owner of the property left by Joy Gopal Mondal in Sarabo Mouza within Savar and Gonesh Mondal in exchange got in his share property in Kanakbari Mouza. Property of the successive heirs of Raj Chandra Mondal and Lechu Mondal and the property of the purchasers from the heirs of said two original owners was recorded in the SA record. It is the further case of the plaintiff-respondents that in 1950 Ananda Mohan Mondal, Gobinda Chandra Mondal, Gouranga Mondal and Fatik Chandra Mondal, sons of Durga Charan Mondal, the relations of the successive heirs of Raj Chandra Mondal and Lechu Mondal, fell in distress and took shelter in the house of Krishna Mondal and others and started living in a small portion of the land of CS Khatian No. 122 and, as such, their names were recorded in SA Khatian No. 185 along with the names of the successive heirs of the original owners. The said relations of Raj Chandra Mondal and Lechu Mondal later on left the house of Krishna Mondal and others. Rajrani Mondal transferred 2.82½ acres of land to Sachi Ram and Sachi Ram sold the said land to the plaintiffs and delivered possession. Krishna Mondal and others transferred 31.04 acres of land out of the land of suit khatian to the plaintiffs. As the plaintiffs purchased land of CS Khatian No. 122 from Kartik Mondal and as there was amicable partition amongst Kartik Mondal and Gonesh Mondal, sons of Joy Gopal Mondal and thereupon Kartik Mondal got land of Mouza Sarabo in his share and Gonesh Mondal got the land or Mouza Ganakbari so to avoid future complication Gonesh Mondal's son Haripada Mondal executed “নাদাবি পত্র” in respect of the land of Mouza Sarabo. The total quantity of land in CS and RS is 34.64 acres of land and out of that plaintiffs are claiming 32.63 acres of land although their kabalas reflect 35.12½  It is the specific case of the plaintiffs that they are in possession of the land in suit and the land recorded in SA Khatian No. 185 was correctly recorded in RS (DP) Khatian No. 170 in the name of the plaintiffs vendor Krishna Chandra Mondal and others but later on in the finally published RS Khatian No. 42 wrongly names of Ananda Mondal, Gobinda Mondal, Fatik Mondal, sons of Durga Charan Mondal, and Genesh Chandra Mondal son of Joy Gopal Mondal were recorded and their address has been shown in India and in the middle of 1992 plaintiffs came to know about the wrong preparation of finally published RS record and as because of the wrong entry in the record of rights serious injury to their right actually arising they are constrained to file the suit. 

 5. On appeal the High Court Division reversed the finding of the trial Court as to limitation holding that against the wrong entry in the SA and RS Khatian suit was not needed be filed within 6 years from the date of knowledge thereof and also from the date of final publication of the said Khatians but from the date of invasion made on the basis of wrong record of rights. The High Court  Division further held that the date of cause of action in the suit is not the essence of the suit and, as such, filing of written statement denying the title and possession of the plaintiff in the land in suit can even be a cause of action of the suit and thus the suit cannot be held to be barred by limitation. The High Court Division was of the view that treating a portion of the land as recorded in SA Khatian later on in RS Khatian as vested property was not legal. The High Court Division further held that from the side of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 no material whatsoever was placed as to how Ananda Mohan Mondal and others became co-sharers in the land as recorded in SA and RS Khatians and thereupon held that Ananda Mohan Mondal and others have got no interest in the land in the suit and, as such, the land in suit cannot be treated as vested property. 

 7. The law is now settled that against the wrong record of rights the person whose interest is affected by such wrong recording need not file suit questioning legality of the record of rights so prepared and finally published within 6 years from said date or from the date of knowledge of such wrong record of rights, but he is required to tile the suit seeking declaration of title within six years from the date the person in whose name record has been wrongly prepared and finally published raises claim denying his claim on the basis of wrong record. But if the entry in the record of rights is made the cause of action one has to file  the suit within 6 (six) years from the date of final publication of the record of rights and not from the date of the certificate of the final publication. In view of the said position of law the learned Counsel for the appellant has not taken any exception to the finding of the High Court Division that the suit was not barred by limitation. 

 8. The land in suit as recorded in CS Khatian belonged to Raj Chandra Mondal and Lechu Mondal. Raj Chandra Mondal died leaving wife Rajrani Mondal and a son by name Rai Charan Mondal and Rai Charan Mondal died leaving wife Maha Dasi. Lechu Mondal died leaving 2 sons Krishna Mondal and Joy Gopal Mondal. Joy Gopal Mondal died leaving sons Kartik Mondal and Gonesh Mondal. The aforesaid genealogical tree of the CS record tenants was not challenged or proved as not correct by the contesting defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The fact of transfer by the successive heirs of Raj Chandra Mondal and Lechu Mondal deposed by PW 1, plaintiff No.1, was not challenged by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2, nor proved the statement made by PW 1 as incorrect. The fact of amicable partition between Kartik Mondal and Gonesh Mondal, sons of Joy Gopal Mondal and thereupon Kartik Mondal got the property in Sarabo Mouza has not been disproved by the contesting defendant Nos. 1 and 2, rather plaintiffs have proved the said fact by the “নাদাবি” deed (Exhibit 6) executed by the son of Gonesh Mondal. It may be mentioned part of the property out of 32.63 acres of land of Sarabo Mouza in Savar PS has been treated as vested property claiming to be the property of Ananda Mohan Mondal, Gobinda Chandra Mondal and Fatik Chandra Mondal, sons of Durga Charan Mondal and Gonesh Chandra Mondal, son of Joy Gopal Mondal. It has already been mentioned that by amicable partition between Kartik Mondal and Gonesh Mondal, sons of Joy Gopal Mondal, the property in Sarabo Mouza was obtained by Kartik Mondal and in exchange thereof Gonesh Mondal got the property of Kanakbari Mouza. It is the definite case of the plaintiffs that Ananda Mohan Mondal, Gobinda Chandra Mondal, Gouranga Mondal and Fatik Chandra Mondal, sons of Durga Charan Mondal having had fallen in distress in the year 1950 took shelter in the homestead of Krishna Mondal and others and later on they left the homestead of Krishna Mondal and others. It is also the case of the plaintiffs that sons of Durga Charan Mondal had no interest in the land owned by Raj Chandra Mondal and Lechu Mondal and later on inherited by their successive heirs. From the contesting defendants' (defendant Nos. 1 and 2) side no material has been placed on the record to show that sons of Durga Charan Mondal had acquired interest in any manner in the land recorded' in CS Khatian No. 122, later on in the SA Khatian No. 185 and RS Khatian No. 42. 

 9. Part ofthe property in suit has been treated as vested property on the basis of the SA Khatian No. 185 and the finally published RS Khatian No. 42. It is the case of the plaintiffs that SA Khatian No. 185 and RS record was wrongly prepared in the name of sons of Durga Charan Mondal and that also the name of Gonesh Chandra Mondal was wrongly entered in the RS Khatian No. 42 since by amicable partition Kartik Mondal, son of Joy Gopal Mondal got the property of Sarabo Mouza and in exchange thereof Gonesh Chandra Mondal, son of Joy Gopal Mondal got the property of Ganakbari Mouza. The plaintiff in support of the fact of amicable partition has put into evidence Exhibit 6, deed of 'nadabi' executed by Haripada Mondal, son of Gonesh Chandra Mondal. 

 10. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the finding that plaintiffs have no title and possession in the land in suit. The contesting defendant Nos. 1 and 2 claimed that they are possessing the land through their men. It may be mentioned defendant Nos. 1 and 2 have not examined any witness in support of their claim of managing the land in suit or the property that has been treated as vested property by examining any witness. The lone witness (DE 1) of the appellant, the Assistant tahshilder of Kashimpur Union Land Office, although has stated that the land in suit is being looked after and enjoyed by the Government and it is not correct to say that plaintiffs are in possession of the land in suit and they have their establishments and structures in the land in suit, but there is no corroboration of the aforesaid statements, nor any material has been brought on record to establish that the land in suit or the land treated as vested property is being looked after and managed by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The plaintiffs in proof of their case that they are in possession of the land in suit by raising structures and they have their establishments in the land in suit have examined PWs 2-4 to corroborate PW 1. These witnesses have stated that the plaintiffs are in possession of the land in suit and they have their structures as well as their establishments therein and they have planted trees in the land in suit. The evidence from the side of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 as against the evidence of the plaintiffs to disprove claim of possession of the plaintiffs is of no worth. In the background of the evidence of the plaintiffs as discussed above we are of the view trial Court was in serious error in holding that plaintiffs have no possession in the land in suit. The plaintiffs by oral and documentary evidence have established that they have acquired title to the land in suit from the undisputed successive heirs of the CS recorded tenants as well as from the transferees of the heirs of the CS recorded tenants. 

 11. The appellant has based its claim as regard the property in suit or part of the property in suit as of being the vested property on the RS Khatian and the census list of the vested property. It may be mentioned census list as it appears has been prepared either on the basis of SA or RS Khatian. In the RS Khatian along with the names of the heirs of the CS recorded tenants and their transferees names of the sons of Durga Charan Mondal have also been recorded and in the RS Khatian address of Durga Charan Mondal's sons and Joy Gopal Mondal's son Gonesh Chandra Mondal has been shown as India and consequent thereupon,. there is an entry in the RS Khatian to the effect "পক্ষে" Custodian land and building". 

 12. The learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that as in the RS Khatian No. 42 prepared under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the Act) names of sons of Durga Charan Mondal as well as Joy Gopal Mondal's son Ganesh Chandra Mondal appear and consequent thereupon as there is presumption of correctness of the entries in the said RS Khatian under section 144A of the Act, as such, treating the property of the said persons as vested property was quite legal. The presumption as regards the entries in the RS Khatian so attached under section 144A of the Act is rebuttable by leading evidence from the side of the person questioning correctness of the entry made therein. It is in the evidence of PW 1 that Durga Charan Mondal's sons having had fallen in distress some time in 1950 came to the house of Raj Chandra Mondal and Durga Charan Mandai's sons had no title in the land of Raj Chandra Mondal and Lechu Mondal and they stayed for some time but later on left the house of Raj Chandra Mondal. It is also in the evidence of PW 1 that names of Durga Charan Mondal's sons were wrongly recorded in the SA and RS Khatian. As against the aforesaid contention of PW 1 the evidence of DW 1 is that Ananda Mohan Mondal and others sons of Durga Charan Mondal were the SA recorded tenants and that they left for India at the time of war of 1965 and thereupon their land has been listed as vested property. This witness in cross-examination has stated that he cannot say on what basis names of sons of Durga Charan Mondal have been recorded in SA Khatian and that he cannot say Durga Charan Mondal's sons and Joy Gopal Mondal's son Gonesh Chandra Mondal at what point of time went to India. Since from the materials on record it is seen that there was no. basis for recording names of Durga Charan Mondal's sons and also name of Gonesh Chandra Mondal in the SA Khatian and also for making entries in the RS Khatian as regards address of Durga Charan Mondal's sons and. Joy Gopal Mondal's son Gonesh Chandra Mondal shown as India has no basis, so the said entries in the RS Khatian were incorrect. Moreover, the Exhibit 6, Nadabi deed executed by Gonesh Chandra Mondal's son of Haripada Mondal reflects the fact of amicable partition of the property of Joy, Gopal Mondal between his, sons Kartik Mondal and Gonesh Chandra Mondal and thereupon Kartik Mondal got the property of Sarabo Mouza wherein the land in suit situates. It is seenfrom the materials on the, record that the entry in the RS Khatian as regards name of Gonesh Chandra Mondal, son of Joy Gopal Mondal reflecting interest in the land of Sarabo Mouza, wherein the land situates, is not correct. Since the presumption of correctness that has been attached to the RS Khatian by  the provision of section 144A of the Act has been rebutted and consequent thereupon recording of names of Durga Charan Mondal's sons and Joy Gopal Mondal's son Gonesh Chandra Mondal was not correct, rather there was no basis for entering their names in the RS Khatian No. 42 and, as such, defendants (defendant Nos. 1 and 2) case of vested property on the basis of wrong entry of the names of persons having no title and interest in the land so listed in the RS Khatian in question has no leg to stand, rather the property in suit has been listed in the census list as vested property without ascertaining the correct position or without ascertaining particulars of the persons who have, in fact, right, title and interest in the land in suit. It appears the vested property authority has prepared the census list merely on the basis of wrongly prepared RS Khatian No. 42, and without ascertaining the real state of the matter is the property in suit in reality belongs to whom. 

 13. The learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that in the background of the gazette notification dated December 3, 1965 property that assumed character of enemy property, later on vested property, vested in the Government, as such, transfers made in 1970 by successive heirs of CS recorded tenants and the purchasers therefrom were not legal and valid and the Exhibit 6, Nadabi deed, executed by Gonesh Chandra Mondal's son Haripada Mondal ought notto have been taken into consideration for the purpose of arriving at a decision that Gonesh Chandra Mondal, son of Joy Gopal Mondal ceased to be the owner of the land of Sarabo Mouza because of amicable partition between the brothers, namely Kartick Mondal and Gonesh Chandra Mondal, sons of Joy Gopal Mondal. We have already observed that part of the land recorded in RS Khatian has been listed as vested property on the basis of entry in the said Khatian. Since incorrectness of the entries in the said RS Khatian No. 42 in so far names of Durga Charan Mondal's sons and the name of Gonesh Chandra Mondal, son of Joy Gopal Mondal have been established by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2, as such, treating the property in suit as vested property on the basis of said wrong entries was illegal. As to treating the property of Gonesh Chandra Mondal son of Joy Gopal Mondal in Sarabo Mouza as vested property is, also not correct, as firstly it is in the evidence of DW 1 that he cannot say when Gonesh Chandra Mondal left for India and second by the Exhibit 6 it has been established by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 that Gonesh Chandra Mondal ceased to have any interest in the land of Sarabo Mouza because of amicable partition with his brother Kartik Mondal. So there being no reliable evidence that the property legally vested in the Government as enemy property, later on vested property, as such, because of the notification of December 3, 1965 it cannot be said property in suit has vested in the Government as enemy property, later on vested property. 

 14. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that the said Division: was of the view that RS record was prepared in terms of the provisions as are in Chapter IV of Part IV of the Act and thereupon expressed the view that presumption of correctness as to the entries in the SA and RS record finally published under section 19(3) in Chapter IV has no presumption of correctness. As against the said finding of the High Court Division the learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that R'S record has been prepared as per provision of section 144 of Chapter XVII of part V of the Act and to the entries in the RS record so prepared under the said section of the Act presumption of correctness has been attached under section 144A of the Act. We have already held that presumption so attached under section 144A of the Act to the Khatians prepared under section 144 of the Act is rebuttable and the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 has rebutted the correctness of the entry made therein as regard the name of Durga Charan Mondal's sons and name or Gonesh Chandra Mondal son of Joy Gopal Mondal and, as such, the finding of the High Court Division that presumption of correctness as regard the entries in the RS Khatian is not available, is not correct, as submitted by the learned Counsel for the appellant, though of merit but for that the decision arrived at by the High Court Division that the property in suit is not vested property has not been materially affected since it has been established by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 that recording of the names of Durga Charan Mondal's sons as well as Gonesh Chandra Mondal, son of Joy Gopal Mondal in the SA and RS record of rights was not correct.

full_judgment:
2. The case of the, plaintiff Nos. 1-4 is that they instituted Title Suit No.113 of 1997 before the Court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Baniachong, Hobiganj for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in respect of the suit land stating, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to 3(three) brother namely, Hashimullah, Nashibullah and Thandai Ullah and they were in possession and accordingly record of right were prepared in their name and they enjoyed the property by digging doba in the suit land. The suit land situated contiguous to the north of plot No.818 belonging to respondents. The respondent admitted the same in the schedule of the plaint as schedule of title suit No.32 of 1984. The respondent brought title suit No.3 of 1991 against the plaintiff with a view to grab the suit property and when the plaintiffs filed written statement he has withdrawn the said suit on condition to sue a fresh. After the withdrawal of the suit the relationship between plaintiffs and defendant developed and on the request of the defendant, the plaintiffs permitted the defendant to keep timbers of his Saw Mills. On 15th Bhadra 1404 B.S. the plaintiffs requested the defendant to remove timbers from the suit land. Defendant refused to remove the timbers from the suit land and denied the title of the plaintiffs. Hence the suit. 

 3. The defendant-petitioner contested the suit filing written statement denying the allegations made in the plaint stating, inter alia, that the suit is barred by limitation and not maintainable on its present form the suit land originally belonged to Majumder Estate and his father Jona Ullah and predecessor of the plaintiffs obtained settlement of the suit land along with other land from Majumder Estate on Srabon 1340 B.S. by executing kabulyat in favour of Manager of Majumder Estate by Jona Ullah and Mir Box and they are in possession in ejmali by paying rent regularly to the Zaminder. At the time of survey operanon Jona Ullah was ill and minor, consequently, the survey officers wrongly prepared the suit land in the name of 3 (three) brothers i.e. the sons of Mir Box but they acquired no right, title and interest in the suit land by dint of wrong recording and the plaintiffs have no possession. That the defendant is in possession of the suit land and continuing his business and as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 4. Mr. Mohammad Nawab Ali, learned Advocate-on-record, appearing for the petitioner submits that the High Court Division has wrongly relied on the observation and finding of the Courts below and has failed to exercise its jurisdiction to determine the issue regarding the acquisition of the suit property by both the predecessors of the plaintiffs and defendants with reference to their possession; that since a khatian of land is not a document of title, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division has wrongly considered the presumptive value of the S.A. Khatian not backed by a trust worthy document or legal testimony. Mr. Ali, lastly, submits that since the possession of the defendant is supported by installation of a Saw Mills, it may not be easily outweighed in pursuance of the story of alleged possession of the defendant as permissive as alleged by the plaintiff. 

 5. Mr. Muhammad Nazrul Islam, learned Counsel, appearing for the respondents submits that Mir Box the predecessor of the plaintiff, obtained pattan from Majumder Waqf Estate, the defendants also admitted in his chief that Mir Box obtained pattan from the Majumder Waqf Estate. He further submits that earlier the defendant filed Title Suit No.32 of 1984 and also filed Title Suit No.3 of 1991 that both the predecessor of the plaintiff and defendant obtained joint pattan from the Zaminder the defendant claimed that they were given pattan and the alleged pattan was obtained by the defendants predecessor and others but no documents were produced. He further submits that under Section 144A of the State Acquisition Tenancy Act an entry in the record of right has a presumptive value of its correctness. All the entry in the record of right appears in the name of the plaintiff’s predecessor Mir Box who obtained pattan from the Zaminder. The trial Court as well as the appellant Court considering all the evidences on record came to a concrete finding that the plaintiff proved their right, title, interest and possession over the suit property and accordingly, decreed the suit. The defendant failed to produced any document of his kabuliyat as claimed. In support of his contention he cited the case of Modarres Ali and others vs. Bishambar Das being dead his heirs reported in 46 DLR 34, the case of Abdur Rahim vs. Tarequl Rahman reported in 50 DIAZ 66 and the case of Doyal Chandra Mondal and others-vs-Assistant Custodian vested and nonresident property reported in 50 DLR 186. 

 6. The Court below found on evidence that I the predecessor of the plaintiff obtained pattan from the Zaminder Majumder Waqf Estate, on the basis of which record of right has been prepared in their name  though the defendant filed Title Suit No.3 of 1991 claiming 50% title thereto on the basis of joint pattan but the suit was withdrawn. The defendant failed to produce the pattan document and ultimately relied on adverse possession. The plaintiffs have I proved the permissive possession of defendant. The defendant though alleged the possession since 1984 but the alleged licence was dated 1994 which have been interpolated by the defendant overwriting 1984. The plaintiff has proved the defendant's possession since 1994 and the suit was filed in 1998. Thus the plea of defendant Nos. 1 and 3 as to adverse possession falls the ground. The plaintiff was paid rent in supported of record of rights in their names. 

 7. The High Court Division under the circumstances rightly held that The findings regarding the title and possession by both the Courts below are concurrent finding of facts and there is no perverse finding and the finding based on evidences on record and there is no allegation of misreading or non consideration of materials on record. Which has been supported in the case of Shambhu Nath Paddar-vs- Bangladesh Railway reported in 43 DLR (AD) 82, the case of Rokeya Begum-vs- Abu Zaher of others reported in 4 MLR (AD) 171. 

 8. The well settled law is that unless there is gross misreading or non consideration of material evidence on record or misconstruction of any document or that finding are perverse and contrary to law or evidence resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice, the concurrent findings cannot be interfered with by the revisional Court under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The judgment and decree passed by the Courts below does not call for interference.

statement denying the material facts of the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit land has been recorded in the name of the Government as khas land and the same has been settled by leased out in favour of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-2 by a registered kabuliyat and the suit land has been mutated in their name; that the plaintiff has no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 "The settled law is that R.S. record has a presumption of correctness but the S.A. record has no such presumptive value." 

 21. Mr. Bhuiyan lastly submits that the trial court correctly decreed the suit on merit upon proper assessment of the pleadings, evidence and other Materials on record, but the court of appeal below misread and mis-appreciated the evidence and materials on record and came to an erroneous decision since as the final court of fact, did not apply its judicial mind and independently assess the evidence and other materials on record in violation of its mandatory obligation under Order 41 Rule 31 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, rather turned down the decision of the trial court on some perverse, unfounded and untenable findings without assigning any reason and also without reversing the findings of the trial court and as, such the impugned judgment and decree being not a proper judgment of reversal, is illegal and liable to be set aside, and in support of his submission Mr. Bhuiyan has placed reliance on the decisions reported in XII ADC 751; 14 BLD 229; 17 BLD 47; 10MLR 255; 15 BLD 96. 

 "After the abolition of all rent receiving interests in the country there is only one class of tenancy under the Government whose rights and liabilities are governed by an uniform law." 

 27. Mr. Shah Hossain finally submits that the trial Court wrongly shifted the burden of proving the correctness of S. A. Khatian on the defendant-opposite parties and held that the defendants failed to proves as to how, why and when the suit land became the khas land of the Government by adducing any evidence, oral and documentary. On this point Mr. Hossain further submits that as plaintiff-the petitioners ought to have proved their case, they cannot take the advantage of the weakness of the defendants. Supporting the impugned judgment and decree Mr. Hossain lastly submits that the appellate court below as the final court of fact arrived at a proper decision upon proper assessment of the pleadings of the parties, evidence and other materials on record and as such the same does not call for any interference from this Court. 

 28. I have meticulously gone through the revisional application, the impugned judgment and decree, the pleadings of the respective parties, evidence led by them and other materials on record and also heard the learned Advocates for both the sides at length and perused the decisions relied upon by both the parties with utmost circumspection and the relevant provisions of law wherefrom it transpires that the evidentiary value of the registered sale deed of the plaintiff-petitioners (Exhibit- 5), the preparation and publication of S. A. record of rights, if any, in the khas khatian of the Government as well as the maintainability of Rent Suit No. 60 of 1957 are predominant issues in this case apart from other connected issues and I will endeavour to address all the issues in proportion to their respective weight and importance. 

 "Registered document prevail upon record of right- SA and RS records were not an evidence of title and that a registered document would prevail upon the records of rights and that the registered document would remain in force unless the same was cancelled by an appropriate civil court." 

 (3) Before entering on a holding under sub-section (2), the Revenue-officer shall cause a notice to be published in the prescribed manner declaring his intention to so enter on the holding and specifying the reasons thereof and also inviting objections from all persons interested in the holding and shall consider any objections that may be submitted to him within the period specified in that behalf in the notice and shall record a decision. 

 35. In the panorama as canvassed in the foregoing paragraph, it can be safely concluded that the defendants are not absolved of their obligation to prove as to when, why and how the suit land was recorded in the khas khatian of the Government and that obligation having not been discharged by any of the defendants, the plea of khas khatian is not proved at all. Moreover, it has already been held in Civil Revision No. 2613 of 2011 arising out of Title Suit No. 55 of 200 to which the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 are plaintiffs that the opposite parties of the present Rule signally failed to prove their plea as to khas khatian. 

 opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 entered into the suit land after the flood of 1988, whereas they allegedly took settlement of the same in 1999 and they did not at all clarify in their pleadings submitted and evidence adduced in all the suits in what capacity they possessed and enjoyed the suit land for the intervening period between 1988 and 1999 and as such I am constrained to hold the view that the plaintiffs entered into the suit land as mere trespassers. Moreover, Court think that if the suit land had ever been recorded in the khas khatian of the Government, it would have settled the same in favour of anyone else, and in the absence of any such lease, Government's title as well as the interest of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 in the suit land is not proved at all. 

 40. As I have already found that the opposite party Nos.1 and 2 are mere trespassers into the suit land, they have got no locus standi to question the accuracy or genuineness of the title deed of the plaintiff petitioners however defective title the latter might have to the suit land. On the 'balance of probabilities' which is the standard of proof in civil jurisdiction as opposed to 'beyond reasonable double' in criminal jurisdiction and also on the weight of evidence and preponderance of documents available in the records of the suit, it appears to me that the plaintiff-petitioners have lawful title to the suit land, which can be questioned only by a person having a better title thereto. That being so, the suit of the plaintiffs succeeds and the defendants having failed to prove their better title to the suit land than that of the plaintiffs, they are entitled to a decree as prayed for. 

 41. On perusal of the pleadings, evidence and other materials on record, I am of the considered view that the judgment of the trial court is very much sound, proper and in accordance with law for, the reasons stated above and it does not suffer from any misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration or misconstruction of any document affecting the merit of the suit and as such I. find no reason to interfere with the same. On the other hand, the court of appeal below misread and mis-appreciated the evidence and materials on record and came to an erroneous decision by failing to apply its judicial mind to the given set of facts and failed to independently assess the evidence and other materials on record in violation of its mandatory obligation under Order 41 Rule 31 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and turned down to the decision of the trial court on some perverse, unfounded and untenable findings without assigning any reason and also without reversing the findings of the trial court and as such the impugned judgment and decree being not a proper judgment of reversal, is illegal and liable to be set aside. 

 44. Send down the lower Court record along with a copy of this judgment to the Court concerned, at once.

full_judgment:
One Syed Hasan Ali was the absolute owner of the said land which devolved on his only son, Syed Mohammad Ali after his demise. Thereafter, the said Syed Mohammad Ali died leaving his only son, Syed Ahsan Ali and his wife Syeda Hosne Ara Begum as his heirs who sold the said land to Md Akkas Ali (father of the petitioner) and Md Abdus Sobhan vide registered Sale Deed No. 2926 dated 7-2-1973. Some clerical mistake having been crept up in the sale deed and Syed Ahsan Ali and Syeda Hosne Ara Begum executed an amended deed vide Registered Amended Deed No. 30146 dated 10-12-1976 before the office of Sadar Sub-Register Dhaka. Md Akkas Ali and Md Abdus Sobhan after having become the absolute owner of the said land applied to mutate their names in the record of rights maintained by the Government. At that stage the said Md Akkas Ali and Md. Abdus Sobhan came to know that in SA Record the scheduled land was recorded in Khas Khatian No. 1 as a road whereas the scheduled land was pond and not a road. In such situation they filed Mutation Case No. 1428 (shoi) of 1977-78 before the Circle Officer, Dhaka who vide Order dated 1-9-1977 directed Tahshildar to give detail report to that effect. The Tahshildar in his report stated that the title of the land vested in Md Akkas Ali and Md Abdus Sobhan and the said land was never a Khas land of the Government. The Tahshildar clearly stated that the land was wrongly recorded in the Akkas Ali and Md Abdus Sobhan in connection with the said land. 

 3. The Circle Officer also sought opinion from Government pleader who also opined that the said land could be mutated in the names of Md Akkas Ali and Md Abdus Sobhan. Thereafter the Circle Officer, Dhaka vide Order dated 19-10-1977 allowed of the Mutation Case No. 1428 (Shoi) of 1977-78 in favour of the said Md Akkas Ali and Md Abdus Sobhan and mutated the names of Md Akkas Ali and Md Abdus Sobhan in respect of the said land and directed Tahshildar to make necessary correction in the record of right and realise the fees for mutation of their names as per law. The said Md Akkas Ali and Md Abdus Sobhan paid the fees for mutation and up-to-date rents on 25-10-1977. The Government never preferred any appeal against the said order dated 19-10-1977 passing the said Mutation Case. Thereafter, their names were also recorded in the R.S. Khatian. In the year 1999 and 2011 their names were recorded in the field survey record and Dhaka City Survey record respectively. Md Akkas Ali died on 26-3-2004 leaving behind his son the petitioner, his wife and his five daughters as his heirs. While the petitioner was in peaceful possession of the said land the Government initiated LA Proceeding No. 13/2010-2011 for acquisation of the said land. The petitioner and other heirs of Md Akkas Ali filed application for getting compensation in respect of the said land. Upon receipt of the said application, the Assistant Land Officer, Gulshan Land Office, Dhaka vide Memo dated 11-4-2012 informed the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Gulshan Circle, Dhaka that the Government does not have any interest in the land. The said Memo dated 11-4-2012 was also endorsed by Assistant Officer (Land), Gulshan land Office, Dhaka. However, as per the direction of the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Gulshan Circle, Dhaka, the Kanungo and Surveyor submitted a report on the same day i.e. on 12-4-2012 on the said land stating that 1.23 acres of land in SA Dag No. 2465 involved in Mutation Case No. 4363/11 has earlier been recorded in No. 1 Khas Khatian and therefore, Government has interest in this land. After receiving the report of the Kanungo and Surveyor, the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Gulshan Circle, in total disregard of the Memo dated 11-4-2012 of the Assistant Land Officer, Gulshan Land Office, vide Memo No. সঃকঃভুঃ(গুল)-১৫ dated 15-4-2012 forwarded the report of the Kanungo and Surveyor. 

 4. Thereafter, the Land Acquisition Officer, Dhaka vide Memo No. 05.41.2600.033.14.001.11-452 dated 24-5-2012 requested the Government Pleader (GP), Dhaka to give his opinion as to whether compensation can be given to those persons whose names were mutated in respect of the land in RS Dag Nos. 6132, 6133 and 6134 (subsequently City Survey Dag Nos. 9662, 9663, 9665 and 17355) which was earlier recorded in the No. 1 Khas Khatian as SA Dag No. 3465. The Government Pleader (GP), Dhaka after considering all the documents and record gave detailed opinion on the scheduled land on 5-6-2012. The Government Pleader (GP) in his report dated 5-6-2012 in clear terms stated that SA Record was duly amended and the names of the predecessor of the petitioner was duly mutated in relation to the scheduled land. In the said opinion, it is also stated that the names of the petitioner and other heirs of the said Md Akkas Ali having been published in the official gazette after the last City Survey, they are entitled to get the compensation in relation to the said land. 

 9. Mr Ahsanul Karim, Advocate appeared with Mr Khairul Alam Choudhury and Ms Farzana Khan on behalf of the petitioner submitted that the Circle Officer vides Order dated 19-10-1997 ordered that the said land can be mutated in the name of Md Akkas Ali and Md Abdus Sobhan. Mr Ahsanul Karim then took us to Dhaka City Survey Record (Annexure D1) published in the names of Md Akkas Ali and another in connection with the said land under section 144(7) of the State Acquisition Tenancy Act, 1950 (the said Act). He submitted that under section 144(7) of the said Act the Revenue Officer finally framed the record and caused the record finally published in the prescribed manner and the publication of such record has the conclusive evidence that the record has been duly prepared. Therefore, the record having been published in the names of Md Akkas Ali and another, such record provides us with the conclusive evidence of the aforementioned. He further submitted that under section 144A of the said Act, The Dhaka City Survey Record (Annexure D1) has the presumption of its correctness. The said land was also mutated in the name of the petitioner and other heirs of Md Akkas Ali and Md Abdus Sobhan (Annexure E) wherein the Assistant Commissioner (Land) gave a declaration that the land in question is not a khas land. Mr Karim then submitted that the Deputy Commissioner Dhaka served a notice upon the petitioner and others under section 7 of the Acquisition and Requisition of the Immovable Property Ordinance, 1882 (the said Ordinance) for compensation. Mr Ahsanul Karim referred to the report of Land Office (Annexure H) dated 12-4-2012 which evidenced that the land was never a khas land. Mr Ahsanul Karim lastly submitted that the Gazzette Notification published by the Government dated 12-4-2009 which also evidenced that the land in question is not a khas land and the respondents were under obligation to pay the compensation as notified day them in their notice under section 7 of the said Ordinance. 

 11. We have considered the writ petition and Annexures contained therein, the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner and the submissions made by the advocates of both the parties. We considered the Annexure "B" of the writ petition, from which it appears vide order dated 19-10-1977 allowed the Mutation Case No. 1428 (Shoi) of 1977-78 in favour of the predecessors of the petitioner and that the Circle Office approved the land was mutated in the names of Md Akkas Ali and another after correction of the record. From Annexure 'C' it appears that the land was mutated in the name of the said persons. From Annexure 'C1' it appears that the Government received rent from the said Md. Akkas Ali and another. From Annexure 'D' it appears that the said land was mutated in the names of Md Akkas Ali and another. From Annexure 'D1' it appears that Dhaka City Survey Report was published in the names of Md Akkas Ali and another in connection with the said land in question under section 144(7) of the said Act. The land Assistant Officer, Gulshan land office by Memo dated 12-4-2012 (Annexure H) sent report to the office of Assistant Commissioner (Land) Gulshan Circle, Dhaka stating that Government has no interest in the said land. The Office of Assistant Commissioner (Annexure I to the writ petition) vide report dated 12-4-2012 stated that from the report of Land Officer it appears that 1.23 acres of land in Dag No. 2465, Mouza-Vatara is khas land. It is a settled principle of law as communicated by the Hon'ble Appellate Division in the case of The Chairman, Board of Investment vs Bay Trawling Limited, 3 MLR (AD) 54 = 51 DLR (AD) 79 that any decision of one lawful Governmental authority is  binding upon all other Governmental authorities.

3. Defendant Nos. 1-2 jointly and defendant No. 3 separately filed written statements to contest the suit contending that the suit is not maintainable, barred by limitation and bad for defect of parties. The positive case of defendant Nos. 1-2 is that during RS operation 0.50 acre land of RS Plot No. 1500 and 0.61 acre land of RS Plot No. 1528 was jointly recorded in the name of Abdul Khaleque Jamaddar and others in RS Khatian No. 670 and on an amicable partition Mozaffar Hossain and others got 0.20 acre land of RS Plot No. 1500 and 0.20 acre land of Plot No. 1528 and while they were owning and possessing said 0.40 acre land settled the same to Amena Khatun by registered patta No. 1259 dated 21-2-1947 and handed over possession thereof to her and on the basis of the pattan and her possession total 0.40 acre land was prepared and finally published in the name of Amena Khatun in separate SA Khatian No. 363. Yousuf Ali Jamaddar and others got 0.31 acre land including 0.08 acre land from suit Plot No. 1500 and said 0.31 acre land was recorded in the name of Yousuf Ali Jamaddar and others in separate SA Khatian No. 730. Moreover, while Kazi Sultan Ahmed and others were owning and possessing 0.22 acre land SA Khatian No. 729 was prepared and finally published in their name. While Amena Khatun was owning and possessing 0.40 acre land transferred the same to Abul Fazal Khan @ Ali Miah by registered sale deed No. 3257 dated 4-7-1962 and handed over possession thereof to him who transferred the same to Sheikh Ramjan by registered sale deed No. 8289 dated 18-10-1976 and after mutating his name and paying rents thereof he transferred 0.20 acre land of suit Plot No. 1500 in favour of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by registered sale deed No. 5498 dated 20-10-1986 and handed over possession thereof to them and they have been owning and possessing the same by payment of rent upon separation of the holding by mutation case. Accordingly, the RS recorded tenants lost their title to .20 acre land out of 0.50 acre land. 

 4. Though in deed No. 3250 dated 8-3-1967, 0.50 acre land was shown to be transferred but the transferors (RS recorded tenants and their successors) had transferable rights to only 0.30 acre land and accordingly, Sultan, Razzak, Enarudin and Anerudin acquired title to 0.0750 acre land each and thereafter, Enarudin Matubbar transferred his share to Sheikh Tara by registered sale deed No. 6873 dated 11-7-1974 who thereafter, transferred the same to Khalil Molla by registered sale deed No. 5711 dated 24-5-1976. Anerudin Sheikh transferred his share to Gonjur Ali by registered sale deed No. 6006 dated 5-9-1972 who thereafter, transferred the same to Sheikh Zaved Ali by registered sale deed No. 7422 dated 27-8-1974 and thereafter, Sheikh Zaved Ali transferred the same to Hossain Matubbar by registered sale deed No. 3156 dated 3-2-1975 and Hossain Matubbar transferred it to Khalil Molla by registered sale deed No. 6037 dated 30-7-1977 and thereafter, Khalil Molla transferred the same to defendant Nos. 1-2 by registered deed No. 120 dated 3-1-1979. Though Enarudin and Anerudin purchased 0.25 acre land but they jointly acquired title to 0.15 acre land and as such the defendants got title to 0.15 acre land instead of 0.25 acre land through Enarudin and Anerudin Sheikh. Said Sultan and Razzak while owning and possessing 0.15 acre land transferred 0.1250 acre land in favour of Taijuddin @ Tajel by registered deed No. 2587 dated 26-4-1972 and after mutating his name and paying rents to the Government Sheikh Taijuddin died leaving behind two sons namely, Sheikh Tara and Sheikh Lal Miah, five daughters namely, Rahela Khatun, Amena Khatun, Komela Khatun, Sufia Khatun (defendant No. 3) and Roki Khatun and one wife namely, Ful Banu and they inherited .1250 acre land as per Muslim law of inheritance. Rahela Khatun sold her share measuring 0.0125 acre land to defendant No. 1 by registered sale deed No. 3901 dated 10-8-1991; Sheikh Lal Miah sold 0.0250 acre land to defendant No. 1 by registered sale deed No. 2686 dated 4-5-1992; Amena Khatun sold 0.0125 acre land to Sheikh Lal Miah by registered sale deed No. 5203 dated 5-9-1992 and after death of Komela Khatun her two daughters and husband Rema transferred 0.0125 acre land Jahangir Molla by registered sale deed No. 5585 dated 4-9-1995 and thereafter, Jahangir Molla and Sheikh Lal Miah sold 0.0250 acre land to defendant No. 1 by registered sale deed No. 2519 dated 15-5-1996. On the other hand, Sheikh Tara Miah and Ful Banu sold 0.04 acre land to defendant No. 1 by registered sale deed No. 2115 dated 12-4-2000 and handed over possession to him. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 became owner in possession of total 0.1025 acre land through Taijuddin. In the aforesaid way defendant Nos. 1-2 become owner in possession of total 0.20 + 0.15 + 0.1025 = 0.4525 acre land and has been owning and possessing the same by erecting dwelling houses and planting different trees therein and they also mutated their names in different mutation cases and have been paying rents and taxes thereof. After transfer of 0.1250 acre land to Taijuddin by sale deed No. 2587 dated 26-4-1975, Sultan and Razzak had title to and transferable right of only 0.0250 acre land and accordingly, the plaintiff acquired title to 0.0250 acre land by purchase from them vide sale deed No. 3176 dated 8-3-1976. Defendant No. 1-2 prayed for a separate saham of 0.4525 acre land. 

 9. Mr Sk. Reajul Hogue learned Advocate appearing with Ms. Shishirkona, learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the Court of appeal, upon misreading and non-consideration of the evidence and misconception of law illegally allotted 0.1250 acre land in the saham of the plaintiff though her vendors had transferable right of 0.0250 acre land and in doing so did not discuss any evidence of the parties. Learned Advocate further submits that as the last court of facts, the Court of appeal did not evaluate or discuss any evidence independently and come to independent findings of fact or reversed the findings of fact of the trial Court but illegally reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court. Learned Advocate further submits that the Court of appeal erroneously held that complicated question of title is involved in the suit and a simple suit for partition is not maintainable but it decided the suit on merit and decreed the suit. Learned Advocate further submits that upon amicable partition among the RS recorded tenants, Mozaffar and others got 0.20 acre land out of 0.50 acre suit land and transferred the same to Amena Khatun by registered deed of pattan dated 21-2-1947 being No. 1259 and on the strength of said pattan separate SA Khatian No. 363 was prepared and finally published in the name of Amena Khatun and accordingly, the said pattan has been acted upon and title of 0.20 acre land vested to Amena Khatun, who thereafter, transferred the same to Abul Fazal Kha vide registered sale date dated 4-7-1962 and accordingly, the RS recorded tenants and their successors lost their title to 0.20 acre land. Learned Advocate further submits that defendant Nos. 1-2 acquired title to 0.20 acre land through Amena Khatun by successive transfers through valid registered sale deeds and mutated their names in respect of 0.20 acre land and have been owning and possessing the same for more than 12 years and accordingly, they have acquired adverse possession in respect of said 0.20 acre land. Learned Advocate further submits that by deed No. 3250 dated 8-3-1967 though 0.50 acre land was shown to have been transferred to Sultan, Abdur Razzak, Enaruddinn and Aneruddin but the vendors of said deed had title to and transferable right of only 0.30 acre land and after deduction of 0.20 acre land, Sultan and three others acquired title to 0.0750 acre land each instead of 0.1250 acre land each. Learned Advocate further submits that after transfer of 0.1250 acre land to Taijuddin by Sultan and Razzak by registered sale deed dated 26-4-1972 they had title to only 0.0250 acre instead of 0.1250 acre land and accordingly, the plaintiff got title to only 0.0250 acre land from Sultan and Abdur Razzak by sale deed No. 3176 dated 8-3-1976. Learned Advocate further submits that the trial Court upon evaluation of evidence of the parties came to the conclusion that the plaintiff is entitled to 0.0250 acre land but the Court of appeal without discussing any evidence of the defendant Nos. 1-2 illegally reduced their share to 0.3525 acre from 0.4525 acre land and illegally increased share of the plaintiff from 0.0250 acre land to 0.1250 acre land. Learned Advocate finally submits that the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment of reversal and, as such, liable to be set-aside. 

 11. As against the above contention, Mr Goutam Kumar Roy learned Advocate appearing for opposite party No. 1 submits that the Court of appeal, as the last Court of facts, upon considering the evidence and materials on record, rightly held that the plaintiff is entitled to 0.1250 acre land on the basis of sale deed dated 8-3-1976 and such findings of fact cannot be reversed in revisional jurisdiction. Learned Advocate further submits that the Court of appeal rightly held that the defendant could not prove pattan dated 21-2-1947 being No. 1255 and accordingly, they could not prove Amena's title to 0.20 acre land and since Amena Khatun could not acquire title to 0.20 acre land the defendants could not acquire title to said 0.20 acre land through Amena. Learned Advocate further submits that the Court of appeal upon considering the evidence held that Sultan Miah, Abdur Razzak, Enaruddin and Aneruddin acquired title to 0.50 acre land by registered sale deed dated 8-3-1967 from the heirs of Ismail and others and accordingly, the vendees of said deed acquired title to 0.50 acre land, in particular, Sultan and Razzak acquired title to 0.25 acre land jointly and after transfer of 0.1250 acre land to Taijuddin they had title to 0.1250 acre land which has been rightly transferred to the plaintiff by registered sale deed dated 8-3-1976 and, as such, the plaintiff has acquired title to said land not only by purchase but by adverse possession by owning and possessing the same by erecting dwelling hurts therein for more than 12 years. Learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiff paid rent to the Government as well as paid municipal taxes in respect of 0.1250 acre land and it is settled principle of law that rent receipts are evidence of possession and may be used as collateral evidence of title. Learned Advocate further submits that the trial Court, upon misreading and non-consideration of evidence of the parties illegally allotted 0.0250 acre land in the saham of the plaintiff and, as such, the Court of appeal committed no error of law in allotting 0.1250 acre land in the saham of the plaintiff by modifying the judgment of the trial Court. 

 13. I have heard the learned Advocates, perused the judgments of the Courts below, the pleadings of the parties, oral and documentary evidence adduced and produced by them and other materials available on record from which it is revealed that the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 1-3 are not co-sharers by inheritance in the suit-jote but they are co-sharers by purchase from the recorded tenants and their successors. The plaintiff filed the suit for partition of 0.50 acre land of Plot No. 1500 claiming 0.1250 acre land in her saham. Defendant Nos. 1-2 jointly filed written statement and claimed a joint saham of 0.4525 acre land and defendant No. 3 filed written statement claiming 0.0250 acre land. Both the Courts below allotted 0.0225 acre land in the saham of defendant No. 3 but she did not challenge those judgments of the Courts. Accordingly, it is to be presumed that defendant No. 3 has accepted the saham allotted to her by the Courts below. 

 15. The plaintiff in her plaint as well as deposition of PW 1 stated that Salim Jamaddar was owner of 0.50 acre land and after his death his four sons namely Abdul Khaleque and others got 0.09 acre land each and three daughters namely Badrunnessa and others got 0.0450 acre land each and thereafter, Badrun-nessa and Kamarunnessa transferred their 0.09 acre land in favour of their brother Ismail who settled the same to his four sons Yusuf and others and thereafter, his two sons who were minors died leaving behind their father Ismail and accordingly, Ismail acquired title to 0.17 acre land and on the other hand Abdul Khaleque sold his share to Sultan Kazi and thereafter, he re-purchased said 0.09 acre land. Further case of the plaintiff that the heirs. of Yeasin, Habibur Rahman and Ismail acquired title to 0.50 acre land on amicable partition among the recorded tenants and their co-sharers and thereafter, they 'transferred the same to Sultan, Abdur Razzak, Enaruddin and Aneruddin by registered sale deed dated 9-3-1967 being No. 3250. The plaintiff produced the certified copy of said deed of sale dated 9-3-1967 which was marked as Exhibit No. 4. The plaintiff did not produce any deed of so-called pattan by which Badrunnessa and Kamarunnessa transferred 0.09 acre land in favour of Ismail and any deed of pattan by which Ismail transferred the same to his four sons. Accordingly, title of 0.09 acre land by Ismail from Badrunnessa and Kamarunnessa and by Yusuf and his three brothers from Ismail has not been established. 

 16. Against the above contention of the plaintiffs the defendants claimed that on an amicable partition among the RS recorded tenants and some of their heirs, Mozaffar and five others ( four sons and one daughter of Yeasin) got 0.20 acre land from the suit plot and other co-sharers got rest land with other land of other khatian and then Mozaffar and five others sold the same vide registered pattan No. 1259 dated 21-2-1947 to Amena Khatun and while she was owning and possessing the same separate SA Khatian was prepared and finally published in her name. The defendant also contended that after such transfer the rest RS recorded tenants and their successors had only transferable right and title to 0.30 acre land and accordingly, by sale deed dated 8-3-1967 Sultan and his three brothers acquired title to 0.0750 acre land each. Defendant Nos. 1-2 claimed title to said 0.20 acre land through successive transfers from Amena Khatun by sale deeds. In support of the transfer of 0.20 acre land in favour of Amena Khatun by Mozaffar and five others defendants Nos. 1-2 produced original copy of pattan dated 21-2-1947 and its related Index from the Sub-registry Office which were marked as Exhibit Nos. Ka and Ka(1)1 without any objection from the plaintiff. The plaintiff and defendant Nos. 1-2 produced certified copy SA Khatian No. 363 showing preparation and publication of 0.20 acre land in the name of Amena Khatun which was marked as Exhibit 1-Ga. Defendant Nos. 1-2 also produced rent receipts in the name of Amena Khatun in respect of 0.20 acre land which was marked as Exhibit No. Kha(3). They further contended that Amena Khatun transferred 0.20 acre land by registered sale deed dated 4-7-1962 to Abul Fazal Kha who transferred it to Sheikh Ramjan by sale deed No. 8289 dated 18-10-1976 who mutated his name and paid rents to the Government and thereafter, he transferred said 0.20 acre land to defendant Nos. 1-2 by registered sale deed No. 5498 dated 20-10-1986. They produced original copy of sale deed No. 3257 dated 4-7-1962, marked as Exhibit-Ja; certified copy of sale deed No. 8289 dated 18-10-1976, marked as Exhibit-Jha; rent receipts showing payment of rent by Ramjan marked as Exhibit Nos. Kha(4)-Kha(5); original sale deed No. 5498 dated 20-10-1986 marked as Exhibit-Ja(1). The defendants also produced rent receipts in the name of defendant Nos. 1-2 showing payment of rent of the suit land by them, marked as Exhibit Nos. Kha(6)-Kha(9). All those documents were marked as exhibits without any objection from the plaintiff. 

 17. While deposing as PW 1 the husband of the plaintiff namely, Muhammad Lalon Fakir stated, "এস, এ ৩৬৩নং খতিয়ানে আমিনা খাতুনের নামে ১৫০০ দাগে ২০ শতাংশ রেকর্ড হয়েছে কি না জানি না।" He further stated in cross-examination "সুলতান মিয়া, আব্দুর রাজ্জাক, এনার উদ্দিন ও আনার উদ্দিন এস, এ রেকর্ডের পরে জমি কিনে। এদের খরিদের আগেই আমিনা খাতুন ২০ শতাংশ কিনে এবং তার নামে এস, এ রেকর্ড হয়।" From the testimony of P.W 1, it is clear that Amena Khatun took settlement of 0.20 acre land and SA khatian was prepared and finally published in her name and thereafter, Sultan, Razzak, Enaruddin and Anaruddin purchased land. Considering above admission of the P.W1 as well as other evidence, the trial Court observed that by registered pattan No. 1259 dated 21-2-1947 [(Pattan Exhibit No. Ka and Index Exhibit No. Ka(1)] some of the RS recorded tenants and their successors transferred 0.20 acre land in favour of Amena Khatun by that pattan she acquired title to 0.20 acre land and SA khatian No. 363 (Exhibit No. Ga=1) was rightly prepared and finally published in her name and she paid rent to the Government [Exhibit (Kha(3)], who transferred the same to Abul Fazal Kha vide registered deed of sale No. 3257 dated 4-7-1962 (Exhibit Ja) who transferred the same to Sheikh Ramzan vide registered deed of sale No. 8289 dated 18-10-1976 (Exhibit Jha) and upon mutating his name he paid rent to the Government [Exhibit Nos. Kha (4) and Kha(5)] and thereafter, he transferred the same to defendant Nos. 1-2 vide registered deed of sale No. 5498 dared 20-10-1986 [Exhibit ja(1)] and upon mutating their names they paid rents to the Government [Exhibit Nos. Kha (6) and Kha(9)]. On relying upon those documentary evidence the trial Court came to the conclusion that after transfer of 0.20 acre land by RS recorded tenants and their successors they had title to remaining 0.30 acre land and accordingly, by sale deed No. 3250 dated 8-3- 1967 (Exhibit No. 4 = Jha(1)] Sultan, Razzak, Enaruddin and Anaruddin acquired title to only 0.30 acre land. 

 19. It appears that the trial Court, upon proper consideration of the evidence of the parties in particular as per admission of PW 1, came to right conclusion that the RS recorded tenants and their successors transferred .20 acre land to Amena and thus they lost title to 0.20 acre land and defendant Nos. 1-2 acquired title to 0.20 acre land through Amena. But that the Court of appeal upon misreading and non-consideration of evidence and upon misconception of law came to the finding that defendant nos. 1-2 could not acquire title to .20 acre land through Amena Khatun and illegally reversed the findings of the trial Court in this regard. 

 20. The plaintiff produced certified copy of sale deed dated 8-3-1967 being No. 3250 (Exhibit-4) and claimed that by said deed the successors of RS recorded tenants and some of their successors have transferred 0.50 acre land in favour of Sultan, Razzak, Enaruddin and Anaruddin. This sale deed is admitted by the defendants in the way that after transfer of 0.020 acre land to Amena Khatun there was only 0.30 acre transferable land and by deed dated 8-3-1967 Sultan, Razzak, Enaruddin and Anaruddin acquired title to only 0.30 acre land. Since the RS recorded tenants and their successors earlier lost title to 0.20 acre land, the trial Court rightly held that Sultan, Razzak, Enaruddin and Anaruddin acquired title to only 0.30 acre land instead of 0.50 acre land by sale deed No. 3250 dated 8-3-1967 (Exhibit-4). The plaintiff claims that she purchased 0.1250 acre land from Sultan and Razzak by sale deed No. 3176 dated 8-3-1976. During trial, the plaintiff could not produce any rent receipts and mutation Khatian showing her possession in said 0.1250 acre land. Though the plaintiff adduced two oral witnesses to support her claim but the trial Court upon evaluation of the evidence of the plaintiff came to the conclusion that the plaintiff acquired title to only 0.0250 acre land. The Court of appeal, while reversing the finding of the trial Court held that the plaintiff adduced rent receipts which were marked as Exhibit Nos. 2(Ga) and 2(Ga)/1 but from perusal of the records it appears that those rent receipts were produced by defendant No. 3 to prove payment of rent by her predecessor Taijuddin in respect of 0.1250 acre land. Accordingly, the findings of the Court of appeal that the plaintiff produced rent receipts to prove her possession are against the evidence on record. 

 23. In the case of Erfan Ali vs Joynal Abedin Mia 35 DLR (AD) 216 it has been held that rent receipts are evidence of possession and may be used as collateral evidence of title. Section 110 of the Evidence Act provides a presumption of ownership in favour of person who is in possession of the property and possession follows title. Moreover, as per section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, every entry in a record of rights prepared or revised under section 144 shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect. By producing SA Khatian No. 363 (Exhibit-Ga) defendant Nos. 1-2 contended that the SA Khatian was rightly prepared and finally published in the name of Amena Khatun on the basis of pattan dated 21-2-1947 (Exhibit-Ka). Though the plaintiff claimed that said deed of pattan was a product of forgery and the SA record was wrongly prepared and finally published in the name of Amena Khatun but she could not rebut the presumption of correctness of the SA Khatian by adducing any reliable evidence. Accordingly, it is to be presumed that deed of pattan dated 21-2-1947 has been acted upon and SA Khatian No. 363 was rightly prepared and finally published in the name of Amena Khatun. Though the plaintiff claimed that the title deeds by which defendant Nos. 1 and 2 claimed title to the suit land were forged documents but the original sale deeds were produced by the defendants and those were marked as exhibits without any objection from the plaintiff. Accordingly, it is to be presumed that those sale deeds are genuine documents. The defendants by producing oral and documentary evidence have been able to prove that they have been owning and possessing 0.4525 acre land for more than 12 years through their predecessors before filing of the suit and, as such, they have acquired title to and possession of 0.4525 acre land by way of adverse possession. 

 27. The High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse the judgment of the courts below when the same has been made either upon mis-reading or non-consideration of the material evidence caused failure of justice; or when the same has been passed on the basis of evidence which cannot be considered legal evidence and had the same been not taken into consideration the judgment would not have been one as has been made; or when the appellate Court in giving a particular finding has committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice or such finding is found to have resulted from glaring misconception of law; or when the findings arrived at by the appellate Court is contrary to the evidence; or when there appears error of law apparent on the face of the record occasioning failure of justice. It is also of the view of our Apex Court that once the conditions in section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure are satisfied and the High Court's jurisdiction to interfere is established, the proceedings as a whole from start to finish can be scrutinized and any order necessary for doing justice may be passed. There is no limit to the area in which the revisional power is to be exercised by the High Court Division in the facts and circumstances of each case. When a finding of fact is based on consideration of the materials on record, those findings are immune from interference by the revisional Court and the High Court Division has no jurisdiction to sit on appeal over a finding of fact. [Ref Md. Shajahan Khan vs Additional Deputy Commissioner 11 BLT (AD) 60; Md. Habibulla vs Sher Ali Khan 15 BLT (AD) 319 : 57 DLR (AD) 55; Md. Habibur Rahman Bhuiyan and others vs Galman Begum and others 33 BLD (AD) 93 : 64 DLR (AD) 133; Government vs Golanz Hossain Kazi and others 22 BLT (AD) 486; KanchanMallik and others vs Saleha Begum and others 22 BLC (AD) 254, Dr. Choudhury Mosaddaqul Isdani vs Abdullah at Mansur Choudhury and others 70 DLR (AD) 1681.

Md Soyeb Khan, AAG ------ For the Petitioners.
