Vs.
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land and others -------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Gobinda Chandra Tagore J : On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why constituting a 7 (seven) member committee comprising of respondent Nos.2 to 8 under Memo No. 31.036.033.00. 00.221.2010-409(7) dated 27-7-2011 (Annexure-D) issued under the signature of respondent No.9 for investigating the finally published Dhaka City Survey Record-of-Rights in respect of 191 mouzas to ascertain the genuinity of such publication and to uphold/cancel the same and the report of the said committee dated 22-5-2012 (Annexure-E) and also the office order under Memo No. মপ/08/2011/83 dated 26-1-2012 issued by respondent No.10 (Annexure-F) forming two committees to investigate the alleged irregularities of the officials engaged in preparing and finally publishing the said Record-of-Rights, and thereby taking departmental actions against the petitioner and/or to initiate criminal cases under the Anti Corruption Law shall not be declared to have been done/issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and as to why the respondents shall not be directed to interfere with the quasi-judicial functions of the field level officers engaged in preparing and finally publishing the Record-of-Rights under the provisions of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and Tenancy Rules, 1955 in any manner, whatsoever other than under the provisions of the aforesaid Act and Rules and/or why such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper, shall not be passed. 

 3. The respondents were also restrained from giving effect to the recommendations made vide report dated 22-5-2012 (Annexure-E) and the said respondents are also restrained from interfering with the quasi-judicial functions of the field level non cadre officers/employees engaged in preparing and publishing the record-of-rights under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and Tenancy Rules, 1955 for a period of 4 (four) months. Subsequently, the order of stay and that of the order of restraint were extended from time to time. 

 The petitioner No.1 is the President of Assistant Settlement Officer Welfare Association and the petitioner Nos.2 and 3 are Secretary and Vice-President of the same Association of Dhaka unit. All of them are serving under the office of the Directorate of Land Records and Surveys as Non-Cadre Servants of the Government and were engaged in the preparation and publication of the recent Dhaka City Survey Khatians following the Dhaka City Survey, which were finally prepared and published in the Gazette Notification on different dates. The Directorate of Land Records and Surveys is empowered to prepare and publish the record-of-rights as per order issued by the Government from time to time by issuing Gazette Notification under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The employees and officers engaged in preparation and publication of the record-of-rights of that office are divided into two categories- Non-Cadre Service Holders starting from Chainman to Assistant Settlement Officer i.e. Chainman, Badar Amin, Sarder Amin, Halka Officer/Sub-Assistant Settlement Officer and Assistant Settlement Officer/Circle Officer and the other group belongs to the Cadre Service, who are deputed to the Directorate. The preparation and publication of the record-of-rights are quasi-judicial functions under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, the Tenancy Rules, 1955, Survey and Settlement Manual, 1935, the Survey Act, 1875 and Technical Rules, 1957. The Rules 26-31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 are the main rules for preparing record-of-rights. Like judicial protection Act, 1850, section 77(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and the rule 39 of the Tenancy Rule, 1955 and also the circular No. ভূঃমঃ/শাঃ-২(অডিট আপত্তি)-৭/২০০৬-৩৯০/১(৯০)dated 2-6-2008 issued by the Ministry of Land have given a safeguard to the persons involved in preparing and publishing the record-of-rights. The record-of-rights of Dhaka City Survey of 191 mouzas prepared under the Dhaka City Survey have already been completed and published in the Bangladesh Gazette as per rule 34 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 as well as, as per section 144(7) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, except some of the khatians of each mouzas against which Writ Petitions or Civil proceedings are pending. When the dispute on finally publishing the record-of-rights were being adjudicated by the Land Survey Tribunals, the Ministry of Land suddenly issued the impugned office order bearing No. 31.036.033.00.00.221. 2010-409 dated 27-7-2011 forming an enquiry committee consisting of the respondent Nos.2-8 for giving an opinion either for affirming or cancelling the finally prepared and published City Survey Khatians of 191 Mouzas under the Dhaka City Survey after 5 years of publication of the same in the Gazette Notification. The said enquiry committee submitted the impugned report dated 22-5-2012 as contained in Annexure-E. In the said report, it was, amongst other, opined that approximately 2815.00 acres of the land of the Government were not recorded in the name of the Government while, most of those properties earlier belonged to the Court of Wards and subsequently, in the name of the private persons by operation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. On receiving the said report dated 22-5-2012, the respondent No. 10, DGDLRS issued the impugned Memo No. মপ/০৮/২০১১/৮৩ dated 26-1-2012 forming two committees-one consisting of respondent Nos.11-15 and the other consisting of respondent Nos.16-19 to enquire into the matter in order to find out the irregularities in not recording the Government land and also to take action against the persons involved in such preparation and publication of the record-of-rights by starting departmental proceeding as well as by filing anti-corruption case against them. The petitioners being aggrieved by the said impugned orders and enquiry report contained in Annexures D, E and F filed the instant Writ Petition and obtained the Rule and the orders of stay and restraint. 

 5. The respondent No.1, the Ministry of Land contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition by denying the material allegations made in the Writ Petition and contending, inter alia, that the respondents, including the respondent Nos.11, 16 and 17 are not only responsible for management and administration of the Directorate or they are not only the supervising officer but they are also engaged in preparing and publishing record-of-rights. Therefore, the allegation made by the petitioners that the respondents are interfering with the so-called quasi-judicial function is not true. The superior officers starting from the post of Charge Officer of the DGLRS are legally authorized to supervise the official activities of the sub-ordinates of the Directorate. They also exercise their revenue powers for preparing and publishing of the record-of-rights in accordance with law as well as the instructions of the Government passed from time to time. Section 149(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 authorizes the Board of Land Administration to pass any order for correction of any entry in a record-of-rights maintained under Part-V of the Act or in a settlement-roll prepared and finally published under Part-V thereof. If there is any bonafide mistake, the superior officer of the Directorate may interfere with the functions and activities of the petitioners and others as per the provision of section 149(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950; rules 27, 28, 31, 36, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42, 42A 42B, and 44 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the Technical Rules, and Chapter (iv) Rule 16, 19, 32 and Chapter (viii) rule-20 of Instructions of the Settlement Department, 1957. The position of a DGLRS is clearly manifested in rule 12 of Survey and Settlement Manual, 1935. The Government can issue circulars, memorandums and other instructions as per rules of Business and Allocation of Business and make rules under section 152 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Therefore, issuing circulars etc. by the Government or the Directorate for making it responsible and accountable is within the legal authority of the Government and the Directorate. Section 77(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 provides safeguard to the petitioners and others only if the acts are done in good faith. The circular dated 2-6-2008 was issued as a directive for the audit team to follow the same during auditing the field level offices. Rule 39 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 authorizes the Revenue Officer with the additional designation, Settlement Officer or Assistant Settlement Officer to exercise power like a Civil Court. The Rules do not give any immunity to the officials from accountability for their activities. The Revenue Officers and others engaged in preparing and publishing the record-of-rights cannot escape the responsibility and liability in securing the public interest in preparing the records-of-the public property. The respondents have every authority to look into whether the petitioners and others had any negligence or committed any deviation from the assigned tasks in preparing the records-of-land properly. Every judicial or quasi-judicial officer has a right to pass an order but it must be guided by the existing laws. The respondent Nos.11, 16 and 17 are empowered to exercise revenue powers and accordingly, they can look into the activities of their subordinate officers. The authority can hold any enquiry or form any committee to look into the allegations of any mischief or gross irregularities and negligence or intentionally done wrong activities committed by any of subordinate revenue officers at any stage of the survey. There are allegations published in different dailies that some revenue officers have recorded the land belonged to different public agencies in the name of some unscrupulous private persons although the previous record i.e. RS Record was in the name of public agencies and thus, helped misappropriation of the public lands by the land grabbers. The respondents are constitutionally bound to look into the serious allegations in public interest in order to take appropriate measures for recovery of the public property and also to take punitive measures against the persons found responsible for the misdeeds and causing losses to the state and public in general. There being serious allegation of irregularities against the finally published record-of-rights of 191 mouzas of City Survey, the respondents formed committee to scrutinize/investigate into the legal aspects as to whether there was any scope for cancellation of the records to redress the public sufferings and accordingly, the enquiry committee was formed by the Memo dated 27-7-2011. Moreover, no penal decision was taken against the petitioners. Accordingly, they cannot be aggrieved thereby and come before this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution for that purpose. No law or any rule gives any immunity to any officials involved in doing irregularities in the name of quasi-judicial functions or any public-office-functions. The petitioners having done gross irregularities in publishing the record-of-rights cannot claim the safeguards under the law and circular as has been claimed by them. The impugned orders were very much within the purview of law. The impugned report contains the facts based on the case studies. The petitioners could have sought relief through normal official procedure and there was nothing to worry about the said impugned order and reports unless he or she is found to have done anything wrong in malafide intention. Hence, the Writ Petition is not maintainable. 

 6. Having placed the Writ Petition, Mr Md Khalilur Rahman along with Mr Junaed Hossen Khan and Mr Md Rashidul Karim, learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that since the record-of-rights prepared finally has already been published in the official Gazette, the Government including the respondents have no legal authority under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to cancel the same and the aggrieved persons including any Government agencies can take recourse to law before the Land Survey Tribunal for correcting the errors, if any, in preparing the said record-of-rights and, as such, the impugned orders as contained in Annexures D and E and the report prepared in pursuance thereof as contained in Annexure-E are liable to be declared to have been passed or prepared without lawful authority and are of no legal effect. 

 7. Then, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the petitioners and others engaged in preparing and publishing, the record-of-rights being protected by section 77(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 as well as by rule 39 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 issuance of the impugned orders as contained in Annexure D and F and the enquiry report prepared in pursuance thereof as contained in Annexure-E are liable to be declared to have been done without lawful authority and are of no legal effect. 

 9. On the other hand, Mr Manzill Murshed, learned Advocate for the respondent No.1 submits that the petitioners and others involved in preparing and publishing the record-of-rights are not immune in law and they are legally bound to discharge their official duties in accordance with law and, as such, there is no legal bar to initiate any proceeding in order to look into whether they have performed their duties in accordance with law or in malafide intention and if anybody is found responsible, they should be taken to book while, in the present Writ Petition, no departmental proceeding has yet been started against the petitioners, not any punitive measure has yet been taken and, as such, there being no cause of action in the Writ Petition, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 10. The learned Advocate for the respondent No.1 further submits that in order to enquire into the allegation brought against the preparation and publication of the Dhaka City Survey Records, the respondents upon issuing Annexure D and E only formed committee to enquire into the allegation and the committee submitted its report as contained in Annexure-E with the clear findings that no wholesale proceeding or punitive measure should be taken but such measures would be taken against the persons, who are found liable and there are only allegation against the petitioners and others and nobody has yet been found even liable and, as such, the Writ Petition being a premature one, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 11. Then, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.1 submits that as per the preliminary enquiry about 2815.056 acres of land of the Government or the Government agencies appertaining to 191 mouzas have been illegally recorded in the name of the private persons through the petitioners and others and, as such, it is the constitutional as well as the legal duty of the respondents to get those record corrected in the name of the Government or the Government agencies whatever may be the case and for that purpose, the impugned orders were issued for ascertaining the liability of the persons involved therein, but the liabilities of the persons including the petitioners have yet not been asserted let alone any proceeding has been drawn against them and therefore, there being no cause of action, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 13. The petitioners and others were involved in preparing and publishing the Dhaka City record-of-rights following the Dhaka City Survey. The record-of-rights have already been finalized and published in the official Gazette. As per the case of the respondents, there were serious allegations of irregularities and illegalities in conducting survey and preparing and publishing the record-of-rights. Even 2815.0569 acres of land appertaining to 191 mouza of Dhaka have been wrongly and illegally recorded in the name of private persons through the petitioners and others, who were involved in conducting the survey and preparing and publishing the record-of-rights. In order to ascertain the liability of the persons involved in such illegalities or irregularities, the respondent No.1, Ministry of Land issued the impugned office order dated 27-7-2011 as contained in Annexure-D forming an Enquiry Committee for a recommendation whether the record-of-rights of the said 191 mouzas should be maintained or cancelled. The Enquiry Committee upon enquiry submitted a report dated 22-5-2012 and the said report was forwarded to the Secretary, Ministry of Land by the impugned Memo dated 22-5-2012. But it appears from the said report dated 22-5-2012 that it was an incomplete report and thereby the liability of the persons involved in preparing such illegal and erroneous record-of-rights was not ascertained. Accordingly, the Directorate of Land Record and Survey by the impugned office order dated 26-1-2012 formed two committees underlining the terms of reference of the committee as under: 

 15. It appears from the Writ Petition that the petitioners filed the Writ Petition with an apprehension only that upon such enquiry, departmental and punitive measures may be taken against them. But it appears from the said office order dated 26-1-2012, Annexure-F that it was intended not to take punitive measures against all the persons, who were involved in preparing and publishing the record-of-rights but only against the persons who are liable for committing any irregularity and illegality. Thus, it appears from the said impugned orders as contained in Annexures D, E and F that the Ministry of Land or the Directorate of Land Record and Survey has yet not completed the enquiry fixing the liability of the persons responsible for any illegality. However, once the record-of-rights, whether it was prepared wrongly or rightly has already been published in the official Gazette, the respondents have no legal authority under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 to cancel the same by any administrative order. The same can only be cancelled or altered or corrected by the competent Court of civil jurisdiction. 

 16. However, the Government has every legal authority to conduct a new survey in respect of the said 191 mouzas of Dhaka City in order to record the land appertaining to those mouzas correctly. 

 17. In such facts and circumstances, it appears that the Writ Petition is pre-mature while, the respondents have no legal authority to cancel the record-of-rights published finally.

3. Opposite party No.1 as plaintiff on 27-11-02 instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 308 of 2002 against the petitioners and another for a decree of declaration that RS record of rights as prepared and finally published in the name of erstwhile DIT now added defendant No.5, RAJUK, in respect of the suit land measuring about 0.3480 acres of RS plot No. 9541 fully described in the schedule 'Kha' a part of schedule 'Ka' measuring about 0.6281 acre was wrong, illegal, ineffective and not binding upon the plaintiff and that the application of defendant No. 4 dated 13-10-02 submitted before defendant No.2 for lease of the suit land was illegal, ineffective and also not binding upon the plaintiff. The plaintiff also prayed for perpetual injunction for restraining defendant Nos. 1 and 2 permanently from leasing out the suit land or any part thereof in favour of defendant No. 4 or any other third party and/or also for restraining them from interfering in any way with the title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. The suit was then renumbered as aforesaid Title Suit No. 124 of 2003. By an order dated 2-4-03 RAJUK was added as defendant No.5. 

 4. Plaint case, in short, is that the land measuring about 0.6864 acre of plot No. 118 appertaining to CS khatian No. 13369 was originally owned and possessed by Indro Mohan and Rajkumar and Mukta Sundari in equal shares. Indro Mohan and Mukta Sundari died without any issue and leaving Rajkumar as their only heir and legal representative. Rajkumar was survived by two sons, namely, Radhagobinda and Pratap Chandra. By successive devolution, Radhagobinda and others became owners in possession of said land. They on 2-1-54 transferred said land to the plaintiff by way of a registered 'Patta' being No. 7441 and a registered sale deed being No. 7442 and delivered possession. Record of rights was accordingly prepared in the names of said recorded tenants and the plaintiff in SA khatian No. 2190 in plot No. 6163. Said land was also recorded as holding No. 47 Lal Chan Mokim Lane in the office of defendant No. 4, the DCC. 

 7. Then RAJUK decided to release the unused land and on the application of the plaintiff, the Ministry of Land by its memo dated 24-3-86 released 0.1482 acre of land in favour of the plaintiff and asked the DC, Dhaka to complete the process of release. When by an order dated 8-4-86 the plaintiff was asked to return Taka 5229.90 proportionate price of the released land out of the compensation received, the plaintiff on 8-4-86 deposited said amount by treasury 'Chalan'. Then, pursuant to the final order of release dated 19-4-86, the government handed over formal possession of said released land to the plaintiff. Meanwhile, in the revision survey, the plaintiff found that said land measuring about 0.3480 acre schedule 'Kha' part of the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of erstwhile DIT and such record of rights had got no basis. 

 9. The tenants of the plaintiff then formed them into a society as defendant No.4 and made an application on 13-10-02 to the DCC for allotment. A server on behalf of the DCC came to the suit land on 6-11-02 for measurement. Then, the plaintiff came to know about the wrong record of rights in respect of 0.3480 acres of land in the name of erstwhile DIT. Hence, the suit. 

 11. Case of the defendant Nos. 1 to 3, in brief, is that land of schedule 'Kha' measuring about 0.3480 acre was acquired in the aforesaid LA Case for building of Dholaikhal Road. Then by a memo dated 5-6-82 the DIT transferred Dholaikhal and the adjacent land to the DCC. Being thus owner in possession, the DCC started development of the road, footpath, drain, etc, which was still pending. Said land was recorded in the name of the DCC. Such record of rights shows possession of the DCC. 

 12. It was further stated that the plaintiff got recorded 0.3292 acre in his name in the DP Khatian No. 5392 behind the back of the DCC. Against said record of rights, an appeal was filed and decided wrongly against the DCC. Then, an application was made for review which was fixed for hearing on 25-6-03. Against the review order, the petitioner moved this Division and got a stay in Writ Petition No. 4522 of 2003. By transfer from the DIT the DCC became owner of the suit land. The plaintiff has got no right or title in the suit land and the suit was therefore not maintainable. 

 16. On the evidence oral and documentary on the record, the trial Court was of the view that seeking declaration in respect of the wrong record of rights without praying for declaration of title in the suit land was not sufficient and upon such view, it dismissed the suit as not maintainable. 

 17. On appeal therefrom at the instance of the plaintiff, the appellate Court on the other hand on the evidence both oral and documentary on record found 0.2435 acre of land was finally released and the plaintiff returned the money as was required for such release of the unused land. It found possession of the plaintiff in the suit land which was admitted by defendant No. 4. It also found RS Khatian was wrongly recorded in the name of defendant No.5. 

 20. He submitted that in the absence of a relief sought for declaration of title in the suit land as was found by the trial Court, the plaintiff was not entitled to a mere decree for declaration that RS record of rights as prepared and published was wrong. 

 26. He submitted that the Court of appeal below rightly decreed the suit in the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record and such decree does not call for any interference. 

 27. He submitted that when the plaintiff was admittedly owner in possession of the entire suit land and after release of schedule 'Kha' land, the plaintiff was not required to seek declaration of title and the suit instituted for declaration that the RS record of rights as prepared and published Was wrong was maintainable in law. In support, he cited Sarashijaksha Chatterjee and others vs Karpor Kamini Devi and others. AIR 1937 Calcutta 745. 

 29. I have perused the record. 

 30. Only issue facing me is, as to whether the Court of appeal below was justified in the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record in reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court and in decreeing the suit in its entirety as prayed for. 

 34. Further case of the plaintiff was that the land of schedule 'Kha' measuring 0.3480 was recorded wrongly in the name of DIT in the revision survey in RS khatian No.6, which had no basis. In support of such case, he adduced evidence both oral and documentary. 

 36. It was also the view of the trial Court that RS khatian might have been prepared in 1969/70 to 1972/73 and the plaintiff got release of the land in 1986. So, there was no occasion for recording the land in the name of the plaintiff. Such record of rights cast a doubt over the title of plaintiff and the declaration sought for in respect of the wrong record of rights was not sufficient in the absence of a declaration of title. 

 39. The trial Court dismissed the suit as not maintainable on the view that after acquisition, there were development works and the record of rights was prepared in the name of DCC. I find no justification for such observation. The finding of the trial Court that there were development works on the suit land has got no basis since it is admitted that the suit land is now occupied by shops and there cannot be thought of and development works by the DCC in the shops, 

 41. The fact that the plaintiff amalgamated derequisitioned land with his other land and built a market there and let out the shops to the tenants was proved and admitted, Consequently, the plaintiff had got title and possession in the entire suit land and preparation and publication of RS record of rights in the name of RAJUK was wrong, illegal, ineffective and not binding upon the plaintiff. 

 45. On the aforesaid findings, there is little difficulty to hold that the plaintiff became owner in possession of 0.3480 acre as described in schedule 'Kha'. Said land was finally recorded and published in the name of the erstwhile DIT. Such record has got no basis. Decree passed by the Court of appeal below declaring such record of rights prepared in respect of said 0.3480 acre in plot No. 9541 in the name of the DIT wrong, illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff is well justified in the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record. 

 46. The trial Court however tried to find that when the record of rights was prepared the plaintiff did not get back possession of said unused land of 0.2480 acre. Such record of rights cast a cloud over the title of the plaintiff Upon such view, it finally found that the suit was not maintainable without declaration of title. 

 47. Such view of the trial Court was reversed rightly by the appellate Court. Because, the decision of the trial Court is based on no authority. Earlier, wrong record of rights could be corrected by a mere application under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. In such proceeding, the aggrieved party was never required to establish title to get an order for correction of the record of rights. Reason is not far away to find. Record of rights does neither create nor destroy title. It is mere a record of physical possession at the time when it is prepared. 

 48. A suit for declaration that the record of rights is wrong and for direction for correction of such record of rights falls under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. I find support from an old judgment of MC Ghosh, J in 1937 AIR Cal 745, 

 "Now in this case the plaintiffs asked for a declaration that the Record of Rights was wrong and they prayed that the said record might be corrected. The suit was therefore maintainable and the learned Judge was wrong to hold that it did not come under section 42." 

 49. The Court of appeal below decreed the suit that the record of rights as prepared in Khatian No. 06 in respect of 0.3480 acre of schedule 'Kha' in the name of DIT (RAJUK) was illegal, ineffective and not binding upon the plaintiff as prayed for. I find such declaration was not sufficient, effective and complete relief. Because, the record of rights would not be corrected even after such declaration and continue to remain as before, with at best a copy of the decree attached with the relevant page. 

 50. It occasioned no doubt, for the omission in the prayer for correction of the record of rights in the name of the plaintiff. What can be done if the art of pleadings does not improve even over a century in this part of the civil law world But a litigant cannot be denied the relief which he is entitled to in law. 

 51. Order VII, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure in such case empowers the Court to give relief to the plaintiff as he is found entitled to but omit to pray. Otherwise, the plaintiff would be driven back to seek another declaration and/or correction of the record of rights in another suit which would not only cost the plaintiff but also consume valuable time of the Court. 

 58. The suit is accordingly decreed declaring the record of rights as prepared and finally published vide Exhibit 11/Ka in respect of land measuring about 3480 described in schedule 'Kha' to the plaint in the name of the then DIT and now RAJUK in RS Khatian No. 6 is wrong, illegal, ineffective and not binding upon the plaintiff. It is directed that the relevant record of rights must be corrected in the name of the plaintiff. 

 Send down the records, at once.

2. Succinctly, the facts of the case, as stated in the writ petition, are that the CS recorded tenants, namely Kalipada Karmakar and Jitendra Nath Karmakar, filed Rent Suit no. 1785 of 1950 for recovery of arrears of rents against two full brothers, namely Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal and Md. Abdul Latif Mondal, in the Court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Satkhira on 27.09.1950 and through a compromise agreement (Solenama) Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal got 3/4 share and his brother Abdul Latif Mondal got 1/4 share of 15.08 acres of land. On 05.04.1956 Md. Abdul Latif Mondal sold out his above 1/4 share i.e. entire 4.00 annas shares of the above entire 15.08 acres of land by the registered sale deed no. 2036 dated 05.04.1956 to Most. Hasne Banu, Most. Futfuti, Most. Bedana and Most. Kamala. Out of above 3/4 share i.e. 12.00 annas share of the entire 15.08 acres of land, Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal gifted .50 annas share of land to his brother’s daughter Ambia Khatun and, accordingly, in the SA Khatian no. 452, 11.50 annas share was recorded in the name of Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal, .50 annas share was recorded in the name of Ambia Khatun and 4.00 annas share was recorded in the names of Hasne Banu, Futfuti Bibi, Bedana Bibi and Kamala Bibi being 1.00 anna for each of them. Thereafter, Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal sold his remaining entire share of 11.50 annas, which is 10.33 acres of land, to the petitioner by the registered sale deed no. 5363 dated 03.06.1985 and, pursuant to the said transfer on 03.10.1985, the Mutation Case no. 380(IX-I)/85-86 was filed before the Assistant Commissioner of Debhatta Land Office (hereinafter referred to as the A/C Land, Debhatta) and vide the order dated 15.10.1985 the mutation was done in favour of the petitioner and, accordingly, the SA Khatian no. 233/2 was prepared in the name of the petitioner in respect of 10.33 acres of land. It is stated that after creation of the SA Khatian no. 233/2, the petitioner conjointly with Bedana Bibi, Kamala Bibi sold 40 decimals of land to one Abdul Gaffur Gazi under the record shown in the SA Khatian no. 233/2. 

 3. On 05.05.2005, Mst. Futfuti Bibi, Mst. Bedana @ Vejali Bibi, Mst. Kamala Bibi and others filed Title Suit no. 25 of 2005 before the Assistant Judge, Debhatta, Satkhira against the petitioner and others praying for partition and cancellation of the petitioner’s aforesaid deed no. 5363 dated 03.06.1985 when the plaint of the aforesaid suit was returned by the said Court under Order 7 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure (shortly, the CPC) by the order dated 25.03.2013. Subsequently, on 20.06.2013 the same was instituted in the Court of learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Satkhira and was renumbered as Title Suit no. 50 of 2013 which is still pending. Thereafter, Mst. Futfuti Bibi, Bedana Bibi, Kamala Bibi and Amina Bibi filed an application to the A/C Land, Debhatta and the said application was registered as Miscellaneous Case no. 02/08-09 under Section 149 of the State Acquisition Tenancy Act, 1950 and (hereinafter referred to as the SAT Act) for review of the order passed in Mutation Case no. 380/85-86 with a prayer for cancellation of the petitioner’s mutation and, thereby, to restore the previous status of the mutation with six names as was recorded in the SA Khatian no. 233. The above review application was rejected on 18.05.2009 and against the said order they moved the Collector who, by his order dated 28.12.2011, registered their representation as Miscellaneous Appeal no. 47 of 2010 and allowed the same. Against the aforesaid order dated 28.12.2011 the petitioner filed Miscellaneous Appeal no. 25 of 2011 before the Divisional Commissioner, Khulna who dismissed it by his order dated 31.02.2012. Against the said order the petitioner filed Appeal no. 5-06/2013 (Mutation), Satkhira before the Land Appeal Board and the same was dismissed on 17.04.2014. Against which the petitioner filed a review case being no. 5-08/2014 (Mutation) Full Board, Satkhira and the Full Board dismissed the said review case by its order dated 18.05.2014. 

 5. Respondent nos. 7 to 9 contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter-alia, that the total land under the SA Khatian no. 233 is 15.08 acres and there were 6 (six) recorded owners and each of them had equal share of 2.51 acres of land. It is claimed that Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal was entitled to have a share of 2.51 acres of land only under the SA Khatian no. 233 and, accordingly, he did not have any right and title to sell 10.33 acres of land. It is alleged that the statements regarding Rent Suit no. 1785 of 1950 are concocted as no such a suit had ever been instituted by the CS recorded tenants against Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal and Md. Abdul Latif Mondal and, further, no Solenama was ever made between the said CS recorded tenants and the two brothers and the judgment and decree dated 27.09.1950 is a forged and fraudulent one. It is further alleged that the registered deed no. 5363 dated 03.06.1985 is also a forged one. It is claimed that the Mutation Case no. 380(IX-1)/85-86 was allowed by the A/C Land, Debhatta without issuing any notice to all the recorded owners of the SA Khatian no. 233. It is stated that the petitioner and respondent nos. 7-10 are 12 brothers and sisters and they have some other paternal land properties and since it was necessary for partition and declaration of title of the property among them, the Partition Suit no. 25 of 2005 was instituted initially in a Court which did not have jurisdiction to entertain the said suit and subsequently the said suit was filed in a competent Court. It is stated that the Collector had rightly allowed the appeal of these respondents and, thereafter, the Divisional Commissioner, then, the Land Appeal Board had correctly dismissed the appeals and, finally, vide the impugned order the Full Board of the Land Appeal Board also rightly dismissed the review case. 

 7. Mr. Subrata Saha, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, at the very outset, takes us through the impugned order in tandem with the preceding orders thereto namely, the orders passed by the A/C Land, Debhatta of Satkhira, the Collector (Additional Deputy Commissioner) of Satkhira and the Divisional Commissioner of Khulna and submits that while the order passed by the A/C Land appears to be in consonance with the provisions of the SAT Act, the subsequent orders passed by the appellate authorities namely, the Collector (the Additional Deputy Commissioner), the Divisional Commissioner and finally the Land Appeal Board, are beyond the provisions of the SAT Act. In an endeavor to elaborate his submission on this point, he places Section 143 of the SAT Act and submits that the Collectors and all other Revenue Officers, while performing the functions of mutation, subdivision, amalgamation etc, are carrying out executive nature of jobs/tasks and their duty is only to record the names of the present tenants as per the papers and information presented to them by the Tahshilders or as per the information provided by the applicant. He continues to submit that in the case at hand, however, the appellate authorities have exceeded their jurisdictions in directing the A/C Land to apportion the shares of the owners of the case land and then mutate their names against their respective shares inasmuch as ascertainment of sahams among the co-sharers can only be done by a competent civil Court, and the Revenue Officers under the SAT Act, having not the status and power of a Court, cannot order for apportionments of the saham. He, then, places Section 143B of the SAT Act and forcefully submits that a revision in the record-of-rights by distribution of the respective shares of any land to the co-sharers can only be done by fulfilling the requirements outlined therein. In continuation of his submission on this point, he argues that if there are conflicting claims by the co-sharers as to the title and possession of a landed property, the A/C Land cannot proceed with a mutation case until the dispute is settled by a competent Court of law. 

 19. It is the submission of the learned Advocate for respondent nos. 7-9 that the functions performed or orders passed by the Revenue Officers are beyond the periphery of the jurisdiction of the civil Courts and, thus, alongside the civil suit, which would determine and adjudicate mainly the saham and title but not be capable of changing the names in the record-of-rights, they had to approach the A/C Land for correction of the record-ofrights. In order to deal with the above submission, we are required to look at the concerned Sections of the SAT Act seeking to oust the jurisdiction of the civil Courts. The following Sections, namely Sections 30, 46B, 69, 72, 86A, 115, 134, 144B and 145F of the SAT Act put an embargo to take recourse to the jurisdiction of the civil Courts. 

 20. From a minute reading of the above provisions, it appears that Section 30 prohibits resorting to the jurisdiction of the civil Courts when an order is made directing preparation or revision of a record-of-rights, Section 46B puts the said embargo when Compensation Assessment-roll has been prepared. Also, as per Section 69, until all the rent receivers’ interests, which were liable to be acquired, have been acquired, the rent receivers were made ineligible to file any execution case for recovery of their interests, Section 72 prohibits resorting to the jurisdiction of the civil Courts when Compensation Assessment-roll has been published, Section 86A puts a bar to sue with regard to the right in any land which re-appears on account of alluvion or abatement of rent on account of diluvion, Section 115 ousts the jurisdiction of the civil Courts in respect of the determination of rentrates, Section 134 prohibits resorting to the jurisdiction of the civil Courts when an order is passed relating to consolidation of holdings of raiyats, Section 144B prohibits resorting to the jurisdiction of the civil Courts when an order has been made under Section 144(1) directing the preparation of revision of the record-of-rights in respect of any area and Section 145F puts an embargo to institute a suit in the civil Court with regard to a matter which is triable by the Land Survey Tribunal. Out of the above Sections, while Sections 30, 46B, 69 and 72 are the relevant provisions for acquisition, the rest Sections are linked up with the provisions of resolving the tenancy issues. 

 22. However, the fact of the instant case does not attract any of the above barring provisions of the SAT Act given that the petitioner’s case is covered by Section 143 of the SAT Act which does not put any bar to seek remedy in the civil Court. In view of the fact that the petitioner is claiming the case property on the basis of a registered sale deed, respondent nos. 7-9 appear to have rightly invoked the civil Court’s jurisdiction where they will have all the opportunity to examine their title & partition vis-a-vis that of their co-sharers on the case land and, then, pursuant to the judgment and decree from the civil Court, the A/C Land shall be duty bound to update the record-of-rights on the case land. It follows that respondent nos. 7-9 were not legally allowed to approach the A/C Land for correction of the record-of-rights at a time, when the same dispute and grievance is being taken care of by a competent civil Court. 

 When Revenue Officer is appointed for the purpose of preparation or revision of a record-of-rights, or for the purpose of preparation of Compensation Assessment Roll under Part IV of the Act, within any district, part of a district or local area, he shall be appointed either with or without the additional designation of ‘Settlement Officer’ or ‘Assistant Settlement Officer’. Every such officer is hereby vested with- 

 36. Power vested in Revenue Officers- When a Revenue-officer is appointed for the purpose of revision of a record-of-rights under chapter XVII of the Act within any district, part of a district or local area, he shall be appointed either with or without the additional designation of “Settlement Officer” or “Assistant Settlement Officer”. Every such Officer shall have,- 

 143. Maintenance of the record-or-rights: The Collector shall maintain up-to-date, in the prescribed manner, the record-or-rights prepared or revised under Part IV, or under this Part by correcting clerical mistakes and by incorporating therein the changes on account of- 

 32. From a minute reading of the above provisions of law, it appears that the duty of maintenance of the record-of-rights has been conferred upon the Collectors and he, with the assistance of the sub-ordinate Revenue Officers, shall perform the said duty apparently on two occasions. Firstly, when a clerical mistake occurs in passing an order on mutation, or after preparation of the record-of-rights or after revision of the same under Part VI of the SAT Act and, secondly, when there is any change in the ownership of the land as a result of transfer/inheritance, or on account of the events having taken place as enunciated in sub-Sections (b) to (d) of Section 143 of the SAT Act. 

 33. To put the provisions of Section 143(a) in a bit detail, it may be said that under Section 89 of the SAT Act, the happening of any transfer of land, upon being registered by the registering officer, must be notified to the Revenue Officer whose duty, then, becomes to open a file for mutation of record of rights and issue notice to the co-sharers of the transferred land, as provided in Section 143C of the SAT Act. However, if the landed property is acquired by inheritance and the partition taken place amicably through a registered instrument upon observing the provisions of the personal laws, Section 143B(2) of the SAT Act empowers the Revenue Officers to cause changes in the record-of-rights. On the other hand, the provisions of Section 143(b) to (d) of the SAT Act provide that if there is any amalgamation of land under Section 116 of the SAT Act, or subdivision of a joint tenancy under Section 117 of the SAT Act, or there happens a consolidation of holdings under Section 125 of the SAT Act, the Revenue Officer under the authority of the Collector shall incorporate the said changes in the record-of-rights. Also, whenever there is the new settlement of the lands or the Government purchases holdings, or there is abatement of rent on account of abandonment, diluvion and acquisition of land, the Collector’s duty is to cause the said changes in the record-of-rights. 

 34. From the facts of the case at hand, it surfaces that there has been a transfer, as per the claim of the petitioner, by Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal, who is the father of the petitioner as well as of respondent nos. 7-9 and, accordingly, the petitioner had approached the concerned Revenue Officer namely, A/C Land, Debhatta, Stakhira, in the year 1985 by filing an application under Section 117 read with Section 143 of the SAT Act and through opening up the Mutation Case no. 380 (IX-I) 85-86 under the authority of Section 143(C) of the SAT Act, the A/C Land, Debhatta, Satkhira, at first, on 03/10/1985 had asked the Tahshilddar to submit a report thereon after making necessary inquires and on 15.10.1985, upon receiving the said report from the Tahshilddar, the record-of-rights was updated by the said Revenue Officer, Debhatta, Satkhira and, accordingly, in our way of scrutiny, we find that the duty performed by the said Revenue Officer namely, A/C Land, Debhatta, Satkhira, was completely in conformity with the provisions of Sections 117, 143 and 143C of the SAT Act and Rules 22- 24 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 inasmuch as under Section 143 of the SAT Act together with the provisions of relevant rules, namely rules 22-24 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the Collectors, with the aid of the Revenue Officers, have been vested with the duty to maintain the record-of-rights of the lands of this country and they are empowered to correct any clerical mistakes occurred in preparation or revision of the record-of-rights and, also, to amend the same when any change takes place in the ownership of the land, be it for sale, inheritance, vesting the property in the Government, acquisition or purchase by the Government etc. 

 36. However, there is no observation by the said A/C Land as to the pendency of the civil suit. Though both the sides now unequivocally admit that a civil suit is pending before the competent Court of law with regard to the claim on the suit property, however, nothing was mentioned about it before the A/C Land, Debhatta, Satkhira neither by respondent nos. 7-9, nor by the writ petitioner. The reasons and motives of non-mentioning about the pendency of the suit are different for the petitioner and respondent nos. 7-9 and, in fact, opposite to each other. While it appears from the contents of the application, which was registered as Miscellaneous Case no. 02/08-09, made by respondent nos. 7-10 before the A/C Land, Debhatta, Satkhira, which has been placed before this Court as annexure-Y, that respondent nos. 7-9 cunningly remained silent about it, in contrast, the petitioner appears to have felt it not necessary to present this information to the A/C Land. Although the A/C Land, Debhatta, Satkhira rejected the said Miscellaneous Case no. 02/08-09 filed by respondent nos. 7-10, however, had the fact of the pendency of the civil suit been stated in the application by respondent nos. 7-10, the A/C Land would have an occasion to make his observation on this fact as well. When these respondents approached the appellate authority namely, Collector the appeal was allowed in absence of the petitioner and, thus, there was no scope for the petitioner to inform the Collector about the pendency of the civil suit on the same claim. Under the circumstance, the petitioner approached the superior appellate authority namely, Divisional Commissioner, Khulna who affirmed the order of the Collector, Satkhira without discussing the fact of institution of the civil suit. Finally, when the petitioner moved the Land Appeal Board where it transpires that the petitioner stated about the facts of the civil suit but the said final appellate authority did not take up the said issue for its consideration and simply arrived at a decision that the order passed by the Collector, Debhatta, Satkhira, to the effect that the record is required to be upgraded by distributing the share to the co-sharers named in the S.A. Khatian no. 233, does not suffer from any infirmity. As the last and final authority on the mutation matters, the Full Board of Land Appeal Board was expected to be astute in discharging their duties, for, a judicious order passed by the said final authority not only minimises the hassle of the parties to a mutation proceeding, which the litigant experience in dealing with the mutation cases, but it also saves the invaluable time of this Court. 

 38. The above core issue of this case surfaces to be a rare one of its kind in this Court as our research could not trace out any similar case on this point. On the other hand, there is no statutory provision as well to guide us a clear-cut path for adjudication upon the point. Under the circumstances, we have no other option but to put our best effort, based on sound and pertinent reasoning to adjudicate upon the issue. It is a universally recognized rule that Parliament or Executive does not take up any sub-judice matter for their consideration. The principle is rooted in our Constitution as well as in many of statutes of our country, including the Rules of the Procedure of Parliament, and, accordingly, it would be a sound and rational view to hold that if there is a case pending in a competent Court of law regarding any dispute over any land property and on the same dispute, pending disposal of the said case, a Revenue Officer is subsequently approached by any claimant with a prayer to update a record-of-rights in the form of amendment or the correction of the record-of-rights, the Revenue Officer should abstain from proceeding with the mutation case. 

 39. In the case at hand, all the Revenue Officers, from the A/C Land to the Land Appeal Board, utterly failed to address this issue. While it is apparent that the parties to this case were at fault at the initial stage before the A/C Land and the Collector for not disclosing the fact of pendency of the civil suit and, later on, when the petitioner had presented the said fact, although belatedly, the Divisional Commissioner and the Land Appeal Board failed to take up the fact for their consideration. Moreover, unless a Revenue authority is presented with a registered instrument of amicable settlement or the contending parties of a mutation case agrees on their respective shares, no Revenue Authority is competent to change the record-of-rights by apportioning/allocating shares to the claimants of any landed property. Thus, in the instant case, the first appellate authority namely, Collector, Satkhira when passed the order stating that the A/C Land, Debhatta, Satkhira should update the record by distributing the share, we find that the said appellate authority exceeded its jurisdiction having attempted to usurp the functions of a civil Court inasmuch as it is for the civil Court to decide the share of the landed property in a situation where the claimed co-sharers are not in agreement as to their respective shares. 

 40. We are of the view that in dealing with the mutation proceedings the Revenue Officers’ duties are only to record the names of the owners of the land upon examining the relevant papers and documents, if the same are produced before them without raising/taking any objection thereto. But the moment the Revenue Officer would come to know, either through an enquiry conducted by him with the assistance of the Tahshilder or any other staff of his office, or through an application filed by a private party for mutation, that there are disputes regarding the produced papers and documents and there are contending claimants over any land and the matter is pending in the Court for disposal, the concerned Revenue Officer must not proceed further with regard to the said mutation case until the said civil suit is finally disposed of. 

 41. In this case, it is an admitted fact that respondent nos. 7-9 have already invoked the competent jurisdiction, namely the jurisdiction of the civil Court, seeking cancellation of the mutation recorded in favour of the petitioner in the year 1985 together with a prayer for partition of the suit land and, thus, we are of the view that until their respective title is settled by the civil Court, the Revenue Officer shall not be in a position to distribute or apportion the respective portions of the share of the petitioner and that of respondent nos. 7-9 for recording the same in their respective record-of-rights. 

 42. Accordingly, we hold that the order passed by all the appellate authorities, starting from the Collector of Satkhira upto the Land Appeal Board, committed illegality in holding that the record-of-rights should be amended upon allocating the sahams among the contending parties. It follows that the impugned order is destined to be declared illegal and, thereby, the same requires to be set aside. 

 (2) Respondent no. 6, being the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Debhatta, Satkhira, is directed to take his decision on updating the record-of-rights of the parties of Miscellaneous Case no. 47 of 2010 only when the adjudication of the Title Suit no. 50 of 2013, now pending before the Court of learned 2nd Joint District Judge, Satkhira, is finally completed. 

 (3) Respondent no. 1, being the Secretary of the Land Ministry, is directed that he shall, in an endeavour to prevent the recurrence of recording a mutation during pendency of a civil suit, issue a circular notifying all the Revenue Officers of Bangladesh and also the that if a civil suit is pending involving claim of title on the basis of transfer or inheritance of an immovable property, the said Officers and the Board shall not, whether suo-motu or upon an application of any person, entertain a case for mutation of names in the record-of-rights under Section 143(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 till a final decision is arrived at in such civil suit through exhausting appeal or revision arising therefrom.
