full_judgment:
A holding of 7.51 acres of land appertaining to C.S. Khatian No.528 of Mouja-Joar Sahra, JL No.271 under former police station -Tejgaon now under police station - Budda, Dhaka belonged to one Joy Durga Das who died leaving behind his daughter's son, namely, Krisna Chandra Debnath to inherit his all properties. While owing and possessing the said properties, Krisna Chandra Debnath sold out 7.51 acres of land by six deeds of sale to Moulana A.K.M. Fazhil Hafiz, Hazi Zohra Khatun and Begum Rahima Hossein, each getting 2.50 acres of the aforesaid land. Subsequently, Begum Rahima Hossain sold out 1.25 acres of land to Ms. Hena Khatun by a deed of sale No.4329 dated 04.10.1961. However, the names of Ms. Hena Khatun and other original heirs were recorded and published in S.A Khatian No.942, but their names were recorded separately during Revisional Survey (R.S. record). Subsequently, the mother of the petitioner, namely Begum Rahima Hossain transferred .1650 acres of land from R.S. Plot No.5306 appertaining to R.S. Khatian No.2100 corresponding to SA Khatian No.942 to the petitioner by a deed of Heba-Bil-Ewaj No.10327 dated 09.6.1994. The petitioner got his name mutated against the case land by Mutation and Separation Case No.443/96-97 and started paying revenue taxes to the Government. However, .1708 acres of ditch land from R.S. Plot No.5306 appertaining to R.S. Khatian No.2100 was recorded in the name of the petitioner's mother and .1200 acres of ditch land from R.S. Plot No.5305 appertaining to R.S. Khatian No.2537 was recorded in the name of respondent No.7. In this way, .2908 acres of ditch land was k recorded in the name of petitioner's mother and respondent No.7 in the present plot No.57227. During land survey in Dhaka City area, .1222 acres Of ditch land from Plot No.57277 appertaining to D.P. Khatian No.7507 was recorded in the name of the petitioner and .0486 acres of land from Plot No.57227 appertaining to D.P. Khatian No.12839 was recorded in the name of petitioner's mother. In this way, .1708 acres of ditch land was recorded in the name of the petitioner and his mother. 

 3. It further appears from the writ petition that respondent No.7 and other purchased .24 acres of land from C.S. Plot No.1242 and .56 acres of land from C.S. plot No.1243 from aforesaid Hena Khatun and Abul Bashar by registered deeds of sale. Subsequently, respondent No.7 and others got their names mutated against the case land by Mutation and Separation Case No.3722/76-77. In the revisional settlement the names of respondent No.7 and others were recorded in plot No.5306 of R.S. Khatian No.2537, but in the Dhaka City Land Survey, only .12 acres of ditch land from plot No.57227 of D.P. Khatian No.2537 was recorded in their names. 

 4. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid draft record-of rights, respondent No.7 and others filed Objection Case Nos.4714 of 2000, 4715of  2000 and 12903 of 2000 before the . Revenue-Officer under Rule 30 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 (in brief, Tenancy Rules, 1955) against the Tashdik record of .1708 acres of land in Plot No.57227 in the name of the petitioner and his mother. The revenue Office, after hearing both the parties and considering their relevant papers and documents, rejected the objection Cases on 8.11.2000. 

 6. Respondent No.7 and others, thereafter, filed an application under Rule 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 before the Settlement Officer who, on receiving the application and on considering the contents thereof, set aside the order passed under Rule 31 and formed a 5-member committee (Appeal Board) headed by a Charge Officer for hearing of the said 3 appeal cases. The said committee heard the parties, recorded their statements, examined the papers and documents, inspected to ascertain the possession of ditch land and unanimously came to a decision making a specific recommendation on 6.3.2002 for restoring the order dated 13.11.2001 passed by the Settlement-Officer in appeal cases. 

 8. For reconsideration of judgment passed in appeal cases under Rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, respondent No.7, thereafter, filed an application under Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 to the Director (land records and surveys) who, by his letter dated 10.06.2002 sent the same to the Settlement-Officer, Dhaka to reopen the aforesaid appeal cases and decide those afresh as per Rules. 

 9. The Settlement-Officer, by his letter bearing Memo .No.12/257/-5(11/528-2075 dated 16.6.2002, informed the Director (land records and' surveys) that there in no scope for reopening the matter in view of the fact that the committee constituted for that purpose has already decided the matter. 

 10. In spite of aforesaid facts and circumstances, the Director (land records and surveys) respondent No.2 by his order under Memo No. Bhu: Re: 6/2002/1471 dated 08.07.2002 passed an order purporting to constitute a committee headed by the respondent No.2 charge officer-3 to hold a fresh hearing in respect of 3 appeal cases and report by 31.07.2002. Respondent No.3, in consequence of above order, issued a notice fixing a date for hearing of 3 appeal cases on 24.07.2002. 

 12. Respondent No.7 contested the Rule Nisi by filling an affidavit-in-opposition and supplementary affidavit-in-oppositions denying the contentions made in the writ petition and supplementary affidavit filed by the writ petitioner. The case of respondent No.7 as set up in the affidavit-in-oppositions, in short, is that respondent No.7 and others produced deeds of purchase in respect of .80 acres of land but the Settlement-Officer prepared record of rights in their favour only in respect of 0.5708 acres of land vide D.P Khatian No.4778. The committee constituted by the Settlement-Officer under rule 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 did not properly consider documents of title in support of their claim and recommended restoring the judgment and order of the appeal cases illegally and as such draft record-of-rights prepared and maintained up to the appellate authority under rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 can not be sustained in the eye of law and the same requires a fresh scrutiny for coming to a correct decision. In view of above facts and circumstances, respondent No.7 made a prayer to respondent No.2, Director (land records and surveys) who being satisfied on material irregularities ordered further scrutiny of the matter under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 and as such the impugned order dated 08.07.2002 contained in Annexure-G to the writ petition for constitution of a committee as well as notice dated 14.7.2002 contained in Annexure-H to the writ petition are lawful and valid and as such the writ petition should be discharged. 

 13. At the very outset, Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Advocate along with Mr. S.R. Khosh Nabish, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that since the appeal cases were decided by the appropriate authority under Rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the judgment passed in appeal cases cannot be. changed, altered and modified by respondent No.2 as Settlement Officer exercising his powers and authority under Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, unless there is an entry that has been procured by fraud in record-of-rights and as such, the order passed by respondent No.2 constituting a committee for reopening the appeal cases earlier decided under Rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 is without lawful authority. He next submits that thought the Rule 42A of the East Bengal Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 gave respondent No.2 as a Settlement-Officer an authority to hear the matter in respect of record-of-rights before final publication thereof, the fact remains that the Settlement-Officer has already exercised such powers and authority by constituting a committee and that the aforesaid forum of law has already been exhausted and as such the order dated 08.07.2002 contained in Annexure-G to the writ petition for constitution of a committee for rehearing of appeal cases is beyond the scope of law. He then submits that similarly, the notice of hearing of the appeal cases as contained in Annexure-H dated 14.07.2002 having been issued in pursuance of an illegal order dated 08.07.2007 contained in Annexure-G has also been issued without lawful authority and as such the Rule Nisi should be made absolute. Learned Advocate for the petitioner, in support of his submissions, relied upon the decision in the case of Md. Aftab Ali Sheikh Vs. Director Land Records, Directorate of land records and surveys, Tejgaon, Dhaka and others, 11 MLR (HC) (2006) 226. 

 15. Be that as it may, Mr. Razik-Al-Jalil, learned Deputy Attorney General appearing of behalf the respondent Nos. l and 2, submits that under Rule 44,of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the director of land records and surveys has been vested with the powers to discharge all the functions of a revenue officer under Chapter XVII of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and, that he shall have all the powers of a settlement officer under Rules 36, 38, 39, 40, 41 and 42A and 42B of the Tenancy Rule, 1955 and that he may correct the fraudulent entry before final publication of record-of-rights under Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rule, 1955. 

 He further submits that since the record-of-rights has not yet been finally published, respondent No.2, may pass an order for necessary correction and as such, respondent No.2 has not committed any illegality in passing the impugned order and similarly, respondent No.3 has also not committed any illegality in issuing the impugned notice in consequence of the order passed by respondent No.2. 

 17. On a close perusal of the writ petition, it appears that respondent No.7 and others filed Objection Case Nos.4714 of 2000. 4715 of 2000 and 12903 of 2000 under rule 30 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Rule, 1955 against the Tasdik record of .1708 of ditch land in Plot No.57227 in the name of the petitioner and his mother, The Objection Officer after hearing both the parties and considering the relevant papers and documents filed by them rejected the objection cases by an order dated 08.11.2000, and the aforesaid facts are evident from Annexure-A and A 1 to the writ petition. 

 19. Respondent No.7 and others thereafter filed an application under Rule 42 of the said Rules before the Settlement-Officer who, on consideration of the contents made in the application, set aside the order passed under Rule-31 of the said Rule and formed a 5-.member committee (Appeal Board) for rehearing of the 3 appeal cases. The committee heard the parties, recorded their statements, considered their papers and documents, inspected the actual possession of the ditch land and recommended restoring the judgment and order dated 13.11.2001 passed by the Appeal Officer and sent the record of the case to the Settlement-Officer to pass the necessary order on the basis of recommendation made by the aforesaid Committee. 

 20. On receiving the record of the case, the Settlement-Officer scrutinized the entire proceeding and affirmed the judgment and order passed under Rule 31 in the said 3 appeal cases. Respondent No.7 and others again filed an application for reconsideration of the order passed in the said appeal cases before the Director (land records and survey), who sent the same to the Settlement-Officer, Dhaka requesting him to re-open the matter and decided the same afresh as per Rules. 

 21. It is seen from the record of the case that the Settlement-Officer delivered judgment in 3 appeal cases by exercising his powers and authority both under rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 after hearing of both the parties. 

 "30. Objection: Blank forms of objection shall be supplied free-of charge, and all objections shall as far as practicable, he made in such forms. Along with the original objection, the objector shall file a copy or copies of the same for service on all other persons who, in the opinion of the Revenue-Officer are materially interested in the case. The Revenue-Officer shall issue notice informing the objector and all other persons so interested of the date and place fixed for the hearing of the objection, and, with each notice to a person, other than the objector, he shall forward a copy of the objection. Objection regarding the ownership or possession of land or of any interest in land shall be decided summarily by the Revenue Officer. The record shall contain a brief summary of the evidence taken and an abstract of the reasons for the decision. Objections shall not be disposed of in the absence of any of the parties materially interested or their representatives, unless the Revenue-Officer be satisfied, for reasons to be recorded, in writing, that the notice was duly served on the person concerned. 

 (2) Before passing the final order on any such appeal, the Appellate Officer shall give the parties an opportunity of being heard and shall record in the proceedings an abstract of the reasons for his decision. 

 42. Special Power of Revenue-officer appointed with the additional designation of Settlement-Officer :- A revenue-officer appointed with the additional designation of 'Settlement-Officer' may, at any time before the publication of final record-of-right, direct that any portion of the proceedings referred to in rules 28 to 32 in respect of any district, part of a district, or local area shall be cancelled and that the proceedings shall be taken up fresh from such stage as he may direct. 

 42A. Correction of fraudulent entry before final publication of record-of-rights :- The Revenue-officer, with the additional designation of 'Settlement-Officer' shall, on receipt of an application or on receipt of an official report for the correction of an entry that has been procured by fraud in record-of-rights before final publication thereof, after consulting relevant records and making such other enquires as he deems necessary, direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act in doing so shall not be open to appeal. At the same time, the Revenue—officer shall make the correct entry after giving the parties concerned a hearing and recording his finding in a formal proceeding for the purpose of future reference. 

 42B. Correction of obvious clerical errors before final publication of record-of-rights :- The Revenue officer, with the additional designation of `Settlement-Officer' shall, have inherent jurisdiction to correct obvious errors e.g., arithmetical or clerical errors before final publication of the record-of-rights. The Settlement-Officer may delegate the said power to some other Revenue officer, with the additional designation of Assistant Settlement Officer, subordinate to him. 

 44. Powers vested in Director of Land Records and Surveys :- In respect of all operations under Chapter XVII of the Act which have been placed under the administrative control of the Director of Land Records and Surveys, East Pakistan, he may discharge all the functions of a Revenue-Officer under the said Chapter and shall have all the powers of a Settlement Officer under rules 36, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42A and 42B. 

 23. It is on record that on 17.06.2002, the Director (land records and surveys), respondent No.2 passed an order constituting a committee headed by respondent No.3 to hold a fresh hearing in respect of the aforesaid 3 appeal cases. In consequence of aforesaid order, a notice was issued directing the parties to appear before the committee for participating in hearing of appeal cases on 24.7.2004. 

 24. Before entering into the merit of the case, let us consider the power and authority of a Director (land records and surveys) as a Revenue-Officer.as contemplated in Rule 44 and Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. 

 25. Rule 44 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 provides that under chapter XVII of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, Director of land records and surveys has been vested with the power to discharge all the functions of a revenue officer who shall have the powers of a settlement officer under Rules 36, 38, 39, 40, 41 and 42B of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 including a power of direction under Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 to correct any entry that has been procured by fraud in the records-of-rights before final publication of the same. 

 26. From a bare reading of Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, it  appears that a revenue officer with the additional designation of settlement officer, on receipt of an application from the aggrieved person or an official report for correction of an entry that has been procured by fraud in the record of rights before final publication, may direct the correction of the fraudulent entry in the record-of-rights after giving the parties concerned a hearing to that effect. 

 27. In view of the propositions of law quoted above, the Director of land records and surveys is the administrative head of the department concerned, but he is not empowered either by any provision of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or by Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 to amend, correct, change, modify or set aside the judgment passed by the Settlement Officer in appeal cases under Rule 31 and 42 of East Bengal Tenancy Rules, 1955 unless there is an allegation of fraudulent entry procured by fraud in the record-of-rights. 

 29. Under the facts and circumstances of the case and the propositions of law, we have no hesitation in holding that since the appeal cases were decided by the settlement officer in exercise of his power under Rules 31 and 42 of the East Bengal and Tenancy Rules, 1955, there is hardly any scope for reopening the matter again by the Director as Settlement-Officer under Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 unless there is any entry procured by fraud in the record-of-rights before final publication of the same. 

 30. The aforesaid view finds support in the 4 decision in the case of Md. Altab Ali Sheikh Vs. Director Land Records, Directorate of Land Records and Survey and others, 11 MLR (HC) (2006) 226, wherein it has been spelt out as under : 

 "Director of Land Records and Survey has no authority to interfere with the judgment passed in appeal under Rule 31 except on the ground of fraud. Director of Land Records and Survey though is the administrative head of the department has no jurisdiction or power under rule 42A to 'amend or set aside judgment of the Settlement Officer passed in appeal under Rule 31 of East Bengal Tenancy Rules, 1955 except on ground of any entry in the record-of-rights obtained by fraud." 

 31. In view of above decision and discussion, it is clear that the judgment and order passed in appeal cases under Rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the same cannot be amended, modified, changed or set aside by the Director of Land Records and Survey under Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 unless there is an entry which was procured by fraud in the record-of-rights. Within the four corners of the writ petition and affidavit-in-opposition, we do not find that respondent No.7 has made out any case of fraudulent entry in the record-of-rights, and as such, we are of the view that since the Settlement-Officer has already exercised his power under Rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the Director of Land Records and Survey does not have the authority to interfere with the same in the absence of an allegation of fraudulent entry in the record-of-rights. 

 36. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the view that since the Settlement-Officer has already decided the appeal cases by exercising his power under Rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the Director of land records and surveys. respondent No.2 has no right and authority to constitute a committee to rehear the appeal cases afresh without having any allegation of fraud in the entry of record-of-rights and similarly, respondent No.3 has also no jurisdiction to issue the impugned notice in consequence of above-order as the constitution of a committee and issuance of notice thereof is beyond the scope of Rules as contemplated in the Tenancy Rules, 1955.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Md. Nazrul Islam Talukder

lawyer:
Azizur Rahman Chowdhury with Mohd Feroz and Md Abdul Mannan, Advocates — For the Appellant. 
Dewan AMS Zaman with Osman Gani, Advocates — For the Respondent.
parties:
Osmanullah being dead his legal heirs, Kasimullah & others ------ Plaintiff-Appellants
vs
Faizullah & others ------ Defendant-Respondent
full_judgment:
This Second Appeal at the instance of the plaintiff appellant is directed against the judgment and decree dated 30-4-1973 passed in Title Appeal No.122 of 1973 by Mr MA Wahab, Special Judge and ex-officio Additional District Judge, Sylhet reversing those dated 24-7-1972 passed in Title Suit No.166 of 1970 by he learned Munsif, 1st Court, Sylhet decreeing the suit on contest against defendant No.1 with cost and ex-parte against the rest without cost and declaring that the ex-parte order dated 14-11-1969 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 491/ 1969 under section 143A East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of the said Court for correction of the record of rights in respect of the suit-land is illegal, void., fraudulent and without jurisdiction. 

 3. The plaintiff later on by a petition got settlement of the suit-property up to 1376 BS from the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property and his petition for renewal of the lease was under consideration; that one Ahsanullah in the meantime filed a Miscellaneous Case No.413 of 1968 under section 143 A of the East Bangal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the plaintiff on his prayer was added as a party in the same under Order 1 rule 10 Code of Civil Procedure and then contested the Miscellaneous Case, but Ahsanullah later on withdrew the case and set up the principal defendant No.1 Faizullah to file another Miscellaneous Case No.419 of 1969 by fabricating some false documents and clandestinely secured an ex parte order on 14-11-69 for correction of the record of rights in his favour, though he has had no right title or possession in the said land; that no notice was served on the said Basanta Kumar Bhatta-charjee or his co-sharers. The plaintiff however came to know about the Miscellaneous Case No.491 of 1969 when defendant No.1 gave out in the locality towards the last part of March, 1970 that he had secured an order for correction of the record of rights in his favour in respect of the suit-land. Hence, the present suit against the defendant No. 1 and the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property, Sylhet as pro-forma defendant No.2. 

 4. The defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement wherein he contended, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable in its present form and it was barred by limitation. He, however denied the case of the plaintiff and stated that he took the jote settlement from Jogendra Kumar Bhattacharjee about 20 years back at a monthly rental of Rs 1.50 per Kedar and since then he had been possessing the suit-land and that during the last survey and settlement operation, the record of rights stood wrongly in the name of the aforesaid Ex-landlord. The defendant No.1 having failed to get the record of right correctly and amicably recorded in his name in the Khatian, filed the Miscellaneous Case No.491 of 1969 and got an ex parte order in his favour for correction of the record of rights and accordingly, the Khatian was modified;. that there was no suppression of notices as alleged in the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case; it was rather the plaintiff who in collusion with the lower rank staff of the Enemy Property Office, Sylhet filed this suit having no subsisting interest in the suit-land and as such, the suit was liable to be dismissed with cost. 

 6. The learned Munsif answered issue Nos.1 and 2 in favour of the plaintiff with the observation that the said issues were not pressed at the time of trial and that the impugned order was passed on 14-11-69 and the plaintiff filed this suit within time on 1-5-1970 and that there was nothing to show against the maintainability of the suit. As to issue No.3, the learned Munsif held that the service of notice upon the plaintiff-opposite party in the Miscellaneous Case No.491 of 1969 was fraudulently suppressed and that defendant No.1 committed fraud in obtaining the ex parte order in that Miscellaneous Case by suppression of facts and also notice and as such, the plaintiff was entitled to get the relief sought for in the suit. With the above findings and observations, the learned Munsif however decreed the suit on contest against the defendant No.1 with cost and ex parte against the rest without costs and further declared that the ex parte order dated 14-11-69 passed in Miscellaneous Case. No.491 of 1969 for correction of the record of rights in respect of the suit-land in favour of the defendant No.1 is void, illegal and without jurisdiction vide his judgment and decree dated 24-07-1972. 

 7. As against the said judgment and decree, the contesting defendant No.1 Faizullah preferred an appeal before the learned Special Judge and ex-officio Additional District Judge, Sylhet, who after hearing both the sides and on consideration of the materials on record was pleased to allow the appeal on contest and set aside the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif and consequently dismissed the suit on contest against defendant No.1 and ex parte against the rest by his judgment and decree dated 30-4-73. 

 10. Mr Azizur Rahman Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant has firstly submitted that the impugned judgment of the Court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal and as such the same should be set aside. To elaborate his argument, the learned Advocate has drawn my attention to the impugned judgment of the Court of appeal below as well as the judgment of the trial Court and then submitted that the trial Court as to the maintainability of the suit and bar of limitation held that the said issues were not pressed before him at the time of trial but still he came to a finding that by suppression of notices the impugned order in Miscellaneous Case No.491 of 1969 was passed on 14-11-69 and the instant suit was filed within time on 1-5-70. He also found that there was nothing to show against the maintainability of the suit; hence he answered the above two issues in favour of the plaintiff. But the lower Appellate Court heard the learned Advocate for the defendant-appellant on the point of maintainability of the suit and ultimately found that the plaintiff had no locus standi to institute the suit and the same was not also maintainable and hence allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned judgment and decree of the trial Court without making any finding as to the question of fraud as determined by the trial Court. It is further submitted by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the lower appellate Court did not at all reverse the findings of the trial Court on the question of fraud and also adverse possession, not to speak of adverting to the reasoning of the trial Court for coming to such findings. The learned Advocate for the appellant further submits that the plaintiff had subsisting interest and possession in the suit-land at the time of passing the order dated 14-11-1969 under section 143A East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act but he was not purposely made a party to the said proceeding. Of course, the original owner of the suit land Basanta Kumar Bhattacharjee and his co-sharer Ranadhir were made parties in that application for correction of the record of rights, but admittedly no notice was duly served upon them. The learned Advocate for the appellant therefore contends that the summons was suppressed by fraudulent means and the ex parte order was obtained surreptitiously. He however asserted that the plaintiff had locus-standi to file the present suit challenging the ex-parte order dated 14-11-1969 of the Miscellaneous Case, though he was not made a party in the same. He claimed his interest in the said property because of his caretaker ship of the interest of the said original owner Basanta Kumar Bhattacharjee, and further on his departure from this country to India, his property became enemy property and the plaintiff then took lease of the same from the Custodian of the Enemy Property by a regular document of lease dated 19-2-1970 and, as such, the plaintiff had every right to challenge the ex parte order passed in the Miscellaneous Case under section 143A of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by filing the present suit and the suit was therefore quite maintainable. 

 11. Mr Dewan AMS Zaman, the learned Advocate for the defendant-respondent, on the other hand, submits that the plaintiff had no locus-standi to institute the suit as he could not show his legal character under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act to be entitled to a declaration of his right, title and interest in the suit-land and a further declaration to the effect that the ex parte order dated 14-11-69 in Misc. Case under section 143A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was false, fraudulent and void ab-initio. The learned Advocate further argued that, it was of course the claim of the plaintiff that he was a lessee in the suit-land which was declared as Enemy Property and thus being a lessee in possession of the suit-land, he was competent to challenge the ex parte order of correction of the record of right in the suit-land by institution of the suit, but a lessee was not a necessary party in a suit like this wherein the lessor was already made a party. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate referred to a decision in the case of Saifuddin Ahmed vs Deputy Custodian, Enemy Property Management Board, reported in 31 DLR 107. He further contended that the suit could be maintainable, had there been a prayer for declaration of plaintiff''s right, title or interest in the suit land together with a prayer for consequential relief. It is further submitted that a suit for a mere declaration to the effect that the impugned ex parte order was false, fraudulent, void, ab-initio and not binding on the plaintiff was not maintainable. Hence that learned Special Judge and ex-officio District Judge rightly held that the plaintiff had no locus standi to institute the suit and the same was not maintainable. 

 12. The learned Advocate for the respondents, of course submitted that there was no finding by the lower appellate Court as to the question of alleged fraud committed in obtaining the ex parte order in the proceedings under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as found by the trial Court, but his contention was that this would not affect the merit of the decision of the lower appellate Court allowing the appeal and dismissing the suit on the ground of maintainability. As to the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant that the minimum requirements for passing the ex parte order dated 14-11-69 in the proceeding under section 143A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act were not complied with, apart from the fraudulent suppression of the process or notice and non-compliance of the provisions of inquiry as required under sub-section (4) of section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by local Revenue Officer in respect of possession of the parties over the land in question before passing such order. It is not clear whether the inquiry as required under the law was properly held in this case. The original records of the Miscellaneous Case are not available before this Court to verify the above contention regarding service of notices and the compliance of the provision of sub-section 4 of section 143A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 143A. (1) Any person aggrieved by an entry or omission of entry in record-of-rights prepared or revised and finally published under Chapter IV may, notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, file an application along with necessary requisites, for the purpose of correcting mistakes in such record-of-rights in the civil Court which would have jurisdiction to entertain a suit for possession of the land to which such entry relates or in respect of which such omission was made. 

 (c) the Court may allow such reasonable time as it may think fit to file objection to the inquiry report referred to in clause (b) and, if no appearance is made by the opposite party within the time mentioned in the notice, and, if no objection is filed to the inquiry report within the time so allowed, the Court may proceed ex parte with disposal of the application after taking into consideration the said report and other material evidence on record; and 

 (5) Any person whose interest has been affected by reason of any entry or omission in the record-of-rights, referred to in sub-section (1), may, within fourteen days of the filing of an application under sub-section (1), appear to be added as co-applicant. 

 (9) Where the Court passes an order under sub-section (4), or sub-section (7), revising the entries or rectifying the omission complained of under-section (1), it shall notify the same to the Collector and the Collector shall correct the record-of-rights accordingly. 

 (10) Any person interested may produce a certified copy of the orders referred to in sub-section (4) or sub-section (7) to the Revenue-Officer and the Revenue-Officer shall make such alterations in the record-of-rights as may be necessary to give effect to such orders. 

 (11) The record-of-rights corrected under sub-section (9) or sub-section (10), shall be deemed to have been prepared and finally published under Chapter IV of this Act. 

 "The Court may allow such reasonable time as it may think fit to file objection to the inquiry report referred to in clause (b) and, if there is no appearance made by the opposite party within the time mentioned in the notice, and if no objection is filed to the inquiry report within the time so allowed, the Court may proceed ex parte with disposal of the application after taking into consideration the said report and other materials on record; and then comes sub-section 4(d) which is as follows: 

 "Any person whose interest has been affected by reason of an entry or omission in the record-of-rights, referred to in sub-section (1), may within fourteen days of the filing of an application under sub-section (1), may appear to be added as co-applicant. 

 "(a) Where the Court passes an order under sub-section (4) or sub-section (7), reversing the entries or rectifying the omission complained of under sub-section (1), it shall be notified to correct the record-of-rights accordingly". 

 "Any person interested may produce a certified copy of the orders referred to in sub-section (4) or sub-section (7) to the Revenue-Officer and the Revenue-Officer shall make such alterations in the record-of-rights as may be necessary to give effect to such order" 

 "The record-of-rights corrected under sub-section (9) of sub-section (10) shall be deemed to have been prepared and finally published under Chapter IV of this Act. 

 18. Now, it may be pointed out that section 143A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is a special provision inserted in East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in 1965, of course the same has been repealed by another Ordinance No. LXIV of 1975. Its purposes was for correcting mistake in the record of rights on the basis of possession of the parties in the case land. However, the scope of section 143A has been discussed in a decision in the case of Assistant Custodiaiv Enemy Property (L&B) Tangail vs Bholanath Guha and ors reported in 36 DLR (AD) 79 and their Lordships have observed in the following terms therein, 

 "An application under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not a suit for declaration of title but is a proceeding for rectification of mistakes in the record of right prepared on the basis of possession in the land in question. The scheme of the section shows the possession is the material question. This was a special provision and this section was inserted after section 143 by East Pakistan. Ordinance VIII of 1965. It was however omitted after a few years by Ordinance LXIV of 1975". 

 "It is well settled that material consideration in a case under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is a question of possession. Whatever may be the defect in title, if it is found that the appellants have been possessing the case land when the record of right was prepared, they are entitled to have their names recorded." 

 From a reading of the above provisions of law and the decisions cited above it is clear that section 143A is meant for a limited purpose for correction of the record of right on the basis of possession of the parties in the case land. Now, the records of the Miscellaneous Case under section 143A are not before this Court. It was also not before the Courts below. Of course, the Courts below could very well call for the same to verify whether the main provisions of sub-section 4 of the said section 143A were complied with before passing the impugned order. The trial Court it appears decided the question wrongly against the contesting defendant mainly on a plea that was non-service of notice upon the opposite parties, i.e. Basanta Kumar and his co-sharer Ranadhir. It has been contended on behalf of the defendant-respondent that mere non-service of notice, cannot be termed as a practice of fraud and it has been further contended that in fact the notice was served upon the principal opposite party, that is the original owner the said Basanta Kumar Bhattacharjee, and in the evidence of both the parties, it has been stated that the suit-land solely belonged to said Basanta Kumar Bhattacharjee. Therefore the learned Advocate submits that there was no fraudulent suppression of notice upon the opposite party No. 1 Basanta Kumar Bhattacharjee as alleged in the Miscellaneous Case. The learned Advocate for the appellant, of course has submitted that it is in the evidence led by defendant No. 1 of the suit that a different address of the said Basanta Kumar Bhattacharjee was given in the application under section 143A from that where he was actually residing and admittedly no notice was served upon the other opposite party namely, Ranadhir. Therefore according to the learned Advocate for the appellant, this kind of non-service of notice constituted fraud and hence the impugned order passed in the miscellaneous case was a nullity in the eye of law. He has relied on a decision in the case of Abul Khair Mia vs Abdul Latif Sarder reported in 32 DLR (AD)167. Now, this question of fraud appears to have been decided by the trial Court in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendant, but the same has been left undiscussed and undecided by the Court of appeal below. The only questions which have been decided by the lower appellate Court are the questions of locus-standi of the plaintiff to institute the suit and its maintainability and those have been decided against the plaintiff-respondent and in favour of the contesting defendant-appellant in TA No. 122 of 1973 and accordingly the trial Court''s decision was found illegal and the same was set aside. Now, question has been raised by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the lower appellate Court erred in law in deciding the question of locus-standi of the plaintiff and maintainability of the suit, particularly when the question of possession of the parties in the suit land was not properly and conclusively decided by a clear finding by both the Court''s below. It is of course the case of the plaintiff-appellant that he had locus-standi to institute the suit as he had subsisting interest and possession in the suit-land on the basis of his alleged caretaker ship of the property and also the alleged lease taken from the Enemy Property Authority. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant contends that the plaintiff was a caretaker, since before the property was declared as enemy-property on the basis of some letters allegedly written to him by the said Basanta Kumar while serving in the Tea Estate in Sylhet in the years 1961-62 and 65 which were marked as Exts. 9 series. But when he left for India leaving his service, his property was declared as enemy property and the plaintiff took yearly lease of the same from the Enemy Property authority by executing a lease deed in the year 1970. He accordingly paid the salamis and got receipts thereof and thereafter he filed an application for renewal of the said lease and therefore: he claims to have locus-standi to institute the suit. 

 20. However for maintainability of the suit as contended there ought to have been a prayer for declaration of right, title and other consequential relief and for that purpose, the plaintiff could be given an option by the lower appellate Court to amend the plaint and incorporate such prayer for the purpose of the maintainability of the suit. Now, in the instant case, it appears that the plaintiff has come with his claims of interest and possession in the suit land at the relevant time on the basis of his caretaker ship of the suit-land, on behalf of the actual owner of the said land i.e. Basanta Kumar Bhattacharjee and to maintain the suit on that basis as I have said earlier that the determination of the question of possession of the parties over the land at the relevant time was very much material but evidence on the question of possession from both the sides appears to be very meagre and insufficient and further the record of the suit does not show as to whether there was an inquiry by the local revenue officer under sub-section 4(b) of the section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act with regard to the possession of the parties at the relevant time and that could be correctly ascertained only by calling for the records of the Miscellaneous case under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and in this respect both the Courts failed to apply their judicial mind and to determine the question of actual possession of the parties in the suit-land at the relevant time. The learned Advocate for the defendant-respondent however raised some question with regard to the lease deed Exhibit 1 which shows that it was granted for one year that is for 1373 BS. But the receipt shows the granting of lease for the period of 4 years at a time which is not permissible in law. Of course, it appears that after 1376, the plaintiff filed an application for renewal of the said lease but nothing available on the record whether such renewal was at all granted. 

 25. Therefore, in this respect, I think there is no bar in the institution of the suit on the ground of fraud without availing of the provision for appeal under the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The plaintiff is however required to establish his locus-standi and the maintainability of the suit. Having considered all aspects of the matter and the relevant provisions of law and the decisions cited above by the parties before me, I am of the view that the lower appellate Court committed gross illegality in determining the question of locus-standi of the plaintiff and maintainability of the suit without coming to a positive finding as to possession of the parties over the suit-land at the relevant time i.e. in 1969 when the application under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was filed in the Court of the learned Munsif for correction of record-of-rights and thereafter when the suit was instituted. At the same time, it is not at all proper for the lower appellate Court to avoid coming to a finding as to the question of fraud on discussion of the materials on record although the trial Court came to such a finding in clear terms. Therefore, the judgment of the Court of appeal below is not at all a proper judgment of reversal and the same is liable to be set aside. 

 In the result, this appeal is allowed and the impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below are set aside and the appeal is sent back on remand to the Court of the learned Additional District Judge and Special Judge for re-hearing and determining the material points as have been pointed out, on the basis of the materials on record and, if necessary, to take further additional evidence from both the sides and particularly with regard to the inquiry report of the revenue officer, if any, of the local. Circle Office, Revenue, concerned and compliance of the provisions of sub-section 4 of section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and for that purpose, if necessary, the records of that Miscellaneous Case under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act may be called for and on consideration thereof to dispose of the appeal by a proper judgment in accordance with law in light of the observations made above. In the facts and circumstances of the case, there will be no order as to costs in this second appeal. The learned Advocate for the appellants is permitted to take back his application for additional grounds in view of the above decision.

full_judgment:
2. The appellant as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 984 of 2014 on 28-10-2014 before the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka, for declaration of title and declaration that the present revisional record of rights are wrong and for staying the proceeding of Miscellaneous Case Nos. 97 of 2014 and 115 of 2014, pending before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Gulshan Circle, Dhaka, the defendant-respondent No. 10. 

 3. Plaintiff's case as stated in the plaint in short, is that, 164 decimals land of CS Plot No. 130 under CS Khatian No. 13 originally belonged to Jamir Bhuiyan, Kadam Bhuiyan and Jabu in 4 annas share each and Sayed Bhuiyan and Hayed Bhuiyan in 2 annas share each and CS, SA and RS record of rights were duly prepared. Sayed Bhuiyan while in possession of his 21.05 decimals of land also purchased 20.5 decimals from Abu Bhuiyan, son of CS tenant Jamir Bhuiyan and 5 decimals from another co-sharer Hayed Bhuiyan by registered kabala dated 16-3-1944 and thus became owner of total 47 decimals. Sayed Bhuiyan sold 17.5 decimals and 24.75 decimals by two registered kabalas dated 26-2-1964 and 27-1-1967 respectively and 4.75 decimals remained with him. Sayed Bhuiyan died leaving behind 3 sons namely Asan Uddin, Basir Uddin alias Kerali and Rustom Ali and a daughter Saleman Nessa. Rustom Ali sold his entire share to his brother Asan Uddin by registered kabala dated 26-10-1978. Asan Uddin also purchased 16 decimals, 20 decimals and 17 decimals from his co-sharers by three separate registered deeds dated 7-2-1973, 5-7-1986 and 25-7-1996 respectively. By that way Asan Uddin became the owner of total 63.10 decimals of land by way of inheritance and purchase. Asan Uddin died leaving behind 6 sons namely Miaz Uddin, Yar Uddin, Saiz Uddin, Taiz Uddin, Azim Udin and Laiz Uddin. Thereafter they sold the suit land to Saidur Rahman Dipu and Mafizul Islam by registered Kabala dated 8-11-2009 who subsequently sold the suit land to the plaintiff through their constituted attorney by registered kabala dated 25-7-2010. 

 7. The defendant Nos. 1-9 filed written statement on 9-6-2015 and also filed written objection against the prayer for temporary injunction on the same date on stating that the plaintiff on creating false documents trying to grab the suit land and also got the mutation of the record of rights beyond the knowledge of the defendants. The present City Khatian also stood in the name of the defendant Nos. 1-9 concerning 1864 decimals of land against which the plaintiff's vendors filed Land Survey Case No. 1111 of 2008 before the Land Survey Tribunal, Dhaka against the defendants, which is still pending. 

 15. It appears from the prayer of the plaint that the plaintiff not only prayed for declaration of title; but, also prayed for further declaration regarding the revisional record of rights and proceedings of Miscellaneous Case Nos. 97 of 2014 and 115 of 2014. 

 16. It appears that the contesting defendants filed an application before the Trial Court for rejection of plaint and the said application has been rejected by the Trial Court on 15-9-2015 and the defendants till today did not challenge the said order. It is settled principle of law that the record of rights are not a document of title and it is always subject to the result of a civil suit, where title is disputed. The revenue authority is bound to give effect of the ultimate decision of the civil court concerning any record of rights. In our view proceeding of a mutation case or a case concerning correction or cancellation of a record of rights will be a futile exercise, while a civil suit is pending concerning the land of that record of rights in between the parties thereto. 

 "Whether the order for enquiry was made before the issuance of the Rule Nisi or thereafter, it was absolutely improper on the part of the learned Advocate for the Writ petitioner-Respondents to pray for postponement of hearing "in order to afford the Government an opportunity of settling the dispute", nor do we think it was proper for the Court to allow the Government "to decide the matter according to law" when the Court itself was in scission of the matter to do exactly the same. The Government is within its rights to conduct any number of internal inquiries into the disputed question of settlement, but as long as the legality or illegality of settlement is before the Court, the Government has no power to decide the issue this way or that way. It is for the Court to decide the matter. The Court cannot simply abandon its judicial responsibility in favour of the Government. It was open to the Writ-Petitioners to withdraw the writ petition and submit themselves to the jurisdiction of the Government, but it was not open to them to keep the writ petition pending and allow the Government to "decide the matter according to law". In other words, the Writ petitioners cannot pursue two remedies at the same time, one at the Governmental level and the other in a Court of law, more so in the constitutional jurisdiction. The High Court Division also misjudge the submission of the learned Advocate for the Writ Petitioners and should not have acceded to his prayers." 

 21. We have gone through the section 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The revenue authority cannot decide the title of the respective parties and it is only the civil court which can decide so and from that point of view section 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not restricting power of a civil court in deciding title which will be reflected in the record of rights. Similarly section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 is also subject to decision of title by a civil Court. 

 "the recent record of right would prevail inasmuch as presumption attached to the State Acquisition record of right." 

 "On reading provision of section 143 of the Act and the Rule 23(4) of the Tenancy Rule, 1955 we are of the view that the Revenue Officer in the facts and circumstances of the instant case in cancelling the mutation obtained by the plaintiff in respect of the land in suit was quite legal. It may be mentioned plaintiff got his name mutated upon sticking out name of Bipin Chandra who said to have acquired the land in suit by settlement from landlords, but in support of claim of settlement no evidence was brought on record. As stated hereinbefore the appellate Court set aside the judgment of the trial Court which dismissed the suit, primarily on the ground that revenue authority had no jurisdiction to correct the record of rights by cancelling the mutation earlier made in the name of the plaintiff on the view that the correction so made affected the right, title and interest of the person whose name was entered in the record of right upon mutation. In view of the provision of section 143 of the Act and the Rule 23(4) of the Tenancy Rule, 1955 in our opinion the appellate Court was in serious error in setting aside the judgment of the trial Court on the view that the revenue officer had no jurisdiction to correct the record of rights prepared upon mutation in the name of the plaintiff." 

 26. On going through the decisions cited by both the learned advocates for both sides it appears that none of the decision directly related with the issue before us. In the present case the only question before this Court is whether a civil court can stay the proceeding concerning record of rights pending before the revenue authority i.e. the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Gulshan Circle, Dhaka by way of temporary injunction. In a suit for declaration of title the civil court can decide both title and possession while the revenue authority only authorized to deal with the record of rights regarding amalgamation subdivision and consolidation of holdings as provided in Chapter XV of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. All the record of rights concerning which any dispute arise shall subject to decision regarding title by a civil Court apart from amalgamation, subdivision and consolidation of holdings as provided in Chapter XV of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. In view of section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the revenue officer is bound to carry on the final order or decree as passed by a civil court. This proposition has been settled in the case of Abdul Moin vs Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land, Secretariat Building, reported in 53 DLR 506, wherein a Division Bench of the High Court Division held that, 

 "When the matter was subsequently brought before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) he was required in law to decide the matter either giving a decision instead of forwarding the same to the Ministry of Land by giving unwarranted and illegal observations. Since the question of title and possession have been settled by the highest Court of the country the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) had, in fact, no option in law but to mutate the name of the petitioner by correcting the record of right. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) not only acted without jurisdiction in sending the matter to the Ministry of Land without deciding the matter himself with untenable observations but also did so in colourable exercise of his official power. The impugned order dated 3-6-1998 passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Sylhet is therefore declared to have been passed without any lawful authority." 

 28. Upon considering the respective cases and the laws and decisions as stated above we are of the view that the civil court can restrain parties from proceeding with any case pending before a revenue authority. The mutation of record of rights does not confer any right title and interest over the concerned land, mores, where there is dispute regarding title, Revenue authority should await till the result of the same by the civil Court. The proceeding before the Revenue authority if not maintain status-quo, then multiplicity of proceedings and conflicting decisions may arise and the proceedings of civil Court should be given precedent then the Revenue proceedings. In the present case though the application filed by the plaintiff-appellant for temporary injunction and stay is to some extend defective inasmuch as they could pray for restraining the defendant No. 10 from proceedings with the mutation proceedings instead of praying an order of stay. However, this is mere a technical defect which cannot disentitle the plaintiff from getting a substantial order.

full_judgment:
2. The short facts of the above mentioned Other Class Suits, in short, are that one Syed Jamshed Hussain Choudhury instituted Other Class Suit No.198 of 1996 before the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Iswardi Upazila, Pabna for declaration of title over the suit property and also observations were made in L.S. Miscellaneous Case No. 11 of 1996 are void, illegal and without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiff. On the other hand the Managing Committee of Marami Joykalimata Thakurani Bighraha instituted Other Class Suit No. 46 of 1999 before the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Pabna impleading Syed Jamshed Hussain Choudhury and others as defendants for declaration of title over the suit property. Thereafter the learned District Judge, Pabna vide Miscellaneous Case No.14 of 1999 transferred the Other Class Suit No.198 of 1996 to the Court of the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Pabna for analogous hearing with Other Class Suit No. 46 of 1999. Eventually on transfer the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Pabna received the suit records and re-numbered the same as Other Class Suit Nos. 8 and 9 of 2003, respectively. 

 3. The plaint case of Other Class Suit No. 8 of 2003, in short, is that Ka Schedule land of Mouza Marami appertaining to D.S. Khatian No. 248 Plot No. 31 measuring 11.02 acres of land, Plot No. 321 measuring 42 decimals of land, Plot No. 337 measuring 18 decimals in total lands are 11.62 acres originally belonged to Joykalimata Thakurani Bighraha as lakheraj of which Kumar Birendra Nath Roy Bahadur was the Shebat of the Joykalimata Thakurani Bighraha. At the time of C.S. operation the record of right finally was published in the name of Joykalimata Thakurani Bighraha showing Kumar Birendra Nath Roy Bahadur as Shebait of Joykalimata Thakurani. 

 5. Paresh Narayan Choudhury died leaving behind 2 sons, Pronab Narayan Choudhury and Pobitra.Narayan Choudhury and widow Shushayna Debi. The heirs of Paresh Narayan Choudhury started a rent case being Rent Case No.551 of 1956 under Section 48 of the B.T. Act against the Naser Hossain for realization of arrear rents. The suit was contested by Md. Nesar Hossain which was decreed in terms of compromise. Decree Execution Case No 8 of 1957 was started and Nesar Hossain Chowdhury paid total rent of the suit property through chalan dated 26.3.1957 and 9.4.1957. The Collector of Pabna District for realization of rent started a Revenue Sale Case being No.12662 of 1958 for 'Ka' Schedule land wherein Nesar Hossain contested the case and filed an application to recognize him as a tenant. Since Nesar Hossain was in possession of the property by purchase, the Collector of Pabna District by his order dated 27.4.1962 exonerated Nesar Hossain from the responsibility of rent on considering his prayer and the suit property was released in his favour. Nesar Hossain at the time of S.A. settlement recorded his name as per his documents, however, due to conspiracy of some unscrupulous employees of the settlement department `Ka' and Kha Schedule lands were wrongly recorded as a result PRR Khatian Nos. 249(ka) and 257/2 were published in the name of landlords, Pronab Naryan Choudhury and Pobitra Narayan Choudhury. However, both the schedules land at the time of final publication of S.A. record neither recorded in the name of Nesar Hossain, Pronab Narayan Choudhury and Pobitra Narayan Choudhury, nor in the name of the Government. Therefore, there was no record of 'Ka' and 'Kha' Schedules land, Md.Nesar Hossain while learn to know about the facts of the record of Ka and Kha Schedule lands filed an application under Section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (SA&T) before the Joint Deputy Commissioner, Revenue Court, which was registered being Case No. 35/1964-65. The Joint Deputy Commissioner, Revenue, Pabna on receipt of the case records ordered to inquire into the matter and to submit a report by the then S.D.O., Pabna Sadar, Pabna by 17.6.1965. The SDO, Pabna Sadar submitted the report stating that Nesar Hossain has right and title over the Ka and Kha Schedules land. In that report it was also pointed out that Ka and Kha Schedule lands neither acquired, nor it was recorded in the Khas Khatian No.1 in the name of the Government. In that report the SDO, Pabna also recommended to settle the same in favour of Md.Nesar Hossain as tenant recognizing his documents and possession. Thereafter, the Joint Deputy Commissioner, Pabna after final hearing on 30.6.1965 under the provisions of SA&T Act recognized Nesar Hossain as tenant of Ka and Kha Schedule lands and ordered to open and prepare a Khatian in his name for realization of rent. Accordingly S.A. Khatian No. 257 was opened in the name Nesar Hossain and in the year 1363 B.S. Nesar Hossain paid rent in favour of the Government and obtained rent receipts. 

 6. The plaintiff on 28.8.1965 purchased the suit property from Nesar Hossain and mutated his name with the government arid office vide Mutation Case No. 245 of 1966- 67 and paid rent and taxes to the government. The holding No. 306 was in the name of the plaintiff and lastly in the year 1399 B.S. the plaintiff paid rent to the Government. After obtaining the suit property at the time of R.S. record of right as per title and possession the record of right was correctly prepared and finally published in the name of the plaintiff. The suit property of previous Plot Nos. 319, 318, 321, 337, 366 and 334 were converted into R.S. Plot Nos. 635, 334, 573, 574, 579 and 575. After publication of the final R.S record of right the plaintiff also paid rent and land development tax to the government and obtained rent receipts and Dhakhilas. The plaintiff denying the right and title of others for more than 31 years peacefully, overtly and without any disturbance from any quater had been owning and possessing the suit property. One Shamsul Alam Dewan only for illegal gain filed an application to the Government for settlement of the aforesaid land treating the suit property as Khash land and the said application was numbered being Miscellaneous Case No. 101 of 80-81. In view of the above application the A.D.C (Rev.), Pabna directed the C.O. (Rev), Iswardi for physical inquiry and after inquiry to submit a report to him. The C.O. (Rev), Iswardi inquired the matter physically and examined the documents of the Tahshil Office including the case diary and Petition Case No. 35 of 1964-65 started before the Joint Deputy Commissioner (Rev), Pabna, who ordered to transfer the property to the new Khatian No. 257 in the name of Naser Hossain who also mutated the property vide the Mutation Case No. 245 of 1966-67, from which it was evident that the plaintiff was the owner of the property. After mutation of the suit property in the name of the plaintiff, he paid rent and development taxes up to 1987. After obtaining the inquiry report from C.O. (Rev), Iswardi, Pabna the A.D.C (Rev), Pabna found the plaintiff is the owner of the suit property and by his order dated 23.6.1981 directed Shamsul Alam Dewan to take the matter to the Civil Court, if he has any grievance, and thereby rejected the application. Thereafter said Shamsul Alam Dewan again filed an application before the A.D.C (Rev) for review of the earlier order dated 23.6.1981, who after hearing the parties and obtaining legal opinion from the Government Pleader, on perusal of the C.S., S.A. and R.S record of rights by his order dated 24.12.1982 rejected the review application on contest. The Revenue Officer of the government recognized the plaintiff as tenant and vendor of the plaintiff Naser Hossain as tenant and also realised the rent from 1363 B.S to 1399 B.S vide Mutation Case No. 35 of 1964-65 L.A. The concerned authority has rejected the Miscellaneous Case No. 101 of 1980-81 and Case No. 1261 of 1948, confirming the result in favour of the plaintiff, therefore the defendant No. 1 has no right, title and possession over the suit property save and except the authority of realization of rent and development taxes from the plaintiff. The plaintiff's further case is that there is no aboriginal in the Marami Mouza of Pabna District, however, some native Christians have been living in the locality near the suit property and only to illegally grab the suit property illegally formed a committee under the leadership of one Filip Somaddar @ Khokon, who used to live in Pabna town and lodged a petition of complaint to the Secretary, Ministry of Land alleging that some local people fraudulently and illegally possessing the property of the aboriginal people. Therefore, the Secretary, Ministry of Land directed the defendant No. 3 to inquire into the matter. The Tahshilder of Dasuriya Union office after getting the direction from the defendant No. 3 started the inquiry secretly and after ex parte inquiry submitted a report to the defendant No. 3 and allegedly recommended for taking steps regarding the suit property that to make a trust for the benefit of the local people treating the suit properties of the government Khash land. On getting the inquiry report the defendant No. 3 A.D.C. (Rev), Pabna most illegally and without lawful authority started a proceeding vide L.S. Miscellaneous Case No. 11 of 1996 showing Government of Bangladesh as plaintiff and the present plaintiff of the instant suit as defendant and served a notice upon the plaintiff of this suit directing him to produce the papers and documents including orders of all Mutation Cases. The plaintiff after getting the notice of L.S. Miscellaneous Case No. 11 of 1996 on 11.12.1996 appeared before the defendant No. 3 and prayed for time to file written statement. However, defendant No. 3 fixed the next date of the case on 18.12.1996 for filling written statement. On I 8.12.1986 plaintiff further prayed for time stating the reasons that due to shortage of time he was unable to procure all the documents to file the written statement while the lawyer of the plaintiff was awaiting for moving the application, the concerned personal officer of the A.D.C (Rev) informed the plaintiffs lawyer to move the application at 4 p.m. The learned lawyer of the plaintiff when rushed to the office of the A.D.C (Rev) at 4 p.m. for moving the application the concerned Bench Assistant informed the lawyer that defendant No. 3 suddenly at about 3 p.m. came to the office and took the only record of L.S. Miscellaneous Case No. 11 of 1996 and rejected the application of the plaintiff and fixed for order on 12.12.1996. Thereafter on the next date the plaintiff also prayed for time but the defendant No.3 without passing any order fixed the case on 22.12.1996 for order. The plaintiff filed a written statement on 22.12.1996 and fixed the case on 26.12.96 for order. The plaintiffs lawyer although placed the case before defendant No. 3 but he did not take any note rather from the behavior posed by him in the Court the plaintiff understood that the defendant No. 3 is biased. Then the plaintiff filed an application before the Secretary, Ministry of Land stating his apprehension that he will not get fair justice from defendant No. 3 and in view of the application the Secretary, Ministry of. Land directed the Divisional Commissioner, Rajshahi to inquire into the matter and submit the report and in the meantime he stayed all further proceedings of L.S Miscellaneous Case No. 11 of 1996. The defendant No. 3 although got the fax massage from the Ministry of land to stay the all further proceedings of L.S. Miscellaneous Case No. 11 of 1996 but most illegally only for getting benefit without staying the Case, on 29.12.1996 by a perfunctory report sent the case record to the Deputy Commissioner for order. The defendant No. 3 in his report made some observations which are beyond the report and also opined that Mutation Case No. 35 of 1964-65 and L.S. Miscellaneous Case No. 101 of 1980-81 and judgment and decree passed by Munsif, Court, Pabna in Suit No. 551 of 1956 is fraudulent and concocted one and farther opined that deed of the plaintiff and his vendor, power of attorney and Kabuliyat all are fraud and forged. Further opined that the order passed in L.S. Miscellaneous Case No. 101 of 1980-81 is fraud, fraudulent and concocted and the suit property is the Khash land. 

 "Ka" schedule land as described in the schedule of the suit along with others property was rightly recorded as Lakharaj property of Joykali Bigraha in D.S. khatian No. 248, Kumar Birendra Nath Roy Bahadur of Natore was the Shebait of Joykali Bigraha whose name was recorded as Shebait in the C.S. record of right. However, Emperor of India was the superior landlord of the suit property. The C.S. Khatian No. 247 of No. 12 Haludchar Mouza under Natore P.S. of District-Rajshahi was also recorded as 'niskar' where in total 30.69 acres of land was in 8 Plots previous Plot No. 314 of Khatian No. 248 measuring .05 acres of land was Halot for the use of general people. Plot No. 316 of the said Khatian measuring 0.53 acres of land was unused land wherein there was a temple in 03 acres of land. Plot No. 318 of the aforesaid Khatian and Mouza also 11.02 acres of land as Debuttar pond on the said Plot. 0.42 acres of land was a jungle. Plot No. 337 was also a Halot which was used for general public. In Plot No. 317 the 1.32 acres of land was a garden. Before the time of C.S record there was a temple of Joykalimata Bigrah, which are very old temple of the locality. Many worshippers perform their worship duties and thereafter they left the portrait of Bigraha in the ponds water. The worshippers of the temple used to come from others locality and use the water of pond from the time of establishment of the temple. The water of the ponds also used for performing Puja Archana of the Bigrah. Besides it aboriginals resided on the bank of the pond also use the pond's water for their personal purpose. There is a pathway adjacent to the temple which went away towards the village, which was developed by the government. The local aboriginal also cultivate the land of Plot Nos. 316, 321, 337 and 317. They also spent the usufruct of the properties for Puja of the Bigraha. The Pond's name is Marami and the aboriginal people use the same. The aboriginal use their local language although there is no words and letters in writing to write the language of the aboriginal, however, they tried to use the same only in their verbal language. The life style and culture of the aboriginal peoples recognize their cultural heritage. The government of erstwhile East Pakistan published Dacca Gazette in 1963 and 1964 recognizing them as aboriginal peoples and got facilities of Section 97 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and became the tenants under the government. Some of them came from Rajshahi area and settled there. Although some got the landed property, however, their properties were not saved from the hand of some local greedy persons. Some people also left the locality due to disterbance of the local people. Very recent master Shamol, a student of Class-V was killed by some miscreants which is the glaring instance of torture by the local peoples upon the aboriginal peoples.
