Therefore, the trial Court ought to have dismissed the suit, rather decreed the same, as such, acted in violation of the provision of law, and as such, committed miscarriage of justice. He referring the cross-examination of D.W.1 submitted that the native village and home District of D.W.1 is not in the District of the suit property, rather he has admitted that his home District is Netrakona and all relative of the D.W.1 have been residing in the District of Netrakona. In cross-examination he further admitted that he is now residing in the District Town, Pabna in a rented house. So, it is crystal clear from the reply of his cross-examination that he is not living within the vicinity of the aforesaid temple or the suit property. Therefore, constituting a Managing Committee by such person not only got up case but also mala fide with a clear mala fide intention to grab the suit property. He referred the cross-examination and pointed that in his cross-examination admitted that the temple is situated within .03 decimals of land, he cannot told anything about to creation and building of the temple. He also admitted that the wall of the temple is no more and the temple was not renovated, since it is established. He could not tell the name of the fisherman who rear and catch the fish from the pond. He categorically in his cross-examination admitted that he has no personal knowledge about Kumar Birendra Nath Roy Bahadur, the Kabuliyat in question, Nesar Hossain, Shishir Kumar Roy and D.S record. He further admitted that he cannot say who was the Borgader of Nesar Hossain and what remarks were written in the D.S. record of rights. He further admitted that he has no idea about the Rent Case No.551/1956. 

 26. We have gone through the plaints, written statements, evidence on record and perused the impugned judgment and also anxiously considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of the respective parties. 

 27. On perusal of the impugned judgment, materials on record and from the submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellant it is clearly manifested that the trial Court in deciding said the two Other Suits came to a conclusion that in respect of Kha and Ga schedule lands of Title Suit No. 8 of 2003 none of the defendants neither denied the plaintiff's right, title and possession nor adduced any evidence claiming the aforesaid land, rather the government and other defendants claimed the Ka schedule land but the plaintiff also claimed the title of the same including Kha and Ga schedule land in Title Suit No. 8 of 2003. Therefore, in the impugned judgment the trial Court opined that there are no necessities to discuss about the right and title of the Kha and Ga schedule lands. Accordingly he did not discuss regarding the right and title of the Kha and Ga schedule lands in the impugned judgment as defendants did not denied the same. Therefore, according to Mr. Siddique the trial Court admittedly found the right, title and possession of the plaintiff's in Kha and Ga schedule lands thus dismissing the suit so far it relates to Kha and Ga schedule land not in accordance with law. The Court below ought to have discussed about right and title about these properties. However, we shall discussed the matter later in this judgment. 

 28. Admittedly the. Emperor of India was original owner who settled the Ka schedule property in favour of Moharaj Birendra Kumar Roy Bhahadur as landlord. It transpires from the materials on record that Moharaj Kumar Birendra Nath Roy Bahadur dedicated the same in favour of the deity permanently. D.S. record of right was finally published in the name of deity treating the same as Lakheraj and showing Kumar Birendra Nath Roy Bahadur as Shebait. Since then Ka schedule property belonged to deity. The plaintiff by producing a Kabuliyat dated 29.11.1943 claimed that the property including Ka schedule and other land had been given Pattan in favour of Paresh Narayan Choudhury who executed the Kabuliyat. In the recital of Kabuliyat it was clearly inscribed that the property belonged to deity Sree Sree Joykalimata Thakurani and Shebait had given Pattan the same for legal necessity. 

 29. Now, the 1st legal issue is as to whether a Shebait can transfer any property of deity permanently or give Pattan year to year basis. The plaintiff in his plaint admitted that Ka schedule property was the property of deity Joykalimata Thakurani. He further admitted that D.S. record of right was correctly published in the name of deity showing Kumar Birendra Nath Roy Bahadur as Shebait. According to him Paresh Narayan Choudhury took Pattan by executing Kabuliyat in favour of Kumark Birendra Nath Roy Bahadur by registered Kabuliyat dated 29:11.1943 which is Ext.3. On perusal of Ext.3 it transpires that it is an unilateral Kabuliyat without supporting any Patta or Dakhila issued by the Shebait as representative of the deity. From the practice and customs at that time without Patta and Dakhila unilateral Kabuliyat is not a acceptable document in the eye of law in respect of settlement of any property by the landlord in favour of Raiyat far away to accept the same from a Shebait of a deity. Moreso, it is pertinent to mention that nothing is found in the recital of the Kabuliyat that the property in question was settled by the Shebait for the legal necessity of the Deity. The plaintiff has claimed the title of the "Ka" schedule suit land in question through his vendor Nesar Hossain who purportedly got the same from Paresh Narayan Chowdhury who also got the same by executing a Kabuliyat in favour of the Shebait of Deity namely Birendra Kumar Nath Roy Bahadur. On perusal of the recital of the Kabuliyat in question, it divulged that the executent of Kabuliyat not only included the property of Deity but also included the land property wherein temple is situated. Accordingly the Poresh Narayan and Nesar Hossain the vendors of the plaintiff also transferred the same property to the plaintiff without any correction or rectification. But it is very interesting that the plaintiff although claimed the property through the aforementioned deed exhibit 16 dated 28.8.1965 and the Kabuliyat in question exhibit-3 but in the plaint and in his testimonies P.W. 1 stand corrected the recital of the Kabuliyat and deed in question stating that 03 decimals land wherein temple is situated never settled in favour of the vendor of the plaintiff. According to the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act landlord can settle any property to Raiyat and Raiyat can settle the property to under Raiyat, but nowhere in the Act there is a provision that Shebait of Deity can settle the Debuttar property to any Raiyat giving right of transper as per provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Moreso, property in question surely belonged to Deity not Shebait, so he is not landlord although has got some responsibility only to look after the property as managerial capacity. Therefore, we are of the view that the claim of settlement in favour of Paresh Narayan Choudhury through unileteral kabuliyat and so on Paresh Narayan Choudhury to Nesar Hossain and to the plaintiff was nothing but a paper transaction without any legal sanction, recognition and basis of title. It is a settled maxim of law that without proving his title deed in accordance with law, by filing some secondary evidence none can claim any title by dint of secondary evidence which are inadmissible in law. The doccuments in question neither produced in original nor proved in accordance with law. Some other private documents were exhibited in violation of provisions of section 63, 64, 65, 66, and 67 of the Evidence Act, a party producing such documents is not relieved of the duty of proving the execution. Even those documents exhibited in trial but the court is to be satisfied as to its execution. 

 30. The plaintiff by producing some copies of Rent Suit Rent Execution Case and Dakhilas in the name of Nesar Hossain issued by Paresh Narayan Choudhury showing Paresh Narayan Chowdhury as Jotddar and decree-holder, which were obtained on compromise basis by Nesar Hossain and also got the property through Rent Suit all were in pursuance of Kabuliyat dated 29.11.1943, however, those papers were not proved by examining the executant scribe or attesting witnesses. Therefore the legality of those documents is not only questionable but highly doubtful. We have already opined that Kabuliyat exhibit 3 was without any legal sanction, thus, subsequent transaction cannot be treated as proper and genuine and as such, the same cannot be sustained in law. After appreciating the recital of power of attorney and deed in question executed in the favour of the plaintiff it reveals that there is no schedule of land in the power of attorney, not only that on further scrutiny it is portrait from the power of attorney wherein 5 (five) persons including the plaintiff, were the Attornies of Nesar Hossain but deed was executed in the name of plaintiff by one of the attorney, namely, Susil in the name of another Attorney, no reason has been disclosed in the deed in question which not only cast and create cloud but also depict serious doubt about the genuinty and execution of the deed exhibit 16. Moreso, it is clearly found from the materials on record that the property of Kha schedule land was purchased by Sushama, wife of Paresh but the power of attorney exhibit 28 in question was not appointed and executed by Sushama but Poresh. In view of the legal proposition as discussed above the purchase of the plaintiff from the Attorney of Naser Hossain through a power of attorney is of no avail. Therefore, we without any hesitation can conclude that the transfer of the suit land described in schedules in favour of Nesar Hossain and thereafter to the plaintiff without any legal sanction and basis of title deed. In such circumstances, we have failed to discover any materials justifying to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree but to hold that the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court in title suit No. 8 of 2003 is not tainted with legal infirmity and perversity. 

 31. Mr. Siddique very humbly and candidly has submitted that after enactment of the state Acquisition and Tenancy Act Paresh Narayan Chowdhury and Nesar Hossain by operation of Law they became tenants under the Government and as such, the plaintiff through his vendors became the tenant under the Government. Now Government cannot deny the title, possession and record of rights which stand in the name of the plaintiff. To examine and consider the above mentioned legal proposition we have meticulously examined the various provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. On scrutiny the provisions of law it appears that most important feature of the suit land must be discussed which comes into effect after insertion of Section 10A in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. For the reference and convenience of discussion we may quote the Section 10A of the said Act, which runs as follows. 

 (4) the tenants referred to in sub- section (3) shall, in respect of the lands held by them subject to the payment of rents immediately before acquisition, be liable to pay rents in respect of such lands at the rates determined in the record of rights finally published under sub-section (3) of section 19, subject to modification under section 53: 

 Provided that pending such final publication of the record of rights, the tenants shall pay rents for such lands at the rates shown in the preliminary rent rolls prepared under the rules made under Chapter IV and in cases where such preliminary rent rolls also have not been prepared, the tenants shall pay rents at the rate existing immediately before acquisition till such preliminary rent-rolls are prepared: 

 Provided further that when any such rent is shown either at an enhanced or at reduced rate in the record of rights finally published under sub-section (3) of section 19 or when any such rent is enhanced or reduced under section 53, the tenant shall be liable to pay the balance or entitled to the adjustment of excess payment against future rent payable by him, as the case may be, with retrospective effect. 

 32. According to the provisions of Section 10A of the said Act it is found that all Debuttar property must he managed, controlled and maintained in accordance with the aforementioned provisions of law. Here we must express our view that the 'Ka' schedule suit property of the present case admittedly was/is a Debuttar property since its inception which was correctly recorded in the name of Deity at the time of preparation of D.S. record of rights during the colonial regime of British showing Kumar Birendra Nath Roy Bahadur as Shebait who was the donor of the property. It further appears from the pleadings of the suit, from the recital of exhibit 3 and deposition of P.W.1 herein he admitted that Ka schedule land was /is a Deity's property. It is further admitted facts that there is a temple with Deity and a big pond from which it is apparent that there was/is nothing cultivable and arable land. Ka schedule total land is occupied by the big pond, temple and Pathway of the temple, so how it would be settled for cultivation to a Raiyat which happened in this case. Since from the time of D.S, record of rights the Ka schedule land belonged to Deity as Debuttar property which never comes within the ambit of the settlement as per the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act or thereafter, by operation of law of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 33. Therefore, we are of the farm view that by executing a Kabuliyat by Shebait of deity in the name of Paresh Narayan Choudhury was never settled as permanent Raiyat Shebait cannot extinguish or alienate permanently the property of Deity in other words Debuttar property and as such, claiming the Deity's property permanently in pursuance of unilateral Kabuliyat Ext.3 cannot be considered as legal instrument. Therefore, including so called record of rights and all further transfer regarding Rent Sale, compromise of Execution Rent Case, settlement of sub-raiyat by Paresh and Naresh and others and thereafter purchase by Nesar Hossein was beyond the provision of law and without lawful authority and jurisdiction. Therefore, in pursuance of such unlawful authority and papers transferred by Nesar Hossein in the name of the plaintiff does not create any legal and lawful authority to have the right, title and possession over Ka schedule land. 

 34. Now we shall discuss the materials on record in respect of Kha and Ga schedule land of the suit to consider the right title of the plaintiff. It is pertinent to look into exhibit 16, deed No. 7238 dated 28.8.65 which was executed in favour of the plaintiff by the Nesar Hossain Siddique through his constituted attorney Mr. Sushil Kumar Roy, on perusal of exhibit 16 it reveals that the said attorney did not disclose anything in respect his power in the said deed but after the name of Neser Hossain Siddique only inserted his name as attorney. 

 D.W. 1 in his deposition stated that Joykalimata Thakurani is the owner of the suit properties as per D.S. Record of rights where in Mr. Birendra Nath Roy Bahadur was the Shabait but on perusal of the materials on record it transpires that Deity's properties only belongs to schedule Ka of the Suit Nos. 8 and 9 of 2003. The plaintiff of the Title Suit No. 9 of 2003 to prove his case did not adduce any documentary evidence except oral, from which it appears that the plaintiff of Title Sun No. 9 of 2003 has failed to prove their locus standi to file and prosecute the suit. Although it is admitted fact that the schedule No. Ka of Title Suit No. 9 of 2003 is the property of Deity, which also admitted by the P.W. 1 Jamshed Hossain Chowdhury. So, it is apparent that the Deity has had the right, title over the Ka schedule land as per the D.S. Khatian and admission of the plaintiffs of T.S. No. 8 of 2003 unless Government take over the property as per the provision of section 10A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950. Since we are affirming the judgment and decree so far it relates to other Suit No. 8 of 2003 hence, the right title of the Deity's is affirmed subject to provisions of section 10A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950. Therefore, the other suit No. 9 of 2003 filed as plaintiff by the defendant Nos. 11 and 12 of other suit No. 8 of 2003 is superbly Hence, the judgment and decree so far it relates to the O.C Suit. No. 9 of 2003 cannot be sustain in law. 

 40. Send down the lower Court records with a copy of this judgment at once.

parties:
Capital Co-operative Housing Society Ltd ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Director, Land Records and Survey, Government of Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Mohammad Gbolam Rabbani, J.: This application under Article 102 of the Constitution by the petitioner, the Capital Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. represented by its Chairman, calls in question two judgments and orders as at Annexures O and N of the two Revenue Officers, respondent Nos. 1(a) and 2 respectively, passed under the Tenancy Rules, 1955 during the preparation and revision of record-of-rights under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in respect of certain lands of mouza Uttarkhan within PS Tejgaon of the district of Dhaka. 

 2. Four plots of land bearing Nos. 881, 890, 893 and 894 recorded in CS Khatian No. 138 (Annexure A-1) and two plots of land bearing Nos. 878 and 879 recorded in CS Khatian No. 330 (Annexure-A) are the subject matter of the instant dispute. These two CS Khatians were recorded in the name of the tenant Sharafatullah under the landlord Bhowal Raj Estate. 

 4. The case of the contesting respondent Nos. 3 to 21 is that the landlord neither auction purchased the said lands nor settled the same in favour of Rahmat Banu. The CS recorded tenant Sharafatullah owned and possessed the said lands till he died and thereafter his successive heirs, respondent Nos. 3 to 8, are owning and possessing the same. Other respondent Nos. 9 to 21 are purchasers in possession from the successive heirs of Sharafatullah. 

 During the aforesaid revision of record of rights the lands appertaining to the aforesaid two CS Khatians were made fifty-three plots on cadastral survey and were recorded in the draft record of right bearing No. 1600, annexure 4 to the affidavit-in- opposition, in the name of said Rahmat Banu to the extent of eight annas' share and in the names of respondent Nos. 3 to 5, 7, 8, 10 to 16 and 18 to 21 and others to the extent of remaining eight annas share. This record-of-right was attested on 6.4.69. After the publication of this draft record-of right under rule 29 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, ten objection cases were filed against it under Rule 30 of the said Tenancy rule on 22.2.71. Out of the said objection cases the objectors in objection case Nos. 377 of 1971 did not contest. The other nine objection cases were heard analogously and were allowed on contest against Rahmat Banu by the judgment and order dated 11.3.71 whereby the name of Rahmat Banu was struck off from the draft record-of-right. The certified copy of this judgment and order is at annexure '5' to the affidavit-in-opposition and against whereof the petitioner filed nine appeals being Nos. 34046 to 34054 of 1984 after eleven years eight months fourteen days claiming that the petitioner had purchased the interest of Rahmat Banu. These appeals filed obviously under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, were heard and disposed of analogously by Mr. Abu Abdullah, the Revenue Officer with the additional designation of Settlement Officer and by the judgment and order dated 16.8.84 he allowed the appeals and directed recording of the name of the petitioner as the sole tenant of the RS Khatian No. 1600. The copy of this judgment and order is' at annexure L to the writ petition. Subsequently, on the prayer of some of the respondents the Director of Land Records, Respondent No.1, directed the Settlement Officer to re-examine the aforesaid judgment and order passed in those nine appeals and accordingly the matter was considered by the respondent No. 1(a) Mr. Md. Shafayet Ali, Revenue Officer appointed with the additional designation of Settlement Officer and he by the impugned order dated 18.1.89 (which is at annexure 'O' to the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner) exercising his power under rule 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, cancelled the portion of the proceeding referred to in rule 31 relating to RS Khatian No. 1600 in question and directed that the proceeding shall be taken up fresh from the said stage of the hearing of those nine appeals. By the said order Mr. Shafayet Ali, made over those appeals to Mr. Kazi Nurur Rahman, Assistant Settlement Officer, for disposal. But as Mr. Kazi Nurur Rahman became ill Mr. Shafayet Ali withdrew the said appeals from the file of Mr. Kazi Nurur Rahman and transferred the same for disposal to the respondent No. 2. Abdul Kader Howlader, another Assistant Settlement Officer. Thereafter upon hearing the parties Mr. Abdul Kader Howlader dismissed all the said appeals by the analogous impugned judgment and order dated 5.2.89 as at annexure N to the writ petition and thereby restored the judgment and order dated 11.3.71 passed in the aforesaid nine objection cues and consequently the name of the petitioner was deleted from the RS Khatian No. 1600. 

 7. Section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act states that the Government may, in any case if it thinks fit, make an order directing that record-of-rights in respect of any district, part of a district or local area be prepared or revised by a Revenue-Officer in accordance with such rules as may be made by the Government in this behalf: 

 8. Chapter VII of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 contains the rules regarding powers of Revenue Officers in preparing and revising record-of-rights under section 144 of the Act. 

 9. According to rule 27, there are ten stages of the work for the preparation of revision of record-of-rights, 6th to 10th stage being respectively attestation, publication of draft record, disposal of objections, filing of appeals and disposal thereof and preparation and publication of final record. 

 10. Rule 28 states the procedure of the work, up to attestation. Rule 29 states that after completion of attestation the Revenue Officer shall publish the draft record-of-rights by placing it for public inspection during a period of not less than one month at such convenient place as he may determine informing the persons concerned about the last date of filing objections under rule 30. 

 15. Rule 42 specially empowers Revenue Officers appointed with the additional designation of Settlement Officer to cancel any portion of the proceeding referred to in rules 28 to 32 any time before the publication of final record-of-rights in respect of any district, part of district, or local area and to take up fresh proceedings from such stage as he may direct. 

 16. Rule 44 empowers Director of Land Records and Surveys to discharge all the aforesaid functions of a Revenue Officer as empowered under the aforesaid Rules including Rules 40 to 42. 

 17. It appears from the impugned order dated 18.1.89 as at Annexure-O to the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner that the respondent No. 1 (a), Md. Shafayet Ali, Revenue Officer, with additional designation of Settlement Officer passed the order under rule 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 directing the proceedings shall be taken up fresh from the stage of rule 31 relating to aforesaid RS Khatian No. 1600 in obedience to the order passed by the respondent No. 1, Director of Land Records, obviously under rule 44. It appears from the subsequent order passed by Mr. Shafayet Ali that at first he transferred these appeals to Mr. Kazi Nurur Rahman, Assistant Settlement Officer, presumably under rule 40, but since this Assistant Settlement Officer became ill, Mr. Shafayet Ali withdrew the appeals from the file of the said Assistant Settlement Officer and transferred them for disposal to the respondent No. 2, Mr. Abdul Kader Howlader, another Assistant Settlement Officer, obviously by exercising his powers under rule 41. 

 18. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that a Revenue Officer appointed with the additional designation of Settlement Officer is not empowered under rule 42 to cancel a single record-of-right as in the instant case, but he may cancel record-of-rights in respect of any district, part of district or local area and that 'local area' means a large area of land appertaining to several record of rights. 

 20. Now if the learned advocate's argument is to be accepted then it was not necessary for the legislature to add the expression 'local area' after the expression 'district or part of district' as the expression 'part of district' would have been sufficient to mean 'large area', It is also illogical to accept as suggested by the learned advocate that the Revenue Officer empowered under rule 42 can cancel a large number of draft record-of-rights, but he cannot cancel such a record of right. The only logical meaning of the expression 'local area', according to us, as understood by this particular statute, namely State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, in the context of revision of record-of-rights is primarily area is respect of which a record-of-right is to be prepared or has been prepared, otherwise we shall have to find out an answer to a queer question, local area means how much area? 

 21. Furthermore, the learned advocate will be caught out in his own argument if we consider the area and other features of the land appertaining to the instant record-of-right. The area is 12.32 acres consisting of 53 plots having several houses, cultivable lands and a tank recorded in the names of 29 persons. 

 22. Thus, considering all the aspects of the case we find it difficult to accept the said contention of Mr. Ahmed and we hold that the area of a record-of-right is a local area as mentioned in rule 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. 

 24. Against this impugned judgment and order Mr. Ahmed has canvassed only one argument, that these appeals should not have been dismissed on the ground of limitation as the appeals were registered after condoning the delay. On perusal of the impugned judgment we find that Mr. Abdul Kader Howlader, Assistant Settlement Officer, incidentally decided the issue of limitation and that too after deciding the appeals on merit. He came to the definite finding that the papers produced by the appellant before him, namely, the petitioner of this writ petition, were not sufficient to record its name in the record of rights and that at the time when the said record-of-right was prepared the other parties including the respondents had got possession in the disputed lands.

full_judgment:
3. The suit was tiled averring that the land in suit measuring 3.30 acres of CS khatian No.6, corresponding the RS khatian No.7, belonged to Bibi Ummat Johara and others and the said landlords settled the land in suit with Bipin Chandra in 1350 BS by granting Dakhila, that said settlement holder Bipin Chandra possessed the land in suit upon payment of rent to the ex-landlords, that RS record was prepared in the name of Bipin Chandra, that Bipin Chandra sold the land in suit to the plaintiff on February 27, 1970, that the plaintiff got his name mutated and possessed the land on payment of rent, that Bipin Chandra in collusing with others filed criminal cases against the plaintiff but he was acquitted. that defendant No.2 filed Title Suit No. 170 of 1980 claiming easement right over the suit land but the same was dismissed for default, that Bipin Chandra filed Title Suit No. 428 of 1979 impleading the plaintiff but later on the same was withdrawn and he tiled fresh suit being No. 159 of 1982 seeking cancellation of the kabala on the basis of which plaintiff claiming the land in suit but the said suit was disposed of in favour of the plaintiff that Bipin Chandra through the defendant No. 2 managed to tile Miscellaneous Case No.37 of 1981-82 before the defendant No.1 tor cancellation of the mutation made in favour of the plaintiff, that defendant No.1 illegally cancelled on June 30, 1983 the mutation which was made in the name of the plaintiff on the view that the land claimed by the plaintiff on the basis of the kabala dated February 27, 1970 is the khas land, that land of the RS khatian No.7 (corresponding to CS Khatian No. 6) was not government khas land and that plaintiff's vendor since settlement from the ex-landlords possessed the land purchased by him on February 27, 1970 and that since purchase plaintiff is in possession of the land in suit, that since the order of the defendant No.1 cancelling the mutation is illegal hence the suit seeking the relief of declaring order of the defendant No.1 illegal void and without jurisdiction. 

 4. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by filing separate written statements. The common case of the defendants was that prior to preparation of CS khatian land of the suit plot was being used as Eidgah, Swashan, Debesthan and that there is a Dighi for the use of the people of the village, that in the CS khatian there is noting that in the plots in question there are Eidgah, Swashan, etc., that there is similar noting in the RS record, that since the acquisition of rent receiving interest of the landlord. the land in suit is being used by the public in general (Muslims and Hindus) for the purposes as mentioned hereinbefore, that Bipin Chandra in collusion with the settlement personnel got the RS record prepared in his name although there was no basis for the preparation of the RS record in his name since Bipin Chandra had never taken settlement from the ex-landlord, that as Bipin Chandra had no right. title, interest and possession in the land in suit, the plaintiff by his so-called purchase did not acquire any interest in the land in suit, that neither Bipin Chandra nor the plaintiff possessed the land in suit, that defendant No.2 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 50 of 1978-79 before the defendant No.1 and the same was decided in favour of the defendant No.2 and the order in the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case was not challenged by Bipin Chandra or by the plaintiff, that Miscellaneous Case No. 50 of 1978-79 was tiled as regard the land of plot Nos. 259 and 34 since the land of those two plots were Swashan, that defendant No.2 later on filed Miscellaneous Case No. 37 of 1981-82 before the defendant No.1, Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Rangpur and the said defendant by the order dated June 30, 1983 quite legally cancelled the mutation earlier made in the name of the plaintiff in respect of the land in suit. 

 5. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the findings that the suit is not bad for defect of party, that the suit as framed is maintainable and not barred by waiver and estoppel, that the plaintiff filed no paper to prove his case of settlement of the land in suit to Bipin Chandra, that plaintiff's case of taking settlement of the land in suit by Bipin Chandra is not correct and that the land in suit was not settled to Bipin Chandra by the landlords, that Bipin Chandra in collusion with survey officials illegally got RS record prepared in his name that in Miscellaneous Case No. 50 of 1978-79 filed by the defendant No. 2 land of plot Nos. 259 and 34 were held to be land used by the Hindu community as Swashan and the said fact was not challenged by Bipin Chandra or by the plaintiff that as Bipin Chandra had no right. title and interest in the land in suit the RS record prepared in his name was not correct, that from plaintiff's side no independent witness was examined to prove the case of settlement said to have been taken by Bipin Chandra, that PW 2 admitted that part of the land in suit is Swashan, that there is no mention which part of the land of respective plots in the land in suit is possessed by the plaintiff, that by the kabala dated February 27, 1970 plaintiff has not acquired any right, title and interest in the land in suit, that the mutation having not been made in the name of the plaintiff upon compliance of the provision of section 117(3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, as such, the same was liable to be cancelled, that the plaintiff is not in exclusive possession of the land in suit, that land in suit being Eidgah, Swashan and Debesthan, etc, the plaintiff did not acquire any title from Bipin Chandra who is said to have taken settlement from the ex-landlords and that settlement to Bipin Chandra by ex-landlords was not proved, that defendants proved by the evidence of DWs 3 and 4 that the land in suit is Eidgah, Swashan and Debesthan, etc., that in view of the evidence and the other materials on record the order dated June 30, 1983 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 37 of 1981-82 is not illegal. 

 6. The plaintiff went on appeal. The appellate Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court primarily on the finding that defendant No. 1 has no jurisdiction to cancel the record of right. It is seen from the judgment of the appellate Court that the said Court proceeded upon the assumption that settlement of the land in suit to Bipin Chandra was not disputed by the defendants and that Bipin Chandra paid rent to the landlord, although the consistent case of the defendants was that there was no settlement of the land in suit by the landlords to Bipin Chandra and that no paper was brought on record in support of the claim that the land in suit was settled with Bipin Chandra by the landlords and Bipin Chandra paid rent to the landlords. The appellate Court, without discussing at all the evidence, arrived at the finding that Bipin Chandra on taking settlement possessed the land in suit and the plaintiff after his purchase possessed the land in suit, that provision of section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act does not authorise the Revenue Officer "to correct Khatians which affects the question of title or possession to land. It has power only to correct Khatian if it has been made as a result of bonafide mistake...............Moreover, revenue officer cannot declare a document to be void". The appellate Court also observed that the defendant No.1 in cancelling the mutation went beyond the limit of his power and the order so passed by the defendant No.1 was without jurisdiction. The appellate Court further observed "I am of the view that if Government thinks that the lands in question belong to or the same are in actual occupation of Hindu Community they should seek redress in the civil Court in an appropriate forum and not in this capricious manner". 

 8. The defendant No.2 moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rule. The High Court Division in the background of the evidence, both oral and documentary, as well as other materials on record, was of the view, as the trial Court was of, that Bipin Chandra did not acquire any title on the basis of his alleged settlement and the RS record prepared in the name of Bipin Chandra had no basis since from plaintiff's side fact of Bipin Chandra's taking settlement was not established either by documentary evidence or by oral evidence. The High Court Division was also of the view similar to that of the trial Court that the plaintiff did not acquire any right, title and interest in the land in suit since his vendor Bipin Chandra did not acquire any right, title and interest in the land in suit. The High Court Division also held since plaintiff had no title in the land in suit, the mutation in the name of the plaintiff was not legal and thus cancellation thereof by the defendant No. 1 was quite legal. The High Court Division while making the Rule absolute observed "Unless the plaintiff proves his title to the suit land he is not permitted to challenge the order of the ADC (Rev) Rangpur. The lower appellate Court has not reversed the finding of the trial Court that the plaintiff acquired no title on the basis of his kabala from Bipin as Bipin had no title to the suit land. The plaintiff 'Could not produce any paper showing settlement in favour of Bipin by ex-landlord Ummat Zohora and others. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties submits that the order of Mutation was passed under section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and an appeal lies against the said order within 30 days which was not filed by the defendant. Section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act relates to Sub-Division of holding and restriction thereon. Mutation proceeding and Sub-division of holding are not identical. Mutation of the khatian or correction of the Khatian may be made by the Revenue Officer on application by interested party or of his own motion under section 50 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the ADC (Rev) Rangpur has the jurisdiction to correct the mistakes appearing in the revenue record committed by the Revenue Officer on bonafide mistake. Accordingly, the ADC (Rev) Rangpur had the jurisdiction to correct the record relating to the khatian which was mutated in the name of the plaintiff by the Upazila Revenue Officer. When it is found that the plaintiff has no title to the suit land, the mutation of the suit land cannot stand in the name of the plaintiff The lower appellate Court therefore committed an error of law in reversing the decision of the trial Court without considering the plaintiff's title to the suit land. The impugned judgment and decree therefore, suffer from illegality and infirmity and cannot be sustained". 

 9. Leave was granted to consider the contention of the appellant that High Court Division while making the Rule absolute did not take into consideration that Bipin Chandra the vendor of the plaintiff having got the settlement from the landlord by Dakhila possessed the land in suit since 1350 B.S. and thereafter transferred the land in suit to the plaintiff by registered kabala dated February 27, 1970 and the plaintiff being in possession since 1350 B.S. got his name mutated in the record of right and, in the background of the said fact, the High Court Division ought to have considered that the plaintiff could also claim adverse possession in the land in suit and thereby acquired title, that the defendant No.2 filed Title Suit No. 170 of 1980 seeking declaration of his easement right over the land in suit but the suit was dismissed and as against that defendant No.2 did not proceed any further, that the trial Court as well as the High Court Division failed to consider that the petition before the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Rangpur filed by the person whose suit for title in the disputed land was dismissed and the order obtained from the defendant No.1 is a product of malice and malafide. 

 11. The learned Counsel appearing for the appellant submitted that issue in the suit was whether the order dated 30-6-1983 cancelling the mutation was legal or, in other words, was beyond the jurisdiction of the defendant No.1 and, as such, before the trial Court there was no question for making decision as to title of the plaintiff in the land in suit, that plaintiff was not required to seek any relief as to title since decision as to legality of the order dated June 30, 1983 in the affirmative would establish his title in the land in suit, that if this Court feels that upon adjudication of the title of the plaintiff at the first instance would entitle him to have the relief sought in the suit, in that case the suit may be sent back to the trial Court to enable the plaintiff to prove his title by adducing evidence, particularly as to the Dakhila by which he took settlement as well as the rent receipt by which he paid rent to ex-landlord, that defendant No.1 i.e. Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Rangpur was wrong in passing order of eviction of the plaintiff from the land in suit and that there is no provision in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to hold that the land in suit was not a retainable land of the ex-landlord, that the High Court Division was in error in holding that the defendant No.1 was quite competent to cancel the order of mutation as per provision of section 50 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, that the question of maintainability of the suit for not seeking consequential relief i.e. declaration as to title, was not raised before the trial Court and, as such, the question about the maintainability of the suit for not seeking the appropriate relief i.e. declaration of title, cannot be raised before this Court, that appellate Court did not commit any error in deciding the suit on the question of jurisdiction of the Revenue Officer as regard correction of the record affecting the title and possession of the parties in whose name mutation was made and, as such, appellate Court was not in error in setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

 12. As against the aforesaid contentions of the learned Counsel of the appellant it was submitted on behalf of the respondent No.1 (defendant No.2), that from plaintiff's side Dakhila on the basis of which Bipin Chandra, as claimed by the plaintiff, was said to have taken settlement, was not produced before the Court, nor the plaintiff produced any rent receipt showing payment of rent to the ex-landlord, that no paper was brought on record to show that Bipin Chandra was recognised by ex-landlord as the tenant, that the subject matter of the suits filed by Bipin Chandra and the defendant No.2 and the issues involved therein are quite distinct and different from the subject matter of the instant suit and, as such, whatever order was passed in the suits filed by the defendant No.2 and Bipin Chandra the same has no bearing on the decision made by the High Court Division in the plaintiff's suit, that the revenue officer was legally quite correct in cancelling the mutation since Rule 23(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules framed under section 143 of the said Act in 1955 authorises the revenue officer to correct the record which appears to him in the background of the materials brought before him was incorrect, that as materials were brought on the record of the Miscellaneous Case No. 37 of 1981-82 and having had noticed the said materials the Additional Deputy Commissioner found that mutation in the name of the plaintiff in respect of the land in suit was wrongly done, the order dated June 30, 1983 cancelling the mutation earlier made in the name of the plaintiff was quite legal. 

 13. One of the points that was raised for determination as to whether Revenue Officer, herein Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), is competent under the provision of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to make correction in the record of rights maintained under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the Act). Provision of section 143 is as follows: 

 "Section 143: Maintenance of the Record of rights-The Collector shall maintain up-to-date, in the prescribed manner, the record of rights prepared or revised under Part IV, or under this Part by correcting clerical mistakes and by incorporating therein the changes on account of- 

 14. As per provision of section 152 of the Act, Rules have been framed relating to matters in Part V and section 143 is in Chapter 8 of the Part V. Rules to carry out the duties given to the Collector for the maintenance of the record of rights as per provision of section 143 of the Act is in Chapter 6 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. For our purpose Rule 23(4) of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 is relevant and the same runs as: 

 "The Revenue Officer shall, either on application or on receipt of a report under clause (j) of sub-rule (1), for the correction of an entry that has been procured by fraud in the record-of-rights after final publication thereof, after consulting the previous-settlement record, preliminary rentrolls, draft record-of-right, sub-divisional and tahsil copies of records modified under section 46 of the Act, holding-wari rentrolls and Register II, and making such other enquiries as he considers necessary, direct excision of the fraudulent entry, and his act in according so being a ministerial act, shall not be open to appeal. At the same time, the Revenue Officer shall make the correct entry, leaving a note against the excised entry that is fraudulent, and make in the record a reference to a proceeding in which the reasons for excision have been stated. He shall also direct similar correction in the record-of-rights maintained in the sub-divisional record room and the tahsil officer and shall supply corrected copies of the record-of-rights to the parties concerned". 

 15. On reading provision of section 143 of the Act and the Rule 23(4) of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 we are of the view that the Revenue Officer in the facts and circumstances of the instant case in cancelling the mutation obtained by the plaintiff in respect of the land in suit was quite legal. It may be mentioned plaintiff got his name untated upon striking out name of Bipin Chandra who is said to have acquired the land in suit by settlement from landlords, but in support of claim of settlement no evidence was brought on record. As stated hereinbefore, the appellate Court set aside the judgment of the trial Court which dismissed the suit, primarily on the ground that revenue authority had no jurisdiction to correct the record of rights by cancelling the mutation earlier made in the name of the plaintiff on the view that the correction so made affected the right, title and interest of the person whose name was entered in the record of right upon mutation. In view of the provision of section 143 of the Act and the Rule 23(4) of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, in our opinion, the appellate Court was in serious error in setting aside the judgment of the trial Court on the view that the revenue officer had no jurisdiction to correct the record of rights prepared upon mutation in the name of the plaintiff. 

 16. It was the case of the plaintiff that his vendor Bipin Chandra took settlement of the land in suit from the ex-landlords who made the settlement by Dakhila and that plaintiff's vendor paid rent to the ex-landlord. From the defendant's side, acquisition of title by plaintiff's vendor Bipin Chandra was challenged contending that at no point of time ex-landlords settled the land in question which is Eidgah, Swashan, Debesthan, etc. and a Dighi for the use of the people of the village to plaintiff's vendor Bipin Chandra. In the background of the case of the respective parties in the suit, in our view, in the absence of determination of title of the person from whom plaintiff said to have acquired title in the land in suit, the plaintiff would not be entitled to the relief sought against the order of the revenue officer cancelling the mutation earlier made in the mime of the plaintiff and the record prepared in the name of the plaintiff's vendor. 

 18. In the instant case, plaintiff sought for a declaration that the order dated June 30, 1983 passed by the revenue officer was illegal and void. To have the relief sought in the suit plaintiff was first required to establish his right, title and interest in the land in suit and in the absence thereof he was not legally competent to take exception to the order of the revenue officer as mentioned hereinbefore. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division as well as the trial Court that from the plaintiff's side no evidence was brought on record to establish that his vendor Bipin Chandra obtained settlement of the land in suit. It was the case of the plaintiff that his vendor Bipin Chandra obtained settlement by the Dakhila granted by the ex- landlords and that Bipin Chandra paid rent to the ex- landlords but no such paper was brought on record. From the plaintiff's side no oral evidence was also led to establish the fact that Zaminder settled the land in suit to Bipin Chandra i.e. vendor of the plaintiff. In the background of the said facts it was held by the High Court Division as well as the trial Court that as Bipin Chandra had no right, title and interest in the land in suit, the plaintiff by purchase from the said Bipin Chandra did not acquire any right, title and interest in the land in suit. 

 19. The plaintiff could have maintained the instant suit in the light of the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act taking exception to the order passed by the revenue officer if he would have any right to the property in question, but, as seen from the materials on record, plaintiff failed to establish that his vendor Bipin Chandra acquired title, interest or right in the land in suit and consequent thereupon, plaintiff by purchase from the said Bipin Chandra as did not acquire any right, title and interest to the land in suit, his suit challenging the legality of the order of the revenue officer cancelling the mutation done earlier in the name of the plaintiff was not maintainable. The plaintiff legally was not competent to challenge the legality of the order of the revenue officer cancelling mutation as regard the land in suit since he did not acquire any right in the land in suit. 

 22. Leave was granted to consider the contention of the appellant that his vendor took settlement of the land in suit by Dakhila in 1350 B.S. and since then plaintiff's vendor possessed the land in suit and thereafter transferred the land on July 27, 1970 to the plaintiff and that since then the plaintiff being in possession and got his name mutated in the record of rights, the High Court Division ought to have considered that the plaintiff could also claim adverse possession in the land in suit and thereby acquired title. 

 24. The other contention of the appellant was that the respondent No.1 filed suit and his suit having been dismissed and that said person having had filed petition for cancellation of the mutation effected earlier in the name of the plaintiff the revenue officer having had passed the order of cancellation on the application of said person the same lacks bonafide and that also malicious. This contention is also of no merit since suit filed earlier by the defendant No.2 i.e. respondent No.1 herein, was absolutely different in nature from the suit filed by the plaintiff and the issue therein was not the one as in the instant suit or in any way close to the subject matter of the instant suit and, as such, even if the same was dismissed the said order of dismissal had no bearing on the subject matter of the suit of the plaintiff. As seen from the provision of section 143 of the Act that the revenue officer is quite competent to maintain the record of rights up to date either on an application or on receipt of a report made under clause (j) of Sub-Rule 1 of Rule 23. In the instant case, application for correction of the record in the light of the provision of section 143 of the Act was filed by the defendant No.2 who earlier obtained an order in respect of the land of plot Nos. 259 and 34 and the order so obtained as regard the said plots was not challenged either by the plaintiff's vendor or by the plaintiff. So, the petition filed by the defendant No.2 was quite in accordance with law and the Revenue Officer was quite within his authority in passing the order challenged in the suit. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has taken exception, that the High Court Division was in error in holding that the Revenue Officer was quite competent to pass the order challenged in the suit, or in other words, the revenue officer was legally competent to make the order for the correction of the record of right under section 50 of the Act. It appears to us that mention of section 50 by the High Court Division as to provision of law relating to correction of record of rights by the Collector was not so vital since the same has not affected the decision made in the case. In all probability mention of section 50 of the Act in the judgment of the High Court Division was a typing mistake and same thus crept in the judgment. As stated hereinbefore, the Revenue Officer, in the light of the provision of section 143 of the Act and Rule 23(4) of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, is quite competent to make necessary entry in the record of right like the one as has been done in the instant case.

full_judgment:
3. The petitioner's case in Writ Petition No. 207/86 is that they purchased the land in question from one Siddique Ahmed by a registered kabala dated 15.8.79. Originally the land was recorded in the name of its owner Abdur Rahman in RS khatian. Subsequently Fazar Rahman, the heir of Abdur Rahman, sold the same to one Nur Mohammad by registered deed of sale and Nur Mohammad sold the same in favour of one Siddique Ahmed by a registered kabala dated 3.12.69. The present petitioners purchased the suit land from the said Siddique Ahmed. The petitioners claim that the suit land be recorded in their names. That one Mohammad Harunur Rashid filed an objection under section 19(1) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in objection Case No. 139 dated 15.10.1980 objecting the entry of the name of the respondent No.2 in the draft record of rights. The objection was not allowed. 

 4. Being aggrieved the petitioners and others filed an appeal case against his objection Case No. 139 dated 15.10.1980. The appeal case was numbered as Appeal case No. 25187/81. The appellate authority after complying with the due formalities and after obtaining the Survey Report and hearing the parties allowed the appeal and directed the inclusion of the names of the petitioners to the extent of 7 annas share in the draft record of rights. Thereafter a Review petition was filed by the respondent No. 2 against the order of the Appellate Authority dated 16.9.1984. The said petition was heard and disposed of by the appellate authority by rejecting the same and maintained the order passed by him in the appeal. The respondent No.2 finding no alternative filed a Second Review petition before the Director of Land Records against the order of the appellate authority dated 16.9.1984. The Director of Land Records by his order dated 31.3.1986 allowed the Second Review petition setting aside the order dated 16.9.1984 passed by the appellate authority and sent back the case to one Mr. Bazlur Rahman for hearing of the appeal afresh. Against this very order of the Director of Land Records dated 31.3.1986, the petitioners have filed this Writ Petition and obtained the present Rule. 

 5. The case of the respondent No.2, as it appears, is that respondent No.2 purchased 12 annas interest from Fazar Rahman the heirs of Hafizur Rahman by a registered Kabala dated 29.11.1976 and subsequently the respondent No.2 also purchased the share of Mofizur Rahman by a registered Kabala dated 2.6.80 and accordingly his name in the draft record of rights has been correctly recorded. 

 6. In Writ Petition No. 208 of 1986 the case of the petitioner Mosammat Sabera Begum is that one Bujarat was instituted by the respondent Nos. 2-3 impleading the petitioner as the second party before the Revenue Authority. The case was disposed of ex parte by order dated 23.6.77 wherein the name of the petitioner in the khatian was directed to be struck off and those of respondent Nos. 2-5 were to be recorded. Against the said order the petitioner filed objection case impleading the respondent Nos. 2-5 as opposite parties. The Revenue Officer considered the objection and disposed of the case by his order dated 31.5.79 maintaining the order recording the name of the respondents passed in the Biujarat dispute case. It is the case of the petitioner that the original owner of the case land was one Abdur Rahman and his name appeared in the RS khatian in Korfa right The said RS khatian was under khatian No. 25 of Jote No. 1 and the owner of the said jote No. 1 was one Abdul Aziz Sarang in raiyati right. The said Jotedar having defaulted in payment of revenue, the Jote was put to auction and ultimately the entire lands vested in the Government. One Abdus Salam prayed for re-settlement of the case land and his prayer was allowed and accordingly he became tenant directly under the Government Abdus Salam also defaulted in payment of rent and a Certificate case was started being Certificate Case No. 357 of 1945-46. The land in question was auction sold to one Ahmedur Rahman on 16.7.1946 and the sale was confirmed on 16.9.1946 and possession was delivered on 18.1.1948. The said Ahmedur Rahman got his name mutated in the RS khatian. The said auction purchaser while in possession sold the land to the petitioner by a registered kabala being kabala No. 4245 dated 21.6.1960 and since then she has been in possession of the case lands. The petitioner's name has been duly recorded in the SA khatian which has been finally published. The petitioner's name was also correctly recorded in the present khatian as per his title and possession. After the Field Survey the present respondent Nos. 5 filed a dispute case and managed to get their names recorded by suppressing notices. 

 7. The case of the respondent that the land originally belonged to one Abdur Rahman to the extent of 16 annas share and RS khatian No. 30/1 has been finally published in the name of the said Abdur Rahman. On his death, the respondent Nos. 2-5 were in possession of the case land as his heirs. That while in such possession they sold the land in favour of Jalalabad Housing Society and delivered possession to the said Society. As against the order the petitioner filed an appeal to the Revenue Authority and the case was registered as Appeal Case No. 23994/80. The Appellate Authority by its order dated 16.9.84 allowed the appeal and directed the recording of the name of the petitioner in the khatian by striking out the names of the respondents. Thereafter the respondent Nos. 2-5 filed a Review petition on 14.10.84 before the said appellate authority and the appellate authority heard the matter and considered the case rejecting the Review petition and maintained his earlier decision by order dated 16.9.84. That thereafter the respondent Nos. 2-5 filed a second appellation for review of the order dated 16.9.84 before the Director of Land Records. The Director of Land Records by the impugned order dated 31.3.86 allowed the second review petition of the respondents by setting aside the order dated 16.9.84 passed by the appellate authority. 

 8. Mr. MH Khondker, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in both the Rules, has submitted that the order dated 16.9.84 in Appeal Case No. 25187/81 having already been reviewed by the learned Appellate officer by his judgment and order dated 27.3.1985, the entertainment of a review petition and of passing the order by the Director of Land Records in reviewing the earlier order of the appeal for the second time is absolutely without jurisdiction and is of no legal effect. Mr. Khandker argued that the Director of Land Records has not been vested with any statutory power to entertain and dispose of any review petition and as such his order is liable to be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and the same is of no legal effect. 

 9. Mr. SC Das, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents submitted that the Director of Land Records has been vested with full powers and authority to revise any order passed by any Revenue Officer under Rule 44 read with Rule 43 of the East Bengal Tenancy Rules, 1955 and as such committed no error of law. 

 10. We have heard the learned Advocates and perused the petition and affidavit filed by the respective parties. The only question that has cropped up in these two Rules is whether the Director of Land Records has been empowered under the statute to entertain and review any order passed by the appellate authority. 

 11. Under section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the Revenue Officer shall publish a draft of the record-of-rights so prepared or revised in the prescribed manner and shall receive and consider any objections relating to any entry therein during the period of such publication. By sub-section 2 of section 19 the forum for appeal is created and any aggrieved person by the order of the Revenue-Officer on any objection made under sub-section (1) of section 19 may appeal to the prescribed Revenue Authority not below the rank of an Assistant Settlement Officer in the manner and within such period as prescribed. 

 12. The petitioner in Writ Petition No. 207 of 1986 filed an appeal being Appeal case No. 25187/81 against the objection order passed in objection case No. 139 dated 15.10.80. The Appellate Authority by his order dated 16.9.84 allowed the appeal and directed the inclusion of the names of the petitioners to the extent of 7 annas share in the draft of record of rights. 

 13. It appears that the respondent No.2 filed a Review petition before the appellate authority who by his order dated 27.3.85 rejected the same and maintained the earlier order dated 16.9.84 passed in the appeal. Thereafter the respondent No. 2 moved the Director General of Land Records respondent No. 1 in a second Review. The Director General of Land Records by the impugned order dated 31.3.86 allowed the second review petition by setting aside the order dated 16.9.84 of the appellate authority directing fresh hearing by one Mr. Bazlur Rahman, an Appeal officer. The Director General appears to have exercised his powers under Rule 44 of the East Bengal Tenancy Rules 1955 and caused interference under Rule 42 of the said Rules by holding that he had powers to correct, modify or set aside any record of rights made or passed in any proceeding following Rule Nos. 28-32 of the said rules. 

 Powers vested in Director of Land Records and Surveys: "In respect of all operations under Chapter XVII of the Act Which have been placed under the administrative control of the Director of Land Records and Surveys. East Pakistan, he may discharge all the functions of a Revenue-Officer under the said Chapter and shall have all the powers of a Settlement Officer under rules 36, 38, 39, 40, 41,42, 42A and 42B," 

 15. Chapter XVII of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 deals with maintenance of the Record-of-Rights. Section 143 of the said Act runs as follows: 

 "The Collector shall maintain up to date, in the prescribed manner, the Record-of-rights prepared or revised under Part IV, or under this Part by correcting clerical mistake and by incorporating therein the changes on account of: 

 This matter has been placed under the Director of Land Records in his Administrative Control. 

 Rule 38 speaks about Revision of record- of-rights under section 31 and Rule 39 deals with powers vested in Settlement and Assistant Settlement Officers and 40 deals with further power vested in Assistant Settlement Officer under Bengal Act V of 1875 and rule 41 empowers the Revenue Officer appointed with the additional designation of 'Settlement Officer' is also hereby vested with all the powers of superintendence of Survey under the Bengal Survey Act of 1875; Rule 42 of the Tenancy Rules reads as follows: 

 "A Revenue Officer appointed with the additional designation of 'Settlement Officer' may at any time before the publication of final record-of-rights, direct that any portion of the proceedings referred to in rules 28-32 in respect of any district, part of district or local area shall be cancelled and that the proceedings shall be taken up fresh from such stage as he may direct" From the aforesaid Rules it appears that the Director General of Land Records is vested with administrative control in respect of all operation under Chapter XVII of the Act and he may discharge all the functions of a Revenue Officer and shall have powers of a Settlement Officer under Rules 36, 38, 39, 42B as such the Director General of Land Records can be said to have at best co-equal powers with that of any Revenue Officer or Settlement Officer with regard to their powers whether they are designated as Additional Designation of Settlement Officer or not but this does not mean that the Director of Land Records has been vested with superior powers to sit over their orders or decisions and to annul the same. In a quasi judicial proceedings like the present one all that is competent to do is that he may exercise any of such powers as is vested in a Revenue or Settlement Officer under Rules 44 and 42 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 in respect of a proceeding which has not attained finality, in either words, in a fresh proceeding the Director General is quite competent to assume his jurisdiction and dispose of the matter which is co-extensive with that of the Revenue or Settlement Officer. But in a matter which has already been disposed of by the Revenue Officer, namely Settlement Officer or Assistant Settlement Officer, in our view the Director of Land Records is incompetent and absolutely without power to lay his hands over such matters. 

 17. In the present cases the Director General of Land Records has interfered with the decisions of the appellate Court which has been done under sub-section 2 of section 19. But in administrative matter under chapter 17 of the Act he has been placed in superior position in matters of control, management of Record of Rights as vested under Rule 44 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Rules. 

 The Respondent No. 1 Director General of Land Records Bangladesh has exceeded his power in entertaining and disposing of the second review petitions reviewing the orders passed by the Settlement Officer in appellate jurisdiction and as such his actions cannot but be said to be without jurisdiction. The Rule 19(1) and 19(2) has vested a power to the Settlement Officer to entertain and hear an appeal arising out of any disputed proceeding and no further power has been provided by way of revision. Although the Code of Civil Procedure has allowed an appellate authority to review any decision but no second review is contemplated under the Rule ref. by any third party namely, the Director of Land Records. Sub-section 3 of section 19 has clearly stated that when all such objections and appeals have been considered and disposed of according to such Rules, the Revenue-Officer shall finally frame the record and shall cause record to be finally published in the prescribed manner and the publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly prepared or revised under this Chapter. So after the forum of appeal being exhausted, the only course left open to the Revenue Officer is to finally frame the record and such record be published in the prescribed manner. So this Rule also does not speak of any forum created for hearing a second review petition as the respondent No. 1 has entertained and disposed of. Since the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of 1950 and the Rules made thereunder do not specifically confer on the Director of Land Records any power to revise the order passed in appeal, in our view, the impugned orders dated 31.3.86 Annexure E in Writ Petition No. 207 and 'G' in Writ Petition No. 208 of 1986 are illegal and void and as such are hereby declared to have been passed without lawful authority and the same are of no legal effect.
